introduction.gainAttention: You can have the most advanced radio in the Marine Corps, but if you use a vertical whip to talk to a horizontal dipole, or try to punch through a concrete jungle with the wrong antenna, you are just carrying thirty pounds of dead weight. Understanding the 'why' behind antenna selection is what separates a radio operator from a communicator.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the technical decision-making process for antenna selection, including polarization, environmental impacts, and the trade-offs between gain and directivity.
objectives: TLO-020: Determine the appropriate antenna type to maximize signal strength and minimize interference.
ELO-051: Explain the relationship between antenna polarization and signal strength.
ELO-052: Analyze the impact of environmental factors on VHF/UHF antenna performance.
ELO-053: Compare antenna gain and directivity characteristics.

mainPoints.title: Polarization Principles
mainPoints.content: Polarization is the orientation of the electric field of the radio wave. For VHF/UHF tactical communications, matching polarization is essential for signal transfer.
subPoints: Vertical Polarization: Standard for most tactical VHF/UHF radios (whips and OE-254s).
Horizontal Polarization: Often used in long-range HF or specialized VHF links to reduce man-made interference.
Cross-polarization (mixing vertical and horizontal) can result in a signal loss of up to 20dB.

mainPoints.title: Environmental Factors in VHF/UHF Propagation
mainPoints.content: VHF and UHF frequencies are primarily line-of-sight and are highly susceptible to the physical environment as detailed in MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 5.
subPoints: Vegetation: Heavy foliage absorbs high-frequency signals; operators may need to increase antenna height to clear the canopy.
Urban Terrain: Buildings cause multipath interference, where signals reflect and arrive at the receiver at different times, causing 'ghosting' or signal cancellation.
Weather: While less impactful than terrain, heavy rain can attenuate UHF signals over long distances.

mainPoints.title: Gain and Directivity
mainPoints.content: Operators must choose between sending a signal in all directions or concentrating it in one direction to reach a distant station.
subPoints: Omnidirectional (e.g., OE-254): Provides 360-degree coverage, ideal for command nets where units are moving in multiple directions.
Directional (e.g., Yagi or Log-Periodic): Concentrates energy in a specific beam, providing higher gain and reducing the chance of enemy intercept from the sides or rear.
Gain: The increase in signal strength achieved by focusing the radiation pattern.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a Reconnaissance team operating in a heavily forested valley. You need to communicate with a higher headquarters located 15km away on a mountain peak. You have a whip antenna and an OE-254 kit.
steps: Analyze the terrain (vegetation and line-of-sight) to determine potential signal loss.
Evaluate the polarization requirements of the receiving station.
Compare the gain of the whip antenna versus the OE-254.
Select the antenna that provides the best chance of clearing the vegetation and providing sufficient gain.
Justify the selection based on MCRP 3-40.3C standards.

conclusion.summary: We have analyzed how polarization, environmental obstacles like foliage and buildings, and the choice between omnidirectional and directional gain affect your ability to communicate.
conclusion.closingStatement: Effective communication is not an accident; it is the result of deliberate antenna selection based on the tactical environment.

tlo.condition: Given a mission requirement, a specific frequency range (VHF/UHF), and a tactical environment.
tlo.behavior: Determine the appropriate antenna type to maximize signal strength and minimize interference.
tlo.standard: Based on the characteristics of the operating area and technical capabilities of the equipment per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires the Marine to evaluate environmental variables (vegetation, multipath, noise) and make a judgment call on which antenna system is most effective. Level 5 (Evaluate) is appropriate for making decisions based on criteria and standards.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a list of antenna types.
elos.behavior: Explain the relationship between antenna polarization and signal strength.
elos.standard: Differentiating between vertical and horizontal polarization and their effects on VHF/UHF propagation per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 2.
elos.justification: Understanding polarization is necessary to evaluate which antenna type maximizes signal.

elos.condition: Given a tactical scenario involving vegetated or urban terrain.
elos.behavior: Analyze the impact of environmental factors on VHF/UHF antenna performance.
elos.standard: Identifying potential signal attenuation and multipath interference factors per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 5.
elos.justification: Analysis of the environment is required before a determination (Level 5) can be made.

elos.condition: Given multiple antenna options (e.g., OE-254, whip, field-expedient).
elos.behavior: Compare antenna gain and directivity characteristics.
elos.standard: To determine which configuration provides the best coverage for the specific mission requirement per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Comparing technical capabilities is a prerequisite for selecting the optimal solution.

title: HF Sky Wave Communications and Ionospheric Propagation

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley where VHF line-of-sight is impossible. Your only link to the Combat Operations Center (COC) is 300 miles away. Without the ability to effectively 'bounce' your signal off the ionosphere, you are isolated. Mastering HF sky wave propagation is the difference between mission success and total communication blackout in a distributed environment.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the principles of HF sky wave propagation, the critical importance of frequency selection relative to the ionosphere, and the technical adjustments required for antenna take-off angles.
objectives: TLO-021: Execute HF sky wave communications.
ELO-054: Define Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and Lowest Useful Frequency (LUF).
ELO-055: Calculate the required take-off angle for sky wave propagation.
ELO-056: Adjust the antenna configuration for NVIS or long-range sky wave.

mainPoints.title: Ionospheric Frequency Selection (MUF and LUF)
mainPoints.content: The ionosphere acts as a refractive medium for HF signals. To establish a link, the operator must select a frequency that is high enough to penetrate noise but low enough to be returned to Earth.
subPoints: Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF): The highest frequency that will be returned to Earth for a given distance; frequencies above this pass into space.
Lowest Useful Frequency (LUF): The frequency below which the signal is absorbed by the D-layer or lost in noise.
Operating Frequency: Ideally 85% of the MUF to account for ionospheric fluctuations (MCRP 3-40.3C, Ch. 1).

mainPoints.title: Take-Off Angles and Skip Distance
mainPoints.content: The take-off angle is the angle above the horizon at which an antenna radiates the bulk of its energy. This angle determines where the signal returns to Earth after reflecting off the ionosphere.
subPoints: High take-off angles (60-90 degrees) are used for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to cover short distances (0-300 miles).
Low take-off angles (less than 30 degrees) are used for long-haul communications to reach distant stations.
The 'Skip Zone' is the area between the end of the ground wave and the first return of the sky wave (MCRP 3-40.3C, Ch. 2).

mainPoints.title: Antenna Adjustments for Propagation
mainPoints.content: Operators must physically manipulate the antenna to achieve the desired take-off angle based on the distance to the receiving station.
subPoints: Height above ground: Lowering a horizontal dipole increases the take-off angle for NVIS.
Orientation: Ensuring the antenna is broadside to the target station for maximum gain.
Configuration: Utilizing vertical whips for low-angle long-range or horizontal wires for high-angle short-range (MCRP 3-40.3C, Ch. 4).

practicalApplication.scenario: The unit is established in a jungle environment. You must establish an HF link with a station 450 miles away. You are provided with an HF radio, a dipole antenna kit, and a frequency propagation chart showing a MUF of 12 MHz and a LUF of 4 MHz.
steps: 1. Analyze the propagation data and select an operating frequency (approx. 10.2 MHz).
2. Determine the required take-off angle for a 450-mile distance using MCRP 3-40.3C charts.
3. Calculate the required height for the dipole antenna to achieve that angle.
4. Erect the antenna and orient it broadside to the distant station.
5. Initiate a radio check to verify the link.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the definitions of MUF and LUF, the calculation of take-off angles, and the physical adjustment of HF antennas to support sky wave propagation.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ionosphere is constantly changing. A Marine who understands these principles can adapt their equipment to maintain the 'always-on' communications required for MAGTF operations.

tlo.condition: Given an HF radio set, a distant station, and ionospheric data (MUF/LUF).
tlo.behavior: execute HF sky wave communications
tlo.standard: by selecting a frequency between the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and Lowest Useful Frequency (LUF) and adjusting the antenna for the correct angle of incidence to establish a reliable communication link per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Establishing sky wave communications requires the Marine to apply ionospheric data and technical procedures to a physical radio set to achieve a specific outcome. This is a direct application of knowledge to a task.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and ionospheric data.
elos.behavior: Define Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and Lowest Useful Frequency (LUF).
elos.standard: Accurately describing their role in HF sky wave propagation per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 1.
elos.justification: Basic terminology is required to understand the frequency selection process.

elos.condition: Given a distant station location and antenna technical data.

title: Directional Antenna Orientation and Interference Mitigation

introduction.gainAttention: You are receiving a critical MEDEVAC request, but a local commercial station or enemy jammer is drowning out the signal. By simply rotating your antenna 90 degrees, you can 'zero out' the noise and hear the call. This is the power of understanding antenna radiation patterns.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the directional characteristics of the horizontal half-wave antenna and how to use its 'nulls' and 'broadsides' to optimize signal-to-noise ratios.
objectives: TLO-022: Demonstrate directional antenna orientation to mitigate interference.
ELO-057: Define the terms 'null' and 'broadside' radiation patterns.
ELO-058: Identify the physical orientation of the antenna's radiation zones.

mainPoints.title: Radiation Patterns: Broadside and Null
mainPoints.content: A horizontal half-wave antenna does not radiate energy equally in all directions. It has a distinct 'figure-eight' pattern.
subPoints: Broadside: The direction perpendicular (90 degrees) to the wire where the signal is strongest.
Null: The direction off the ends of the wire where the signal is weakest or non-existent.
Reciprocity: The antenna receives best from the same directions it transmits best (MCRP 3-40.3C, Ch. 2).

mainPoints.title: Interference Mitigation Strategy
mainPoints.content: To maximize the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), the operator must position the antenna so the desired station is in a 'lobe' and the interference is in a 'null'.
subPoints: Identify the azimuth of the desired station and the interfering source.
Orient the wire so the ends (nulls) point directly at the source of interference.
Ensure the broadside (maximum gain) is facing the friendly station.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are operating a horizontal dipole. A friendly station is located at an azimuth of 090 degrees. An enemy jamming source is identified at an azimuth of 180 degrees. You must orient your antenna to maintain the link while mitigating the jammer.
steps: 1. Identify the azimuth of the desired signal (090).
2. Identify the azimuth of the interference (180).
3. Lay out the antenna wire along the 180-360 degree axis.
4. Verify that the ends of the wire (nulls) are pointing toward the interference (180).
5. Verify that the broadside of the wire (maximum gain) is facing the friendly station (090).
6. Conduct a signal quality check.

conclusion.summary: We have defined the radiation patterns of a half-wave antenna and practiced orienting the antenna to use nulls for interference mitigation.
conclusion.closingStatement: Antenna orientation is a 'free' way to increase your signal strength and defeat electronic warfare without needing more power or better equipment.

tlo.condition: Given a horizontal half-wave antenna, a desired signal source, and an identified interfering station.
tlo.behavior: demonstrate directional antenna orientation to mitigate interference
tlo.standard: by placing the interfering source in the antenna's null and the desired source in the antenna's broadside to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The Marine must physically manipulate the antenna based on the spatial relationship between signal sources. This requires the application of antenna theory to a real-world scenario.

elos.behavior: define the terms 'null' and 'broadside' radiation patterns
elos.standard: ensuring definitions accurately reflect the areas of minimum and maximum radiation intensity per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Knowledge of these terms is a prerequisite for physically orienting the antenna to achieve the desired signal-to-noise ratio.

elos.condition: Given a horizontal half-wave antenna and a compass.
elos.behavior: identify the physical orientation of the antenna's radiation zones
elos.standard: by correctly indicating the broadside direction (perpendicular to the wire) and the null direction (off the ends of the wire) per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The Marine must understand the spatial relationship between the physical wire and the invisible radiation pattern before attempting mitigation.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a hide site, and your only link to the Quick Reaction Force (QRF) is a weak, scratchy HF signal. You have plenty of wire, but if you don't know the exact length to cut that wire for your assigned frequency, your signal might never leave the clearing. Precision in antenna length is the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mathematical principles required to calculate the physical length of half-wave and quarter-wave antennas using the standard formulas found in MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-023: Calculate antenna length to within one inch of the mathematical requirement.
ELO-059: State the mathematical formulas for half-wave and quarter-wave antenna lengths.
ELO-060: Calculate the length of a half-wave dipole antenna in feet and inches.

mainPoints.title: The Physics of Resonance and the Velocity Factor
mainPoints.content: An antenna is most efficient when it is resonant, meaning its physical length matches the electrical wavelength of the frequency being transmitted. Because radio waves travel slower in wire than in free space, we use a 'velocity factor' to adjust our calculations.
subPoints: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.
The constant 468 accounts for the velocity factor in wire for a half-wave antenna.
The constant 234 is used for a quarter-wave antenna (half of 468).

mainPoints.title: The Half-Wave Dipole Formula
mainPoints.content: To find the total length of a half-wave dipole in feet, divide the constant 468 by the operating frequency in Megahertz (MHz).
subPoints: Formula: L (feet) = 468 / Frequency (MHz).
Example: For 10 MHz, 468 / 10 = 46.8 feet.
To convert decimals to inches: Multiply the decimal remainder by 12 (0.8 * 12 = 9.6 inches).

mainPoints.title: The Quarter-Wave Formula
mainPoints.content: Quarter-wave antennas (often used for vertical whips or field expedients) use half the length of a dipole.
subPoints: Formula: L (feet) = 234 / Frequency (MHz).
This calculation provides the length of the radiator element only.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a reconnaissance team. Your primary frequency is 7.250 MHz. You need to construct a half-wave dipole antenna using WD-1/TT field wire.
steps: Identify the assigned frequency (7.250 MHz).
Apply the half-wave formula: 468 / 7.250.
Calculate the total length in feet (64.55 feet).
Convert the decimal portion to inches (0.55 x 12 = 6.6 inches).
Measure and mark the wire to 64 feet, 7 inches.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the importance of resonance, the use of the 468 and 234 constants, and the step-by-step process for converting frequency into a physical wire length.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who can do the math is an operator who can communicate under any condition. Master these formulas to ensure your signal always hits the mark.

tlo.condition: Given a specific operating frequency, a calculator, and reference material.
tlo.behavior: calculate antenna length
tlo.standard: to within one inch of the mathematical requirement based on the formula for a half-wave or quarter-wave antenna per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Calculation is a Level 3 cognitive task involving the application of mathematical formulas (468/f) to a specific technical requirement.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: state the mathematical formulas for half-wave and quarter-wave antenna lengths
elos.standard: including the constant (468 for half-wave in feet) used to account for velocity factor per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Recall of the specific formula is required before the Marine can perform the calculation for a specific frequency.

elos.condition: Given a specific frequency in MHz and a calculator.
elos.behavior: calculate the length of a half-wave dipole antenna in feet and inches
elos.standard: to within one inch of the mathematical requirement per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: This is a direct component skill of the TLO, applying the formula to a specific operational requirement.

introduction.gainAttention: Have you ever touched a radio chassis and received a painful 'RF burn'? Or noticed your signal strength drop significantly when the soil dries out? That is the result of a poor ground. In the Marine Corps, a good ground isn't just about signal quality—it's about operator safety and equipment survival.
introduction.overview: This lesson explains the theory and implementation of grounding systems, including ground rods, counterpoises, and ground screens as per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-024: Implement an antenna grounding system to establish a low-resistance path to earth.
ELO-061: Describe the purpose of a counterpoise and ground screen.
ELO-062: Install a grounding rod.
ELO-063: Connect a counterpoise to the radio's ground terminal.

mainPoints.title: Grounding Theory and Safety
mainPoints.content: Grounding provides a low-resistance path to the earth. This serves two purposes: it protects the operator from hazardous voltages and completes the electrical circuit for the antenna, especially for vertical radiators.
subPoints: Reduces 'RF feedback' in the handset.
Protects equipment from static discharge and lightning.
Improves radiation efficiency by reducing ground loss.

mainPoints.title: Artificial Grounds: Counterpoise and Ground Screens
mainPoints.content: When the soil is too rocky, sandy, or dry to provide good conductivity, we must create an artificial ground.
subPoints: Counterpoise: A network of wires elevated above the ground or laid on the surface, not necessarily in contact with the earth.
Ground Screen: A mesh of wires placed directly on the ground to reduce ground resistance.
These systems act as the 'missing half' of the antenna system.

mainPoints.title: Installation Procedures
mainPoints.content: Proper installation requires physical effort and attention to layout.
subPoints: Ground rods must be driven at least 2 feet deep; deeper is always better for lower resistance.
Counterpoise wires should be laid out radially (like spokes on a wheel) from the base of the antenna.
Ensure all connections to the ground terminal are tight and free of corrosion.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a desert environment with high-resistance sandy soil. You are tasked with grounding an HF manpack radio to improve its performance for a long-haul link.
steps: Select a site for the ground rod near the antenna base.
Drive the ground rod into the earth to a minimum depth of 2 feet using a sledgehammer.
Connect the ground strap from the radio's ground terminal to the rod.
Deploy four counterpoise wires radially from the ground terminal, each cut to 1/4 wavelength of the operating frequency.
Verify all connections are secure and the wires are clear of foot traffic.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the critical role of grounding in safety and efficiency, the use of counterpoises in poor soil, and the physical requirements for installing ground rods.
conclusion.closingStatement: Never settle for a 'good enough' ground. The safety of your team and the reliability of your comms depend on the path you provide to the earth.

tlo.condition: Given a radio set, antenna, grounding rod, and counterpoise or ground screen materials.
tlo.behavior: implement an antenna grounding system
tlo.standard: to establish a low-resistance path to earth to improve radiation efficiency and ensure operator safety per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Constructing a grounding system requires the Marine to follow a technical procedure and apply it to the physical environment (soil conditions) to meet safety and efficiency standards.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a list of grounding materials.
elos.behavior: describe the purpose of a counterpoise and ground screen
elos.standard: explaining how they provide an artificial ground for antennas in areas of poor soil conductivity per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding the function of these components is necessary to ensure they are implemented correctly in varying terrain.

elos.condition: Given a radio set, grounding rod, and sledgehammer.
elos.behavior: install a grounding rod
elos.standard: to a depth of at least 2 feet or until reaching a low-resistance contact point to ensure operator safety and equipment protection per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Physical installation of the ground rod is the primary component skill for implementing a complete grounding system.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-intensity conflict environment where your unit's survival depends on a single SITREP reaching the Combat Operations Center. You have a functional radio and a directional antenna, but the signal is too weak to break the squelch. Without proper orientation, your signal is literally being broadcast into empty space instead of toward your target. Mastering antenna orientation is the difference between mission success and total communication blackout.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the technical application of antenna orientation, focusing on understanding radiation patterns, calculating precise azimuths between stations, and the physical alignment of directional antennas to maximize signal gain.
objectives: TLO-025: Apply antenna orientation techniques for maximum signal strength.
ELO-064: Identify the radiation patterns of directional antennas.
ELO-065: Calculate the azimuth between the local station and the distant station.
ELO-066: Orient the antenna's physical boom or radiator.

mainPoints.title: Radiation Patterns and Lobe Theory
mainPoints.content: Directional antennas do not radiate energy equally in all directions. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 2, Section I, energy is concentrated into specific areas called lobes.
subPoints: Major Lobe: The area of maximum radiation where the signal is strongest.
Minor Lobes: Areas of weaker radiation (side and back lobes) that represent wasted energy in directional applications.
Nulls: Directions where virtually no signal is radiated or received.

mainPoints.title: Azimuth Calculation and Map Work
mainPoints.content: Before physically moving the antenna, the operator must determine the exact direction of the distant station using a map and protractor.
subPoints: Identify grid coordinates for both the local and distant stations.
Draw a line between stations and measure the grid azimuth using a protractor.
Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth using the G-M angle found in the map's marginal data.

mainPoints.title: Physical Orientation Techniques
mainPoints.content: The final step is the physical alignment of the antenna hardware with the calculated magnetic azimuth.
subPoints: Use a lensatic compass to identify the magnetic azimuth on the ground.
Align the antenna's boom (for Yagi antennas) or the center line of the radiation pattern (for wire antennas) with the compass heading.
Ensure the alignment is within +/- 5 degrees to maintain maximum gain within the major lobe.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a reconnaissance team. You must establish a directional HF link with a higher headquarters located 25 miles away at grid 12S UF 4567 8901. Your current position is 12S UF 4000 8000.
steps: Plot both sets of coordinates on the provided tactical map.
Calculate the grid azimuth using a protractor.
Apply the G-M angle to determine the magnetic azimuth.
Use a lensatic compass to orient the directional antenna's major lobe toward the distant station within 5 degrees.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the identification of radiation lobes, the mathematical calculation of azimuths, and the physical orientation of antennas. These skills ensure that the maximum amount of radiated energy reaches the intended receiver.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio is only as good as its antenna. By precisely orienting your equipment, you overcome distance and terrain to ensure the Marine Corps maintains its command and control edge.

tlo.condition: Given a directional antenna, a compass, and the grid coordinates of a distant station.
tlo.behavior: apply antenna orientation techniques for maximum signal strength
tlo.standard: by aligning the antenna's major radiation lobe with the distant station's azimuth within +/- 5 degrees per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires the application of land navigation skills (azimuth conversion) and signal theory to the physical placement of equipment.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a list of antenna types,
elos.behavior: identify the radiation patterns of directional antennas
elos.standard: ensuring the major and minor lobes are correctly distinguished per Chapter 2, Section I of MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Knowledge of radiation patterns is a prerequisite for understanding how to orient the antenna's major lobe toward a target station.

elos.condition: Given a map, grid coordinates for two stations, and a protractor,
elos.behavior: calculate the azimuth between the local station and the distant station
elos.standard: to within +/- 1 degree of the mathematical bearing.
elos.justification: The Marine must be able to determine the correct direction of the distant station before the antenna can be physically aligned.

elos.condition: Given a lensatic compass and a directional antenna,
elos.behavior: orient the antenna's physical boom or radiator
elos.standard: to the calculated azimuth within +/- 5 degrees per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: This is the final component skill required to achieve the TLO's standard for signal maximization.

introduction.gainAttention: In mountainous terrain or dense jungle, standard line-of-sight radios often fail. The AS-2259/GR antenna is the Marine Corps' primary solution for these 'skip zone' gaps. It allows you to shoot your signal straight up into the atmosphere to rain back down on your target, bypassing terrain obstacles that would stop other antennas cold.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the knowledge and skills required to identify, assemble, and employ the AS-2259/GR antenna for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications.
objectives: TLO-026: Perform the assembly and erection of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
ELO-067: Identify all components of the antenna system.
ELO-068: Describe the characteristics of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
ELO-069: Measure the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR).

mainPoints.title: NVIS Propagation Principles
mainPoints.content: NVIS is a technique used to provide reliable communications in the 0-300 mile range, effectively eliminating the 'skip zone'.
subPoints: Requires high take-off angles (70 to 90 degrees) to reflect signals off the ionosphere.
Operates typically in the 2 to 12 MHz frequency range.
Ideal for overcoming terrain masking in valleys or heavily forested areas.

mainPoints.title: AS-2259/GR Component Identification
mainPoints.content: The AS-2259/GR is a tactical, man-portable antenna kit. Operators must be able to identify all parts to ensure rapid deployment.
subPoints: Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that form the vertical support.
Top Truck: The assembly at the top of the mast where the radiators connect.
Radiator Cables: Two crossed dipole cables that also serve as guy wires for stability.
Base Plate and Stakes: Provide the foundation and anchoring for the system.

mainPoints.title: Erection and VSWR Verification
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly must be followed by technical verification to prevent damage to the radio set.
subPoints: Assemble the mast and radiators in a clear area, ensuring the cables are taut and the mast is vertical.
Connect the antenna to the radio and perform a VSWR check.
A VSWR of 2:1 or less is required for safe and efficient operation; high VSWR indicates assembly errors or cable damage.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your platoon is operating in a deep valley. You are tasked with establishing a communications link to the Battalion CP located 40 miles away. You have been issued an AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
steps: Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit to ensure all mast sections and radiator cables are present.
Assemble the mast and top truck, then erect the antenna using the radiator cables as guy wires.
Connect the radio and measure the VSWR to ensure it is 2:1 or less.
Configure the radio for an HF frequency between 2-12 MHz to support NVIS propagation.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the theory of NVIS propagation, identified the components of the AS-2259/GR, and practiced the assembly and testing of the system.
conclusion.closingStatement: The AS-2259/GR is a critical tool for the tactical radio operator. When terrain stands in your way, NVIS allows you to go over it, ensuring the MAGTF remains a connected and lethal force.

tlo.behavior: Perform the assembly and erection of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
tlo.standard: To support Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications, ensuring the VSWR is within acceptable limits per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This is a procedural, hands-on task requiring the Marine to apply technical steps to achieve a physical result in a field environment.

elos.standard: to include the mast sections, top truck, and radiator cables per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Component recognition is essential for safe and correct assembly of the specific antenna system.

elos.standard: including the typical frequency range and take-off angles required for short-range HF communications.
elos.justification: Understanding the 'why' behind the AS-2259/GR's configuration (NVIS) ensures the Marine understands the purpose of the specific erection technique.

title: Assembly and Erection of the OE-254 Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-intensity conflict where your unit's survival depends on calling in immediate fire support. You pull your radio, but the signal is dead because the terrain is blocking your manpack antenna. The OE-254 is the difference between silence and the support you need to win. It is the workhorse of VHF communications, and knowing how to put it up fast and right is a life-saving skill.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the identification of OE-254 components, the technical requirements for siting a VHF antenna to ensure line-of-sight, and the physical procedures for erecting and securing the mast using the 120-degree guying method.
objectives: TLO-027: Perform the assembly and erection of an OE-254 antenna.
ELO-070: Identify all components of the antenna system.
ELO-071: Describe the siting requirements for VHF line-of-sight (LOS) communications.
ELO-072: Secure guy ropes and anchors.

mainPoints.title: OE-254 Component Identification
mainPoints.content: Before assembly, the operator must inventory the OE-254 kit to ensure all mission-essential parts are present and functional.
subPoints: Base Stake and Base Plate: Provides the foundation and grounding for the mast.
Mast Sections: Interlocking tubular sections that provide the required height for LOS.
Bicone Assembly: The radiating element consisting of the feedcone and elements.
Guy Ropes and Anchors: Used to stabilize the mast against wind and weight.
Coaxial Cable (RG-213): Connects the antenna to the radio set.

mainPoints.title: VHF Siting and Signal Propagation
mainPoints.content: VHF signals (30-300 MHz) primarily travel via line-of-sight. The physical environment directly impacts signal reliability.
subPoints: Terrain: High ground is preferred to clear the curvature of the earth and physical obstacles.
Vegetation: Heavy foliage can absorb VHF signals; antennas should be cleared of immediate brush or raised above the canopy.
Man-made Obstacles: Avoid power lines and large metal structures which cause signal reflection or interference.

mainPoints.title: Erection and Guying Procedures
mainPoints.content: Structural stability is achieved through proper guying. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, the mast must be secured to prevent collapse and ensure safety.
subPoints: Guying Intervals: Guy ropes must be spaced at 120-degree intervals around the mast.
Anchor Placement: Anchors should be driven into the ground at a distance from the base equal to approximately 1/2 to 2/3 of the mast height.
Tensioning: Ropes must be taut but not over-tightened to avoid bowing the mast sections.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your platoon has established a patrol base in a wooded area. You are tasked with erecting an OE-254 to establish a VHF link with the Company Command Post located 15km away.
steps: Conduct a layout and inventory of the OE-254 kit.
Select a site that maximizes elevation and minimizes foliage interference.
Assemble the bicone and attach the coaxial cable.
Connect mast sections and raise the antenna.
Drive anchors and secure guy ropes at 120-degree intervals.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the identification of the OE-254 kit, the critical nature of VHF line-of-sight siting, and the technical standards for securing the mast with 120-degree guying.
conclusion.closingStatement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier. When you master its assembly and siting, you ensure that your commander's intent can be heard across the battlefield, regardless of the terrain.

tlo.behavior: Perform the assembly and erection of an OE-254 antenna.
tlo.standard: To support VHF line-of-sight communications, ensuring guy ropes are secured at 120-degree intervals per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Physical assembly and erection of equipment is a direct application of technical knowledge and manual skills.

elos.behavior: identify all components of the antenna system
elos.standard: to include the base stake, mast sections, and bicone assembly per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Component recognition is the first step in the assembly process for the OE-254 system.

elos.behavior: describe the siting requirements for VHF line-of-sight (LOS) communications
elos.standard: including the effects of terrain and vegetation on signal propagation.
elos.justification: VHF communications are limited by LOS; understanding siting is critical before physical erection occurs.

warnings: Standard should include measurable criteria (time limits, accuracy percentages) or reference authoritative sources (per MCRP..., IAW TM...).

introduction.gainAttention: A poorly planned antenna farm is a beacon for enemy Direction Finding (DF) and a self-inflicted wound of signal interference. If your antennas are too close, your radios will 'talk' to each other instead of the distant end. To keep our communications secure and clear, we must plan our layouts with mathematical precision.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the tactical and technical considerations for antenna farm placement, the principles of mutual interference, and the calculation of separation distances to ensure electromagnetic compatibility.
objectives: TLO-028: Plan the layout of an antenna farm.
ELO-073: Identify siting considerations for an antenna farm.
ELO-074: Explain the principles of mutual interference.
ELO-075: Determine minimum separation distances between antennas.

mainPoints.title: Siting Considerations
mainPoints.content: Planning an antenna farm requires balancing three primary categories of considerations per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8.
subPoints: Doctrinal: Proximity to the Command Post (CP) and accessibility for operators.
Tactical: Use of natural concealment (reverse slopes) and security from enemy ground observation.
Technical: Soil conductivity for grounding and clear paths for signal propagation.

mainPoints.title: Mutual Interference Principles
mainPoints.content: Mutual interference occurs when multiple transmitters operate in close proximity, degrading the performance of nearby receivers.
subPoints: Cosite Interference: When a transmitter desensitizes a receiver on a different frequency due to physical proximity.
Frequency Separation: The requirement to maintain a minimum 'buffer' between assigned frequencies to prevent bleed-over.
Harmonics: Secondary signals generated at multiples of the fundamental frequency that can interfere with other nets.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Separation and Layout
mainPoints.content: To mitigate interference, antennas must be physically separated based on their operating characteristics.
subPoints: Horizontal Separation: The physical distance between masts; generally, the further the better, but limited by cable length.
Vertical Separation: Placing antennas at different heights to reduce coupling.
Polarization: Using different polarizations (vertical vs. horizontal) can provide up to 20dB of isolation.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Comm Chief for a Battalion Main CP. You have five VHF nets and two HF nets that must be operational within a 100m x 100m area. You must create a layout that prevents cosite interference.
steps: Analyze the frequency list to identify potential interference pairs.
Determine the minimum horizontal separation distances based on frequency bands.
Plot the antenna locations on a site overlay, considering terrain and concealment.
Designate cable runs to avoid power line interference.
Submit the completed antenna farm diagram for approval.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the tactical and technical requirements for siting, the dangers of mutual interference, and the methods for determining proper antenna separation.
conclusion.closingStatement: Effective antenna farm planning ensures that our electronic signature is managed and our internal communications remain crystal clear. Plan with the enemy's DF capability in mind, and execute with technical discipline.

tlo.condition: Given a mission, a list of communication nets, and a tactical area of responsibility.
tlo.behavior: Plan the layout of an antenna farm.
tlo.standard: To minimize mutual interference and maximize signal propagation while meeting tactical concealment and security requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Siting requires the synthesis of terrain analysis, frequency management, and tactical requirements to create a new layout or configuration.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a deep reconnaissance hide site and your primary whip antenna snaps. You have a spool of copper wire and a radio, but without the exact mathematical length for your assigned frequency, your signal will never reach the Combat Operations Center. Precision in antenna length is the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mathematical requirements for determining the physical length of half-wave dipole and quarter-wave vertical antennas using standard military formulas found in MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-029: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole or quarter-wave vertical antenna.
ELO-076: State the mathematical formula for calculating the length of a half-wave dipole.
ELO-077: Calculate the length of a single leg of a half-wave dipole.

mainPoints.title: The Standard Antenna Formula
mainPoints.content: To achieve resonance, an antenna must be cut to a specific fraction of the wavelength of the operating frequency. MCRP 3-40.3C provides constant values to simplify this calculation.
subPoints: For feet: 468 divided by the frequency in MHz (468/f).
For meters: 143 divided by the frequency in MHz (143/f).
These constants account for the 'end effect' where the velocity of propagation is slightly slower in wire than in free space.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Half-Wave Dipole Total Length
mainPoints.content: The half-wave dipole is the most common field-expedient antenna. The formula provides the total length of the radiating element.
subPoints: Example: For 7.0 MHz in feet: 468 / 7.0 = 66.85 feet.
Example: For 7.0 MHz in meters: 143 / 7.0 = 20.42 meters.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Individual Leg Lengths
mainPoints.content: A center-fed half-wave dipole consists of two distinct 'legs' or elements. To construct the antenna, the total length must be divided by two.
subPoints: Formula: (Total Length) / 2 = Individual Leg Length.
Using the 7.0 MHz example: 66.85 feet / 2 = 33.42 feet per leg.
Accuracy is critical; MCRP 3-40.3C standards require precision within +/- 1 inch to maintain a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a platoon-sized patrol. Your frequency is 14.250 MHz. You must calculate the total length and individual leg lengths for a half-wave dipole in both feet and meters.
steps: Identify the frequency (14.250 MHz).
Apply the formula for feet: 468 / 14.250.
Apply the formula for meters: 143 / 14.250.
Divide both results by 2 to determine the length of each individual wire leg.
Record results on the calculation worksheet for instructor verification.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the standard formulas for antenna calculation (468/f and 143/f) and the process for determining both total and individual leg lengths for dipole antennas.
conclusion.closingStatement: Math is a weapon. By mastering these calculations, you ensure that your equipment is tuned to the exact frequency required to maintain the command and control link.

tlo.standard: To within +/- 1 inch of the mathematical requirement based on the formula provided in MCRP 3-40.3C.

introduction.gainAttention: A radio is simply a heavy box of electronics until it is connected to an efficient antenna system. In the field, you cannot rely on issued whips alone. Building a field-expedient dipole allows you to push your signal further, hide your signature, and overcome terrain obstacles that would stop other units in their tracks.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the technical skills to identify antenna components, understand the effects of polarization, and physically construct a resonant half-wave dipole antenna.
objectives: TLO-030: Demonstrate the construction and employment of a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-078: Identify the components of a field-expedient antenna system.
ELO-079: Describe the effects of antenna polarization and orientation.
ELO-080: Perform wire cutting and stripping for an antenna radiator.

mainPoints.title: Components of the Dipole System
mainPoints.content: A standard field-expedient dipole consists of four primary components that must be properly integrated for the system to function.
subPoints: Radiator: The wire elements cut to the specific frequency.
Insulators: Non-conductive materials at the ends and center to prevent signal grounding.
Transmission Line: Coaxial cable (e.g., RG-58) that carries the signal from the radio to the antenna.
Balun: A 'balanced-to-unbalanced' transformer used at the feed point to improve efficiency.

mainPoints.title: Polarization and Orientation
mainPoints.content: The physical orientation of the antenna determines the direction and 'shape' of the radio wave.
subPoints: Horizontal Polarization: Antenna is parallel to the earth; best for long-range HF skywave and reducing man-made noise.
Vertical Polarization: Antenna is perpendicular to the earth; best for omni-directional ground wave communication.
Directivity: A horizontal dipole radiates energy best broadside (perpendicular) to the wire.

mainPoints.title: Construction Techniques
mainPoints.content: Proper mechanical construction ensures electrical reliability. Poorly stripped or loose wires create resistance and heat, which can damage the radio.
subPoints: Measure twice, cut once: Always add 6-12 inches for 'pigtails' or tying off to insulators before cutting.
Stripping: Remove insulation without nicking the copper strands to prevent wire fatigue.
Strain Relief: Ensure the weight of the transmission line is supported by the center insulator, not the wire connections.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team must establish a point-to-point HF link with a station 100 miles away. You have been provided with a frequency of 5.200 MHz, a spool of WD-1/TT wire, and two insulators.
steps: Calculate the required leg length for 5.200 MHz.
Measure and cut two lengths of wire, adding 6 inches for attachment points.
Strip 2 inches of insulation from the feed-point end of each wire.
Attach the wires to the center and end insulators using a standard fisherman's knot or wire wrap.
Connect the transmission line to the center feed point.
Raise the antenna to a horizontal position at least 1/4 wavelength above the ground.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the components of the dipole, discussed how orientation affects your signal, and practiced the physical skills of cutting and stripping antenna wire.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ability to build an antenna from scrap wire is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Ensure your connections are tight and your measurements are exact.

title: Employment and Assembly of the AS-2259/GR Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine your unit is operating in a deep mountain valley. Your standard vehicle whip antenna is failing to reach the Combat Operations Center (COC) because the signal is being blocked by the surrounding terrain. To get your message out, you need to shoot your signal straight up into the atmosphere so it can bounce back down over those mountains. This is the power of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) and the AS-2259/GR antenna.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the identification of AS-2259/GR components, the principles of NVIS propagation, and the step-by-step assembly of the antenna system to support short-range HF communications.
objectives: TLO-031: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit, an HF radio, and a designated site, perform the assembly and erection of the AS-2259/GR antenna to support NVIS communications.
ELO-081: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
ELO-082: Explain the characteristics of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
ELO-083: Assemble the mast and radiator elements of the AS-2259/GR.

mainPoints.title: NVIS Propagation Principles
mainPoints.content: Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) is a technique used to establish reliable communications over distances of 0-300 miles, bypassing terrain obstacles.
subPoints: Uses high take-off angles (near 90 degrees) to reflect signals off the ionosphere.
Requires specific frequency selection, typically between 2 and 12 MHz.
Eliminates the 'skip zone' common in standard HF skywave propagation.

mainPoints.title: AS-2259/GR Component Identification
mainPoints.content: The AS-2259/GR is a tactical, omnidirectional antenna designed specifically for NVIS.
subPoints: Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that form the vertical support.
Top Mast Assembly: Contains the feed point for the radiator elements.
Radiator Elements: Two crossed-dipole wire assemblies that also serve as guy wires.
Base and Ground Stake: Provides stability and electrical grounding.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Erection Procedures
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly ensures maximum signal radiation and structural integrity.
subPoints: Site selection: Choose a level area clear of overhead obstructions.
Mast assembly: Ensure each section is fully seated to prevent collapse.
Radiator tensioning: Wire elements must be pulled taut at 90-degree intervals to maintain the 'crossed-dipole' configuration.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team has been dropped at a remote patrol base in a canyon. You must establish an HF link back to the Battalion COC using the AS-2259/GR to overcome the terrain masking.
steps: Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit to ensure all components are present and serviceable.
Layout the base and drive the ground stake into the center of the site.
Assemble the mast sections and attach the top mast assembly.
Deploy the radiator wires at 90-degree angles from each other.
Erect the mast and secure the radiator wires to the ground stakes with proper tension.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the components of the AS-2259/GR, the theory of NVIS propagation for short-range HF, and the physical steps required to erect the system.
conclusion.closingStatement: Mastering the AS-2259/GR ensures that no matter the terrain, the Marine Corps maintains the ability to communicate and coordinate across the battlespace.

title: Employment and Assembly of the OE-254 Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: In the VHF world, 'Height is Might.' If you are operating at the edge of your radio's range, every foot of elevation you gain can mean the difference between a clear transmission and total silence. The OE-254 allows you to put your antenna 30 feet in the air, significantly extending your Line of Sight (LOS) capabilities.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the OE-254 antenna system, including component identification, critical siting considerations for safety and performance, and the team-based guying and erection process.
objectives: TLO-032: Given an OE-254 antenna kit, a VHF radio, and a designated site, demonstrate the assembly and erection of the OE-254 antenna to its full height.
ELO-084: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.
ELO-085: Describe siting considerations for the OE-254 antenna.
ELO-086: Perform the guying of the OE-254 mast.

mainPoints.title: OE-254 System Components
mainPoints.content: The OE-254 is a biconical, omnidirectional antenna designed for the 30-88 MHz VHF range.
subPoints: Feed Cone and Radiating Elements: The 'top' of the antenna that handles the signal.
Mast Sections: Lightweight aluminum tubes used to reach the 30-foot height.
Guy Ropes and Plates: Used to stabilize the mast at two different levels.
Base Stake and Base Plate: The foundation of the mast system.

mainPoints.title: Siting and Safety Considerations
mainPoints.content: Because the OE-254 stands 30 feet tall and is made of conductive aluminum, site selection is a matter of both performance and life safety.
subPoints: Line of Sight (LOS): Ensure the site is the highest available ground with minimal obstructions.
Power Line Safety: The antenna must be placed at a distance at least twice its height (60 feet) from any overhead power lines.
Grounding: Always use the provided ground stake to protect against static buildup and lightning.

mainPoints.title: Guying and Team Erection
mainPoints.content: Erecting a 30-foot mast requires a coordinated three-person team to prevent the mast from buckling or falling.
subPoints: Guying Intervals: Secure guy ropes at 120-degree intervals (three directions).
Team Roles: One person on the mast, two people managing guy ropes to maintain verticality during the lift.
Tensioning: Ensure ropes are tight enough to withstand wind but not so tight they bend the aluminum mast.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your platoon is establishing a static observation post. You are tasked with erecting an OE-254 to ensure the VHF net remains reliable over the 15-mile distance to the company headquarters.
steps: Conduct a site survey to ensure clearance from power lines and optimal LOS.
Assemble the feed cone and radiating elements on the ground.
Connect the coaxial cable to the feed cone before raising the mast.
Assemble the mast sections while the team members prepare the guy stakes at 120-degree intervals.
Raise the antenna to its full 30-foot height using the three-person lift method, securing guys at each level.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the OE-254 components, discussed the critical safety distances from power lines, and practiced the team-based guying techniques required for a 30-foot erection.
conclusion.closingStatement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier for VHF communications. Erecting it quickly and safely ensures your unit stays connected when the distance gets long.

elos.justification: Identification of components is the foundational step before complex assembly of a 30-foot mast system.

elos.standard: Including Line of Sight (LOS) requirements and safety clearances from overhead power lines per MCRP 3-40.3C, page 8-6.
elos.justification: Safety and technical siting are critical for VHF communications and the physical safety of the Marines erecting a tall mast.

elos.justification: Guying is a critical component skill for the OE-254 to prevent equipment damage and ensure structural integrity.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a high-tempo environment where your signal is barely breaking the squelch of the receiving station. You have the right frequency and the right power setting, but your signal is still weak. The difference between mission success and communication failure might literally be beneath your feet. By properly implementing a ground system, you can reclaim lost energy and turn a marginal link into a crystal-clear circuit.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the theory and practical application of antenna ground systems, specifically focusing on how ground screens and counterpoises improve radiation efficiency for vertical whip antennas.
objectives: Explain the purpose of an antenna ground system per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Differentiate between a ground screen and a counterpoise per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Install a counterpoise system using four radial wires of the correct length per MCRP 3-40.3C.

mainPoints.title: Purpose of Antenna Ground Systems
mainPoints.content: A ground system is essential for vertical antennas to provide a low-resistance return path for radio frequency (RF) energy. Without an adequate ground, energy is lost to the earth as heat rather than being radiated as a signal.
subPoints: Reduces ground loss by providing a highly conductive path.
Improves radiation efficiency, ensuring more power reaches the distant station.
Acts as the 'other half' of the antenna system for unbalanced radiators like the vertical whip.

mainPoints.title: Ground Screen vs. Counterpoise
mainPoints.content: While both improve performance, they are utilized in different tactical scenarios based on the soil and the antenna height.
subPoints: Ground Screen: A series of buried or surface-laid wires used to reduce resistance in the immediate vicinity of the antenna base.
Counterpoise: An artificial ground system used when a standard ground is unavailable or the soil is poorly conductive. It is typically elevated above the earth.
Functional Difference: Ground screens rely on contact with the earth; counterpoises act as a capacitive substitute for the earth.

mainPoints.title: Counterpoise Installation Requirements
mainPoints.content: To be effective, a counterpoise must be constructed according to the operating frequency to ensure resonance and efficiency.
subPoints: Requires at least four radial wires.
Radials must be cut to the correct length (1/4 wavelength) for the operating frequency.
Wires should be spread out evenly (90 degrees apart) from the base of the antenna.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team is tasked with establishing an HF radio site in a rocky, arid region where the soil conductivity is extremely poor. You must implement a counterpoise system for your vertical whip antenna to ensure reliable communications with the Battalion COC.
steps: Identify the operating frequency and calculate the 1/4 wavelength for the radial wires.
Measure and cut four lengths of copper wire to the calculated length.
Connect the four wires to the ground terminal of the antenna base or the radio's ground lug.
Deploy the wires radially from the antenna, ensuring they are approximately 90 degrees apart.
Secure the ends of the radials using ground stakes, ensuring they are taut and elevated if required by the specific antenna kit.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed how ground systems reduce loss and improve efficiency. We differentiated between buried ground screens and elevated counterpoises, and we covered the specific requirements for installing a four-radial counterpoise system.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who understands the ground is an operator who can communicate anywhere. Never neglect your ground system; it is the foundation of your signal's strength.

tlo.behavior: Implement an antenna ground system.
tlo.standard: By installing a ground screen or counterpoise to improve radiation efficiency per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The Marine must apply knowledge of soil conductivity and wavelength to physically install a grounding solution. This is a direct application of technical principles.

elos.justification: Different tactical environments require different grounding solutions; the Marine must know which to apply.

introduction.gainAttention: A directional antenna is like a sniper rifle; it concentrates all its energy into a narrow beam to hit a specific target. However, if that rifle is misaligned by even a few degrees, you will miss the target entirely. In the world of radio, a misaligned directional antenna means your signal is being wasted on empty space while your intended receiver hears nothing but static.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the precise orientation of directional antennas, including the calculation of azimuths and the identification of radiation patterns to maximize signal gain.
objectives: Define the term 'azimuth' as it relates to antenna orientation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Identify the major lobe of an antenna pattern per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Calculate the required azimuth for antenna orientation within +/- 3 degrees.

mainPoints.title: Azimuth and Orientation Fundamentals
mainPoints.content: Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from a north reference (typically grid north or magnetic north) to the direction of the distant station.
subPoints: Proper orientation ensures the antenna's energy is concentrated toward the receiver.
Orientation is critical for directional antennas like the Yagi, Vee, or Sloping Wire.
Reference MCRP 3-40.3C Appendix A for standardized definitions.

mainPoints.title: Understanding Radiation Patterns
mainPoints.content: Every antenna has a radiation pattern that shows where the energy is strongest.
subPoints: Major Lobe: The area of maximum radiation intensity where the most gain is achieved.
Minor Lobes/Side Lobes: Areas of unintended radiation that waste power and can increase the chance of detection by the enemy.
Nulls: Directions in which the antenna radiates little to no energy.

mainPoints.title: Calculating and Applying the Azimuth
mainPoints.content: To achieve maximum gain, the major lobe must be aligned precisely with the distant station's location.
subPoints: Determine your location and the distant station's location using grid coordinates.
Calculate the grid-to-magnetic conversion (G-M angle) if using a lensatic compass.
The standard for alignment is within +/- 3 degrees to ensure the peak of the major lobe is utilized.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are located at Grid 12S VF 1234 5678. You need to establish a directional link with a station located at Grid 12S VF 2234 6678. Using a map and a directional antenna, you must calculate the bearing and orient the antenna's major lobe.
steps: Plot both stations on the map and draw a line between them.
Use a protractor to determine the grid azimuth from your position to the distant station.
Apply the G-M angle for your current location to convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth.
Physically rotate the directional antenna so that its primary radiating element (the major lobe) is aligned with the calculated magnetic azimuth.
Verify the alignment using a compass, ensuring the error is no more than +/- 3 degrees.

conclusion.summary: We defined azimuth, identified the importance of the major lobe in radiation patterns, and practiced the calculations necessary to align a directional antenna.
conclusion.closingStatement: Precision in orientation is the hallmark of a professional communicator. By mastering azimuth calculations and lobe alignment, you ensure that your signal reaches the target with maximum intensity.

tlo.condition: Given an erected directional antenna and a distant station's location.
tlo.behavior: Apply orientation techniques to a directional antenna.
tlo.standard: Aligning the major lobe toward the receiving station to achieve maximum gain per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires using tools (compass/map) and technical data (radiation patterns) to perform a physical adjustment. Level 3 is appropriate for using information in a specific situation.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a list of antenna terms.
elos.behavior: Define the term 'azimuth' as it relates to antenna orientation.
elos.standard: Ensuring the definition matches the glossary in MCRP 3-40.3C Appendix A.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the term azimuth is a fundamental prerequisite for performing orientation techniques.

elos.condition: Given a radiation pattern diagram for a directional antenna.
elos.behavior: Identify the major lobe of the antenna pattern.
elos.standard: Correctly locating the area of maximum radiation intensity per MCRP 3-40.3C Section 2-4.
elos.justification: The Marine must be able to recognize the major lobe before they can align it with a distant station.

elos.behavior: Calculate the required azimuth for antenna orientation.
elos.standard: Within +/- 3 degrees of the actual bearing to ensure maximum signal gain.
elos.justification: Application of map reading skills is necessary to determine the physical direction the antenna must face.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley in a mountainous region. Your standard whip antenna is failing to reach the Combat Operations Center (COC) only 50 miles away because the terrain is blocking your line-of-sight. Understanding HF propagation is the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence. Today, we will learn how to 'bounce' signals off the atmosphere to overcome terrain and distance.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of HF propagation including Groundwave, Skywave, and NVIS, and provides the criteria for selecting the optimal antenna based on mission requirements.
objectives: TLO-035: Determine the appropriate HF antenna type.
ELO-093: Describe the characteristics of Groundwave, Skywave, and NVIS propagation.
ELO-094: Compare the gain and take-off angle characteristics of each antenna.

mainPoints.title: HF Propagation Fundamentals
mainPoints.content: Radio waves travel from the transmitter to the receiver in three primary ways depending on frequency and antenna type.
subPoints: Groundwave: Follows the curvature of the earth; best for short distances (0-50 miles) using vertical polarization.
Skywave: Reflects off the ionosphere; used for long-range communication (100 to thousands of miles) but has a 'skip zone' where no signal is received.
Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS): Radiates at high angles (70-90 degrees) to reflect back down locally (0-300 miles), effectively 'filling in' the skip zone and overcoming terrain.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Characteristics and Take-off Angles
mainPoints.content: The 'Take-off Angle' is the angle above the horizon that an antenna radiates its energy. This determines the distance the signal will travel.
subPoints: Vertical Whip: Low take-off angle; excellent for Groundwave but poor for NVIS.
Half-Wave Dipole: Variable take-off angle based on height above ground; highly versatile for medium to long-range Skywave.
AS-2259/GR: High take-off angle (near 90 degrees); specifically designed for NVIS and short-range communication in restrictive terrain.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Selection Criteria
mainPoints.content: To select the right antenna, the operator must evaluate the distance to the distant station, the frequency assigned, and the environmental obstacles.
subPoints: Short Range (0-300 miles) with terrain: Select NVIS (AS-2259 or low Dipole).
Medium Range (300-1500 miles): Select Dipole or Inverted Vee at moderate heights.
Long Range (1500+ miles): Select low take-off angle antennas like the Sloping Vee or Vertical Half-Rhombic.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Radio Supervisor for a Reconnaissance team inserted 150 miles from the extraction point. You are located in a heavily forested ravine. You have been assigned a frequency of 5.0 MHz. You have an AS-2259 kit, a Dipole kit, and a 10ft Whip.
steps: Analyze the distance requirement (150 miles = NVIS/Short Range Skywave).
Evaluate the terrain (Ravine = High take-off angle required).
Compare available antennas based on MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 4.
Select the AS-2259/GR as the primary antenna to ensure NVIS propagation.
Justify the selection based on the 90-degree take-off angle required to clear the ravine walls.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the three types of HF propagation and how antenna take-off angles dictate the effective range of our communications. Selecting the right antenna is not a guess; it is a technical decision based on distance, frequency, and terrain.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ability to communicate is a weapon system. By mastering antenna selection, you ensure that the MAGTF commander maintains command and control, regardless of the distance or the height of the mountains between you and your objective.

elos.justification: Analysis of antenna characteristics is a prerequisite for the higher-level task of determining the best antenna for a specific mission.

introduction.gainAttention: The AS-2259/GR is the most effective tool in the Marine Corps inventory for short-range HF communications in jungle or mountainous environments. However, if installed incorrectly, it becomes a 15-foot lightning rod or a source of RF burns for your team. Precision in installation is a matter of both mission success and physical safety.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the knowledge and skills to safely and effectively install the AS-2259/GR antenna kit for NVIS operations.
objectives: TLO-036: Perform the installation of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
ELO-095: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
ELO-096: Explain safety precautions for HF antenna installation.
ELO-097: Assemble the mast sections and radiating elements.

mainPoints.title: Safety and Siting Considerations
mainPoints.content: Before unpacking the kit, the site must be surveyed for hazards according to MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8.
subPoints: Power Lines: Ensure the site is at least twice the height of the antenna away from any power lines.
RF Hazards: Establish a keep-out zone to prevent personnel from touching the radiating elements during transmission.
Grounding: The antenna must be properly grounded to the radio set to prevent equipment damage and electrical shock.

mainPoints.title: AS-2259/GR Component Identification
mainPoints.content: The AS-2259/GR is a specialized kit. Operators must ensure all components are present and serviceable.
subPoints: Mast Sections: Seven fiberglass sections, including one top section and six interchangeable lower sections.
Top Assembly: Contains the matching transformer and connections for the radiating elements.
Radiating Elements: Four wire elements that also serve as the guy wires for the mast.
Base Stake and Ground Cable: Provides the physical foundation and electrical ground path.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Erection Procedures
mainPoints.content: Follow a structured sequence to ensure the mast is stable and the elements are properly tensioned.
subPoints: Drive the base stake into the ground and attach the base of the first mast section.
Assemble the mast sections on the ground, attaching the top assembly and radiating elements.
Carefully raise the mast vertically, ensuring it remains straight.
Secure the four radiating elements to the ground stakes at 90-degree intervals, providing tension to stabilize the mast.
Connect the coaxial cable to the radio and perform a VSWR check.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit has just arrived at a new Patrol Base. You are tasked with establishing an NVIS link back to the Battalion HQ. You have been provided an AS-2259/GR kit and must set it up within 15 minutes.
steps: Conduct a site survey to ensure clearance from power lines and overhead obstructions.
Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit against the technical manual.
Drive the base stake and assemble the seven mast sections.
Attach the radiating elements to the top assembly.
Raise the mast and secure the elements to the ground stakes, ensuring the mast is perfectly vertical.
Connect the ground cable and the RF feed line to the radio set.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the components, safety requirements, and assembly steps for the AS-2259/GR. This antenna is essential for NVIS comms, but its effectiveness depends entirely on the quality of your installation.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio is only as good as its antenna. By following these procedures, you ensure that your team has a stable, safe, and effective communication link when it matters most.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-intensity conflict where your manpack whip antenna is failing to reach the Combat Operations Center (COC) due to terrain. According to MCRP 3-40.3C, the antenna is the one variable an operator has the most control over. By properly installing the OE-254, you can transform a marginal, static-filled net into a crystal-clear link that ensures your unit's calls for fire and medical evacuations are heard.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the identification of OE-254 components, tactical siting considerations to maximize signal propagation, and the step-by-step assembly and installation of the antenna system.
objectives: TLO-037: Perform the installation of an OE-254 antenna.
ELO-098: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.

mainPoints.title: OE-254 Component Identification
mainPoints.content: Before deployment, every operator must verify the serviceability of the OE-254 kit. Missing or damaged components will directly degrade VHF line-of-sight communications.
subPoints: Mast Base and Mast Sections: The structural foundation of the antenna.
Guy Plates and Guy Ropes: Essential for maintaining a vertical, stable mast under wind load.
Radiator Elements: The active components that facilitate signal transmission and reception.
Base Stake and Grounding Equipment: Critical for safety and signal stability.

mainPoints.title: Tactical Siting and Signal Propagation
mainPoints.content: The effectiveness of a VHF antenna is heavily dependent on its physical location. Operators must analyze the terrain to avoid signal masking.
subPoints: Ground Slope: Ensure the site is level enough to support a vertical mast without risking collapse.
Overhead Obstructions: Avoid power lines (safety hazard) and heavy foliage which absorbs VHF energy.
Distance to Radio: Keep the cable run within technical limits to minimize signal attenuation (line loss).

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Vertical Installation
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly ensures the antenna operates at the correct resonance and prevents physical damage to the equipment.
subPoints: Locking Mast Sections: Each section must be fully seated and locked to prevent the mast from telescoping downward.
Radiator Seating: Elements must be securely attached to the feed cone to ensure electrical continuity.
Tensioning Guy Lines: Use a 'star' pattern to ensure the mast is perfectly vertical and tensioned equally.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your platoon has established a patrol base in a wooded valley. You are ordered to establish a VHF retransmission point on a nearby ridge to maintain comms with the Company HQ.
steps: Conduct a site survey of the ridge, identifying a level area clear of overhead power lines.
Inventory the OE-254 kit, laying out all mast sections and radiator elements.
Assemble the radiator assembly and attach the coaxial cable.
Erect the mast sections one at a time, securing guy lines at the 15-foot and 30-foot levels.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength and verticality of the mast.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the identification of the OE-254 components, the critical nature of siting for VHF propagation, and the technical steps required for a stable, vertical installation.
conclusion.closingStatement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier. Your ability to install this system correctly ensures that the MAGTF remains a connected, lethal force regardless of the terrain.

introduction.gainAttention: In a modern Command Post, dozens of radios are transmitting simultaneously. Without a plan, these systems will interfere with each other, creating 'electronic fratricide' that can shut down our own communications more effectively than the enemy. Mastering the antenna farm layout is the difference between a functional COC and a useless pile of interference.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the framework for planning an antenna farm, focusing on the types of command post configurations, technical placement considerations, and the calculation of separation distances to prevent cosite interference.
objectives: TLO-038: Plan an antenna farm layout.
ELO-101: Describe the types of antenna farms.
ELO-102: Analyze technical considerations for antenna placement.
ELO-103: Determine minimum separation distances between antennas.

mainPoints.title: Command Post Antenna Farm Configurations
mainPoints.content: The layout of an antenna farm is dictated by the echelon of command and the tactical mission.
subPoints: Tactical CP: Small, mobile, and rapidly deployed; focuses on immediate maneuver nets.
Main CP: High density of systems (HF, VHF, UHF, SATCOM); requires complex interference management.
Rear CP: Focuses on sustainment and long-haul links, often utilizing more permanent antenna structures.

mainPoints.title: Technical Placement Considerations
mainPoints.content: Technical factors must be balanced against tactical security to ensure the farm remains operational and survivable.
subPoints: Frequency Separation: Grouping similar frequency bands while maintaining distance between high-power transmitters and sensitive receivers.
Polarization: Ensuring all antennas in a net use the same polarization (vertical vs. horizontal) to avoid 20dB+ signal loss.
Power Line Interference: Siting antennas away from civilian power grids to reduce man-made noise floors.

mainPoints.title: Separation Distances and Cosite Interference
mainPoints.content: Cosite interference occurs when a transmitter's signal overwhelms a nearby receiver. This is mitigated through physical distance and frequency management.
subPoints: Horizontal Separation: The primary method for reducing interference between antennas in the same frequency band.
Vertical Separation: Utilizing different mast heights to create isolation between antennas.
Power Output Analysis: High-power HF transmitters require significantly more 'buffer' space than low-power VHF handhelds.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Comm Chief for a Battalion Main CP. You are given a list of 12 radio nets (4 HF, 6 VHF, 2 UHF) and a 100m x 100m plot of land. You must design the layout.
steps: Group radios by frequency band (HF, VHF, UHF).
Identify the highest power transmitters and place them on the perimeter.
Calculate minimum separation distances based on MCRP 6-22D Chapter 8 standards.
Draft a site map showing the location, polarization, and frequency of every antenna.
Brief the layout, justifying the placement based on terrain and interference mitigation.

conclusion.summary: We have analyzed the different types of antenna farms, the technical requirements for polarization and frequency management, and the necessity of maintaining strict separation distances.
conclusion.closingStatement: A well-planned antenna farm is invisible when it works, but a failure in planning is felt by every Marine on the net. Plan with precision to ensure the Commander's intent is always communicable.

tlo.behavior: Plan an antenna farm layout.

tlo.justification: Siting an antenna farm requires the synthesis of tactical requirements, terrain analysis, and electromagnetic interference principles to create a unique spatial configuration.
