title: Construction of the Half-Wave Dipole Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley where your standard vehicle whip antenna cannot clear the terrain. Your mission depends on establishing a reliable HF link back to the COC. By the end of this period of instruction, you will know how to turn a spool of copper wire and a few insulators into a high-performance half-wave dipole that can punch through atmospheric noise and terrain obstacles.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mathematical calculation, physical configuration, and construction techniques required to build a center-fed half-wave dipole antenna using field-expedient materials and MCRP 3-40.3C standards.
objectives: TLO-039: Given a frequency, wire, insulators, a transmission line, and MCRP 6-22D, construct a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-104: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-105: Describe the configuration of a center-fed doublet.
ELO-106: Measure and cut antenna wire elements.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Antenna Length
mainPoints.content: To ensure resonance at the desired operating frequency, the antenna must be cut to a specific length. The standard formula for a half-wave dipole in feet is 468 divided by the frequency in Megahertz (MHz).
subPoints: Formula: L (feet) = 468 / Frequency (MHz)
This result provides the total length of the antenna from end to end.
Accuracy must be within 1% to ensure a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

mainPoints.title: Center-Fed Doublet Configuration
mainPoints.content: A half-wave dipole, also known as a center-fed doublet, consists of two distinct elements. Each element is a quarter-wavelength long.
subPoints: The transmission line (coax or twin-lead) connects at the center insulator.
Two wire elements extend in opposite directions from the center.
Insulators are used at the center and both ends to isolate the antenna from the support structures.

mainPoints.title: Measuring and Cutting Techniques
mainPoints.content: Precision in measurement is critical. When cutting wire, the operator must account for the 'pigtails' needed to secure the wire to the insulators.
subPoints: Measure the total calculated length first.
Divide the total length by two to determine the length of each quarter-wave element.
Add 6-12 inches of 'service loop' or excess wire to each end for wrapping around insulators and soldering/connecting to the transmission line.

practicalApplication.scenario: The platoon is assigned a primary HF frequency of 8.45 MHz. You are tasked with constructing a horizontal half-wave dipole to support long-haul communications.
steps: Calculate the total length: 468 / 8.45 = 55.38 feet.
Divide by 2 for each element: 27.69 feet per side.
Measure two lengths of WD-1/TT or copper wire to 28.5 feet (including excess for ties).
Attach the two elements to a center insulator and connect the transmission line.
Secure the far ends to insulators and prepare for hoisting.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the calculation of antenna length using the 468 formula, the physical layout of the center-fed doublet, and the practical steps to measure and cut the wire elements.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ability to fabricate an antenna from raw wire is a hallmark of a proficient communicator. This skill ensures that even if your primary equipment is damaged, the MAGTF maintains its ability to command and control.

tlo.justification: Construction involves the synthesis of raw materials and mathematical calculations to produce a functional communication tool tailored to a specific frequency.

introduction.gainAttention: Radio waves travel at the speed of light—300 million meters per second. However, because electricity travels slightly slower in wire than in free space, our antennas must be mathematically 'tuned' to match the wave. If your math is wrong, your signal stays in the radio as heat instead of going into the atmosphere as a wave.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the theoretical relationship between frequency and wavelength and the precise calculations required to determine antenna element lengths for HF operations.
objectives: TLO-040: Calculate the physical length of antenna elements.
ELO-107: Identify the constant values used in the antenna length formula.
ELO-108: Explain the inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength.
ELO-109: Calculate the length of a half-wave dipole antenna in feet.

mainPoints.title: Frequency and Wavelength Relationship
mainPoints.content: There is an inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength. As the frequency of a signal increases, the physical length of the wave decreases.
subPoints: Higher Frequency = Shorter Antenna.
Lower Frequency = Longer Antenna.
Understanding this prevents common errors when switching between day and night frequencies.

mainPoints.title: Standard Constants for Calculation
mainPoints.content: MCRP 3-40.3C provides specific constants to simplify the calculation of half-wave and quarter-wave antennas.
subPoints: For length in feet: Use the constant 468 for a half-wave antenna.
For length in meters: Use the constant 143 for a half-wave antenna.
These constants account for the 'velocity factor' of electricity traveling through wire.

mainPoints.title: Mathematical Precision
mainPoints.content: Calculations must be accurate to two decimal places to remain within the 1% tolerance required for tactical radios.
subPoints: Step 1: Identify the assigned frequency in MHz.
Step 2: Divide the constant (468) by the frequency.
Step 3: Round to the nearest hundredth.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are provided with three frequencies for a 24-hour period: 4.25 MHz, 12.10 MHz, and 22.50 MHz. You must calculate the exact half-wave dipole length for each to prepare the wire kits.
steps: Calculate for 4.25 MHz: 468 / 4.25 = 110.12 feet.
Calculate for 12.10 MHz: 468 / 12.10 = 38.68 feet.
Calculate for 22.50 MHz: 468 / 22.50 = 20.80 feet.
Verify that as the frequency increased, the calculated length decreased.

conclusion.summary: You have learned the inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength, the constants 468 and 143, and the method for precise length calculation.
conclusion.closingStatement: Precision in your calculations is the difference between a clear voice link and a radio that overheats and fails. Master the math, and you master the spectrum.

tlo.condition: Given a specific operating frequency and a requirement to construct a wire antenna.
tlo.behavior: Calculate the physical length of antenna elements.
tlo.standard: To within 1% of the theoretical requirement based on the formula provided in MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Calculation is the direct application of a mathematical formula to a specific problem set to determine a precise value.

elos.justification: Understanding the theory of wavelength ensures the Marine can identify logical errors in their calculations.

elos.justification: This is a direct application of the formula required to meet the TLO standard.

title: Installation of the AS-2259/GR NVIS Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley, only 50 miles from your higher headquarters. Your standard whip antenna is failing because the signal is being absorbed by the surrounding terrain. This is the 'skip zone'—where tactical communications go to die. The AS-2259/GR is your solution to bridge that gap using Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS), allowing you to communicate over obstacles by bouncing your signal off the ionosphere at a steep angle.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of NVIS propagation, the identification of AS-2259/GR components, and the step-by-step procedures for assembling and erecting the antenna system to support short-range HF communications.
objectives: TLO-041: Demonstrate the installation of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
ELO-110: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
ELO-111: Describe the characteristics of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
ELO-112: Assemble the AS-2259/GR mast and radiating elements.

mainPoints.title: NVIS Propagation Characteristics
mainPoints.content: Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) is a technique used to provide reliable communications in the 0-300 mile range, effectively eliminating the skip zone common in HF communications.
subPoints: Requires high take-off angles (60-90 degrees) to ensure the signal reflects back to Earth locally.
Operates typically in the 2-12 MHz frequency range depending on atmospheric conditions.
Ideal for mountainous terrain or heavily vegetated areas where line-of-sight is impossible.

mainPoints.title: AS-2259/GR Component Identification
mainPoints.content: The AS-2259/GR is a tactical HF antenna designed specifically for NVIS. Operators must be able to identify all kit components to ensure rapid deployment.
subPoints: Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that provide the vertical structure.
Top Truck: The assembly at the top of the mast that houses the matching transformer.
Radiating Elements: Two crossed-dipole wire assemblies that also serve as guy wires.
Base Plate and Stakes: Provides the foundation and anchoring for the system.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Installation Procedures
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly ensures both electrical performance and structural integrity. All connections must be hand-tight to prevent damage while maintaining conductivity.
subPoints: Site Selection: Choose a level area approximately 60x60 feet.
Mast Assembly: Connect mast sections sequentially while attaching the radiating elements to the top truck.
Erection: Carefully raise the mast while tensioning the radiating elements/guy wires.
Connection: Attach the RF cable to the base and ensure the system is grounded.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a patrol base located in a canyon. You are tasked with establishing a command net with the Combat Operations Center (COC) located 45 miles away. You must deploy the AS-2259/GR to overcome the terrain masking.
steps: Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit using the technical manual.
Select a suitable site and layout the base plate and stakes.
Assemble the mast sections and attach the top truck.
Deploy the radiating elements at 90-degree angles from each other.
Erect the antenna and secure the guy wires to the stakes.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength and NVIS propagation.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the mechanics of NVIS propagation, identified the critical components of the AS-2259/GR, and practiced the assembly of the antenna. These skills allow for reliable HF communications in environments where standard antennas fail.
conclusion.closingStatement: Mastering the AS-2259/GR ensures that no matter the terrain, the Marine Corps maintains the ability to command and control the battlespace.

elos.standard: In accordance with the sequence of events outlined in MCRP 3-40.3C, ensuring all connections are hand-tight.
elos.justification: Assembly is a component skill of the terminal demonstration of installation.

warnings: Verb "Assemble" is not in the standard Bloom's Taxonomy verb list. Consider using one of: Demonstrate, Perform, Calculate, Apply, Execute, Implement, Use

title: Installation of the OE-254 VHF Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: In the world of VHF communications, height is king. Without a clear line-of-sight, your mission-critical data and voice traffic won't reach the receiver. The OE-254 Omni-Directional Antenna is the workhorse that extends your reach and ensures your signal clears the trees and terrain that would otherwise block your path.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the siting considerations for line-of-sight (LOS) communications, the identification of OE-254 components, and the physical assembly and erection of the antenna system.
objectives: TLO-042: Demonstrate the installation of an OE-254 antenna.
ELO-113: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.
ELO-114: Explain the siting considerations for a line-of-sight (LOS) antenna.
ELO-115: Perform the assembly of the OE-254 bicone antenna head.

mainPoints.title: Siting and LOS Propagation
mainPoints.content: VHF signals travel primarily via line-of-sight. Understanding how terrain and placement affect this signal is critical for the radio operator.
subPoints: Terrain Masking: Hills and buildings can completely block VHF signals.
Vegetation: Heavy foliage absorbs high-frequency energy, reducing range.
Antenna Height: Increasing the height of the antenna directly increases the radio horizon and signal clarity.

mainPoints.title: OE-254 Component Identification
mainPoints.content: The OE-254 is a rugged, bicone antenna. Familiarity with its components is essential for assembly under low-light or high-stress conditions.
subPoints: Feedcone: The central hub where the elements attach and the signal is fed.
Antenna Elements: The screw-in rods that form the bicone shape.
Mast Sections: Lightweight aluminum tubes used to elevate the antenna.
Guy Ropes and Stakes: Essential for stabilizing the antenna at its full 30-foot height.

mainPoints.title: Assembly of the Bicone Head
mainPoints.content: The bicone head is the heart of the antenna. It must be assembled correctly to ensure the antenna is resonant across the 30-88 MHz VHF band.
subPoints: Ensure all elements are fully seated into the feedcone to prevent signal loss.
Check the frequency configuration; the OE-254 is broadband and does not require tuning, but physical integrity is paramount.
Attach the coaxial cable to the feedcone before elevating the mast.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your platoon is tasked with providing a retransmission site on a designated hilltop. You must site and erect the OE-254 to ensure the company net maintains connectivity across the valley floor.
steps: Analyze the terrain to identify the highest point with the clearest line-of-sight.
Unpack the OE-254 kit and verify all components are present.
Assemble the bicone antenna head by securely threading all elements into the feedcone.
Connect the RF cable to the feedcone and secure it to the mast.
Assemble the mast sections and raise the antenna using the guy ropes for stability.
Secure the guy ropes to stakes at the proper distance to ensure the mast is vertical and stable.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the importance of siting for LOS communications, identified the OE-254 components, and demonstrated the assembly of the bicone head and mast.
conclusion.closingStatement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier. By properly siting and erecting this antenna, you ensure that the commander's intent is heard clearly across the entire AO.

tlo.condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit and a requirement to provide VHF line-of-sight communications.
tlo.behavior: Demonstrate the installation of an OE-254 antenna.
tlo.standard: The antenna must be erected to its full height and secured to withstand environmental conditions while maintaining a clear line of sight to the receiving station per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Installation of standard antenna kits is a procedural application of technical manual instructions. Level 3 (Apply) reflects the requirement to perform the physical task in a field environment.

elos.condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit.
elos.behavior: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.
elos.standard: Including the feedcone, elements, mast sections, and guy ropes per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Inventory and identification are the first steps in VHF antenna employment.

elos.condition: Given a map and a requirement for VHF communications.
elos.behavior: Explain the siting considerations for a line-of-sight (LOS) antenna.
elos.standard: Identifying the impact of terrain, vegetation, and antenna height on signal propagation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: VHF antennas require specific siting to function; understanding LOS is critical for successful installation.

elos.condition: Given an OE-254 antenna kit and a site.
elos.behavior: Perform the assembly of the OE-254 bicone antenna head.
elos.standard: Ensuring all elements are fully seated and the feedcone is properly configured for the frequency range per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The assembly of the head is a distinct technical skill required before the mast can be erected.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a dense jungle or a deep urban canyon where your standard whip antenna cannot reach the distant station. Your mission depends on getting a SITREP out, but your primary antenna is broken or insufficient. By the end of this lesson, you will possess the 'black magic' of radio communications: the ability to turn a spool of field wire and some basic math into a high-performance antenna system that can reach across the battlespace.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for calculating, assembling, and employing field-expedient wire antennas using WD-1/TT field wire and improvised insulators.
objectives: TLO-043: Construct a field-expedient wire antenna.
ELO-116: Calculate the physical length of a wire antenna.
ELO-117: Assemble antenna components including the radiator, insulators, and feed line connections.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Length Calculation
mainPoints.content: To achieve resonance, an antenna must be cut to a specific length relative to its operating frequency. Per MCRP 3-40.3C Section III, the standard formula for a half-wave dipole is used to ensure the antenna efficiently radiates energy.
subPoints: Formula: 468 divided by the frequency in MHz equals the total length in feet.
For a half-wave dipole, this total length is then divided by two to create two equal elements (legs).
Accuracy is critical; even a few inches of error can result in high VSWR and potential damage to the radio set.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Component Integration
mainPoints.content: Construction requires the integration of the radiator (wire), insulators, and the feed line. Following MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 6, Marines must ensure mechanical strength and electrical conductivity.
subPoints: Use WD-1/TT field wire as the primary radiating element.
Insulators (improvised from plastic, glass, or dry wood) must be used at the ends and center to prevent the signal from grounding out.
Utilize the clove hitch or square knot to secure wire to insulators to prevent slipping under tension.
Electrical connections must be stripped of insulation and twisted tightly to ensure metal-to-metal contact.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team is established in a patrol base. You are assigned a frequency of 14.250 MHz and must establish a long-range HF link using a Half-Wave Dipole configuration. You have a spool of WD-1/TT, two plastic MRE spoons to use as insulators, and a multi-tool.
steps: Calculate the total antenna length (468 / 14.250).
Measure and cut two equal lengths of WD-1/TT wire.
Attach the wire ends to the improvised insulators using clove hitches.
Strip 2 inches of insulation from the center ends and connect them to the coaxial feed line or radio adapter.
Hoist the antenna into the air using para-cord, ensuring it is clear of metal obstructions.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the mathematical requirements for antenna resonance and the physical assembly techniques required by MCRP 3-40.3C. Remember: 468/Freq is your baseline for success.
conclusion.closingStatement: A Marine's ability to innovate with available materials is a force multiplier. Don't let a broken whip antenna be the reason your unit loses comms.

tlo.condition: Given field wire (WD-1/TT), insulators, a radio set, and a requirement to establish communications when standard antennas are unavailable.
tlo.behavior: Construct a field-expedient wire antenna.
tlo.standard: The antenna must achieve resonance at the assigned frequency and enable communication (such as a Half-Wave Dipole or Inverted Vee) in accordance with MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires the Marine to synthesize knowledge of radio frequency theory, perform mathematical calculations for wire length, and use non-standard materials to create a functional system. Level 6 (Create) is required because the Marine is producing a new artifact from raw components.

elos.condition: Given a specific operating frequency and the formula for a half-wave dipole (468 / Frequency in MHz).
elos.behavior: Calculate the physical length of a wire antenna.
elos.standard: The calculation must be accurate to within one inch of the theoretical length required for resonance per MCRP 3-40.3C, Section III.
elos.justification: Calculating the specific length is a prerequisite mathematical application required before physical construction can begin.

elos.condition: Given field wire (WD-1/TT), insulators, and a multi-tool.
elos.behavior: Assemble antenna components including the radiator, insulators, and feed line connections.
elos.standard: Components must be securely joined using approved knots (such as the clove hitch or square knot) and electrical connections must be stripped and twisted to ensure metal-to-metal contact per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 6.
elos.justification: This is the component skill of physical assembly required to achieve the terminal objective of construction.

warnings: Verb "Assemble" is not in the standard Bloom's Taxonomy verb list. Consider using one of: Demonstrate, Perform, Calculate, Apply, Execute, Implement, Use

introduction.gainAttention: The most sophisticated radio in the world is nothing more than an expensive paperweight if the antenna system is compromised. In the field, antennas are snagged by trees, snapped by vehicles, or degraded by corrosion. Your ability to quickly identify the fault and apply a 'combat fix' is what keeps the command and control loop closed.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying common antenna faults and performing the Western Union splice to restore electrical and structural integrity to wire antennas.
objectives: TLO-044: Troubleshoot a damaged antenna system to restore functionality.
ELO-118: Identify common antenna system faults.
ELO-119: Perform a Western Union splice on broken antenna wire.

mainPoints.title: Identifying Antenna System Faults
mainPoints.content: Troubleshooting begins with a visual inspection and an understanding of how electrical faults manifest in radio performance. Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 6, operators must look for three primary issues.
subPoints: Shorts: Occur when the radiating element touches the ground or a metal structure, causing energy to bleed off.
Opens: A break in the wire or a loose connection that prevents the signal from reaching the antenna.
High VSWR (Voltage Standing Wave Ratio): Indicated by the radio's internal meter; usually caused by incorrect length or poor grounding.

mainPoints.title: The Western Union Splice
mainPoints.content: When a wire antenna is severed, a simple knot is insufficient because it lacks electrical continuity. The Western Union splice is the military standard for repairing field wire (MCRP 3-40.3C, Page 6-2).
subPoints: Strip approximately 4-6 inches of insulation from both broken ends.
Twist the wires together tightly, ensuring at least five wraps on each side of the center.
The splice must be mechanically strong enough to withstand the tension of being hoisted.
Seal the connection with electrical or friction tape to prevent moisture from corroding the copper/steel strands.

practicalApplication.scenario: During a night move, a vehicle drove over your inverted-vee antenna's leg, snapping the WD-1/TT wire. Your radio is showing a 'Check Antenna' fault. You must restore the link immediately using your field repair kit.
steps: Locate the break in the wire through visual and tactile inspection.
Strip the insulation from both ends of the break using a multi-tool.
Perform a Western Union splice, ensuring the wraps are tight and the connection is rigid.
Apply electrical tape to the splice, overlapping the insulation on both sides.
Re-tension the antenna and perform a radio check to verify the fault is cleared.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the symptoms of shorts and opens and mastered the Western Union splice. These skills ensure that antenna damage is only a temporary setback, not a mission failure.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the fleet, you won't always have a fresh antenna in the warehouse. Master these repairs now so you can keep the net alive when it matters most.

tlo.condition: Given a damaged antenna (whip or wire) and a field repair kit.
tlo.behavior: Troubleshoot a damaged antenna system to restore functionality.
tlo.standard: Electrical continuity and structural integrity must be restored to allow for immediate resumption of communications per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Repairing damaged equipment requires the Marine to first analyze the system to identify the point of failure before applying a fix. Level 4 (Analyze) is appropriate for diagnostic tasks involving system restoration.

elos.condition: Given a radio system with degraded performance and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Identify common antenna system faults.
elos.standard: Must correctly identify symptoms of shorts, opens, and poor grounding that lead to high Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 6.
elos.justification: Understanding the symptoms of failure is the first step in the troubleshooting (analysis) process.

errors: Verb "Identify" is a Level 1 verb, but Level 2 was specified. Approved verbs for Level 2: Describe, Explain, Summarize, Classify, Discuss, Interpret

elos.condition: Given a damaged wire antenna and a field repair kit.
elos.behavior: Perform a Western Union splice on broken antenna wire.
elos.standard: The splice must be mechanically sound and wrapped with friction tape or electrical tape to prevent moisture entry per MCRP 3-40.3C, Page 6-2.
elos.justification: Physical repair of the radiator is a necessary skill to restore functionality during troubleshooting.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a hide site, your radio is functioning perfectly, and your antenna is cut to the exact frequency, yet your signal is barely breaking the squelch of the receiving station. In many tactical environments, the difference between a failed mission and successful communication is the quality of your ground. Without a low-resistance path to the earth, your radio energy has nowhere to go, effectively turning your equipment into an expensive paperweight.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for establishing a field-expedient ground, the environmental considerations for site selection, and the physical preparation of materials to ensure maximum conductivity.
objectives: TLO-045: Demonstrate the fabrication of a field-expedient ground connection.
ELO-120: Explain the requirements for a field-expedient ground.
ELO-121: Prepare the contact surfaces for a ground connection.

mainPoints.title: Grounding Requirements and Environmental Safety
mainPoints.content: According to MCRP 3-40.3C, Section II, a ground must provide a low-resistance path to the earth to support efficient radio wave radiation.
subPoints: Resistance: The goal is the lowest resistance possible; high resistance leads to power loss and potential equipment damage.
Moisture: Conductivity is directly related to soil moisture. In dry conditions, grounding effectiveness decreases significantly.
Environmental Safety: Ground rods must never be installed near drinking water supplies to prevent contamination of the water table.

mainPoints.title: Surface Preparation and Oxidation Prevention
mainPoints.content: Electrical conductivity is only as good as the point of contact. Metal-to-metal contact is mandatory for a low-resistance bond.
subPoints: Cleaning: Use sandpaper or a scraper to remove all paint, rust, and oxidation from the ground rod and the wire.
Bare Metal: Surfaces must be polished to bare metal to ensure maximum surface area contact.
Protection: Once the connection is made using a clamp or wire wrap, it should be taped to prevent moisture from causing rapid oxidation.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit has established a temporary patrol base in a wooded area. You are tasked with setting up a manpack radio for long-range HF communication. You have a length of copper wire and a galvanized steel pipe to use as a ground.
steps: Identify a location for the ground rod that is away from known water sources.
Drive the pipe into the ground, seeking moist soil if available.
Use a scraper or sandpaper to clean a 2-inch section of the pipe until bare metal is visible.
Clean the end of the ground wire to remove any insulation or corrosion.
Secure the wire to the cleaned section of the pipe using a ground clamp or tight wire wrap.
Seal the connection with electrical tape to prevent oxidation.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the necessity of low-resistance grounds, the impact of soil moisture, and the critical requirement to protect water supplies. We also demonstrated the proper method for cleaning contact surfaces to ensure a solid electrical bond.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who ignores the ground is an operator who ignores their primary weapon system. Master these field-expedient techniques to ensure your message gets through, regardless of the terrain.

tlo.condition: Given a radio system requiring a ground, a pipe or conduit to serve as a ground rod, ground wire, ground clamp, cleaning materials (sandpaper or scraper), and tape.
tlo.behavior: Demonstrate the fabrication of a field-expedient ground connection.
tlo.standard: The connection must be low-resistance, support radio wave radiation, prevent oxidation, and be installed without contaminating nearby drinking water supplies per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: While this involves fabrication, it follows a specific technical procedure to ensure electrical safety and signal propagation. Level 3 (Apply) is the correct level for implementing these technical standards using available materials.

elos.condition: Given a tactical scenario and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Explain the requirements for a field-expedient ground.
elos.standard: Explanation must include the necessity for low resistance, the role of moisture in conductivity, and the prohibition of grounding near drinking water per MCRP 3-40.3C, Section II.
elos.justification: Marines must understand the 'why' and the safety constraints (water contamination) before physical implementation.

elos.condition: Given a ground rod (pipe), ground wire, and cleaning materials.
elos.behavior: Prepare the contact surfaces for a ground connection.
elos.standard: Surfaces must be scraped or sanded to bare metal to remove paint, rust, or oxidation to ensure a low-resistance electrical bond per MCRP 3-40.3C, Page 2-21.
elos.justification: Surface preparation is a critical skill for ensuring the effectiveness of the ground connection.

warnings: Verb "Prepare" is not in the standard Bloom's Taxonomy verb list. Consider using one of: Demonstrate, Perform, Calculate, Apply, Execute, Implement, Use

introduction.gainAttention: What do you do when the ground is too rocky to drive a rod, or you are operating in a desert where the sand is so dry it acts as an insulator? In these environments, a traditional ground is impossible. To maintain communications, you must create an artificial ground—a counterpoise—to complete your radio circuit.
introduction.overview: This lesson defines the counterpoise, explains its role in high-resistance soil environments, and details the physical installation requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-046: Perform the installation of an antenna counterpoise.
ELO-122: Define the term 'counterpoise' and its purpose in a radio circuit.
ELO-123: Describe the physical requirements for a counterpoise installation.

mainPoints.title: The Counterpoise Concept
mainPoints.content: A counterpoise is a substitute for a ground connection used when the earth's resistance is too high for a standard ground rod to be effective.
subPoints: Purpose: It acts as the 'other half' of the antenna system, providing a return path for RF current.
Application: Essential in desert, rocky terrain, or when operating from the upper floors of buildings.

mainPoints.title: Physical Installation Standards
mainPoints.content: MCRP 3-40.3C specifies strict physical parameters to ensure the counterpoise functions correctly without losing energy to the earth.
subPoints: Insulation: Unlike a ground rod, a counterpoise must be insulated from the ground. It should be suspended above the earth or laid on insulators.
Sizing: The counterpoise must be at least equal to, or larger than, the physical size of the antenna it is supporting.
Connection: The counterpoise wire must be connected directly to the radio's ground terminal or the antenna's matching network ground.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are operating in a rocky plateau where the soil depth is less than 3 inches. You are deploying a vertical whip antenna and must install a counterpoise to ensure the radio can tune the frequency.
steps: Measure the length of your primary antenna radiator.
Cut a counterpoise wire that is at least the same length as the antenna (preferably slightly longer).
Connect one end of the counterpoise wire to the ground terminal of the radio or antenna base.
Lay the wire out away from the radio, ensuring it is supported by insulators (like dry wood or plastic) to keep it from making direct contact with the high-resistance soil.
Ensure the wire is clear of foot traffic to prevent trip hazards and signal interference.

conclusion.summary: A counterpoise is your primary alternative when the earth refuses to provide a natural ground. By ensuring it is properly sized and insulated, you can maintain a high-performance radio circuit in the most difficult geographical conditions.
conclusion.closingStatement: Adaptability is a hallmark of Marine Corps communications. When the ground fails you, the counterpoise ensures the mission continues.

tlo.condition: Given an antenna system, wire, and insulators, in an environment where a direct ground connection is impractical due to high soil resistance.
tlo.behavior: Perform the installation of an antenna counterpoise.
tlo.standard: Ensuring the counterpoise is at least equal to or larger than the antenna size, insulated from the ground, and connected to the radio system ground terminal per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Installation of a counterpoise is a procedural, hands-on task that requires the Marine to apply technical steps in a field environment to achieve a specific physical result.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a classroom environment.
elos.behavior: Define the term 'counterpoise' and its purpose in a radio circuit.
elos.standard: Accurately stating that it is a substitute for a ground connection when soil resistance is high, per MCRP 3-40.3C Section II.
elos.justification: Marines must first recall the definition and purpose of the equipment before they can perform the installation.

elos.condition: Given a list of antenna components and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Describe the physical requirements for a counterpoise installation.
elos.standard: Including requirements for insulation from the ground and size relative to the antenna per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding the physical constraints (insulation and size) is a prerequisite to successful physical execution.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes tactical environment. You have the correct frequency, your radio is powered on, and you are within range, but your transmission is barely audible through a wall of static. You check your connections, but everything looks solid. The culprit? Your antenna is oriented horizontally while the receiving station is vertical. In the world of radio communications, being 'off' by 90 degrees can mean the difference between a clear command and a total communications failure.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of antenna polarization, the distinction between vertical and horizontal orientations, and how to select the correct polarization based on the transmission type and tactical environment.
objectives: TLO-047: Apply antenna polarization requirements.
ELO-124: Define vertical and horizontal polarization.
ELO-125: Explain the advantages of vertical versus horizontal polarization for different transmission types.

mainPoints.title: Defining Polarization
mainPoints.content: Polarization is determined by the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) of the electromagnetic wave relative to the earth's surface. If the E-plane is perpendicular to the earth, it is vertically polarized. If it is parallel, it is horizontally polarized.
subPoints: The physical position of the antenna radiator determines the polarization.
Vertical antennas (like whips) produce vertical polarization.
Horizontal antennas (like dipoles suspended between trees) produce horizontal polarization.

mainPoints.title: Tactical Application of Polarization
mainPoints.content: The choice of polarization significantly impacts signal propagation and noise reception. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, specific transmission types favor specific orientations.
subPoints: Vertical Polarization: Preferred for ground wave transmission as it follows the earth's curvature more effectively and is standard for mobile/whip antennas.
Horizontal Polarization: Often used for sky wave (HF) to reduce the pickup of man-made noise, which is predominantly vertically polarized.
Cross-Polarization: When the transmitting and receiving antennas have different polarizations, a significant signal loss (up to 20dB or more) occurs.

practicalApplication.scenario: A Marine radio team is tasked with establishing a long-range HF sky wave link back to the COC while operating in an urban environment with high man-made electrical noise. They have a wire antenna kit and two masts.
steps: Identify the transmission type (Sky wave).
Determine the noise environment (High man-made noise).
Select the appropriate polarization (Horizontal) to minimize noise and optimize the sky wave path.
Orient the wire antenna parallel to the ground to achieve horizontal polarization.

conclusion.summary: We have defined polarization as the orientation of the E-plane and discussed why vertical is used for ground waves while horizontal is often preferred for sky waves to mitigate noise.
conclusion.closingStatement: Understanding polarization ensures that your signal reaches its destination with maximum strength. Do not let a 90-degree mistake compromise your mission.

tlo.condition: Given a communication mission, a specified frequency band (LF, MF, HF, VHF, or UHF), and tactical antennas.
tlo.behavior: Apply antenna polarization requirements.
tlo.standard: To optimize signal strength and radiation patterns based on frequency and transmission type (ground wave vs. sky wave) per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires the Marine to use knowledge of wave propagation and frequency characteristics to make a tactical decision (selecting the correct polarization) for a specific mission scenario.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and diagrams of electromagnetic waves.
elos.behavior: Define vertical and horizontal polarization.
elos.standard: Identifying the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) relative to the earth's surface per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the basic types of polarization is required before application to tactical scenarios.

elos.condition: Given a tactical scenario involving ground wave and sky wave propagation.
elos.behavior: Explain the advantages of vertical versus horizontal polarization for different transmission types.
elos.standard: Correctly identifying that vertical polarization is preferred for ground wave and horizontal is often used for sky wave to reduce man-made noise per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Comprehending the 'why' behind polarization choice is necessary for the Marine to 'apply' requirements in the TLO.

introduction.gainAttention: In a survival or tactical scenario, your issued antenna might break or be lost. As a communicator, you must be able to fabricate an antenna from a spool of WD-1/TT field wire. However, if you cut that wire to a random length, your radio's energy will reflect back into the transmitter, potentially frying the internal components and ensuring your message is never heard. Precision in length is precision in lethality.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the mathematical formulas and procedures required to calculate the physical length of half-wave and quarter-wave antennas to ensure resonance at a specific frequency.
objectives: TLO-048: Calculate the physical length of the antenna wire.
ELO-126: Identify the standard formula for calculating a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-127: Calculate the physical length of a quarter-wave vertical antenna.

mainPoints.title: The Half-Wave Dipole Formula
mainPoints.content: To achieve resonance, an antenna must be cut to a specific fraction of the wavelength. For a half-wave dipole, the standard formula accounts for the velocity factor of wire.
subPoints: Formula: Length (in feet) = 468 / Frequency (in MHz).
This formula provides the total length of the dipole from end to end.
Example: For 10 MHz, the length is 46.8 feet.

mainPoints.title: The Quarter-Wave Vertical Formula
mainPoints.content: A quarter-wave antenna (often used for whips or ground-plane antennas) is half the length of a dipole for the same frequency.
subPoints: Formula: Length (in feet) = 234 / Frequency (in MHz).
This represents the length of the vertical radiator element.
Accuracy is critical; calculations should be within a 1% margin of error to maintain a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

practicalApplication.scenario: You are assigned a frequency of 14.250 MHz. You need to construct a field-expedient half-wave dipole and a quarter-wave vertical antenna using field wire.
steps: Apply the half-wave formula: 468 / 14.250 = 32.84 feet.
Apply the quarter-wave formula: 234 / 14.250 = 16.42 feet.
Measure the wire using a tape measure, ensuring no kinks or loops.
Cut the wire and prepare the center insulator for the dipole or the base mount for the vertical.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the critical formulas for antenna construction: 468/f for half-wave and 234/f for quarter-wave antennas.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ability to calculate and cut an antenna to the exact frequency is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Master these numbers, and you will never be without a way to reach the net.

tlo.condition: Given a specific operating frequency, a requirement for a half-wave or quarter-wave antenna, and reference material.
tlo.behavior: Calculate the physical length of the antenna wire.
tlo.standard: Ensuring resonance at the assigned frequency by applying the standard formula (468/frequency for half-wave) and accounting for velocity factors per MCRP 3-40.3C Section III.
tlo.justification: Calculation is a direct application of mathematical formulas to technical requirements, falling under the Apply level of Bloom's Taxonomy.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a specific frequency.
elos.behavior: Identify the standard formula for calculating a half-wave dipole antenna.
elos.standard: Correctly stating the formula as 468 divided by the frequency in megahertz to find length in feet per MCRP 3-40.3C Section III.
elos.justification: Recalling the mathematical constant and formula structure is the first step in the calculation process.

elos.condition: Given a requirement for a quarter-wave antenna and an operating frequency.
elos.behavior: Calculate the physical length of a quarter-wave vertical antenna.
elos.standard: Applying the formula (234/frequency) to determine the length in feet within a 1% margin of error per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Calculating a component part (quarter-wave) supports the broader TLO of calculating various antenna lengths.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes tactical environment, and your life depends on a single transmission. You key the handset, but the distant station hears nothing but static. You have the right frequency and the right power, but your antenna is pointed 30 degrees off-target. In the world of radio communications, 'close enough' is a failure. Proper antenna orientation is the difference between a clear command and a lost connection.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of antenna radiation patterns, the difference between omnidirectional and directional antennas, and the technical process of calculating and applying an azimuth to ensure maximum signal-to-noise ratio.
objectives: Identify the radiation patterns for omnidirectional and directional antennas (ELO-128).
Calculate the azimuth for antenna orientation (ELO-129).
Demonstrate antenna orientation for maximum signal strength (TLO-049).

mainPoints.title: Radiation Patterns and Directionality
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 2, Section I, radiation patterns represent the energy distribution of an antenna in space. Understanding these patterns allows an operator to predict where the signal will be strongest.
subPoints: Omnidirectional Antennas: Radiate energy equally in all directions (360 degrees) on the horizontal plane, typically used for mobile operations or net control stations.
Directional Antennas: Concentrate energy in a specific direction, providing 'gain' toward the distant station while reducing interference from other directions.
Nulls and Lobes: Lobes are areas of high signal strength; nulls are areas of little to no signal. Operators must align the main lobe with the distant station.

mainPoints.title: Azimuth Calculation and Orientation
mainPoints.content: To achieve maximum signal transfer, the antenna must be physically aligned with the distant station's location using a calculated azimuth.
subPoints: Determining Grid Azimuth: Use the grid coordinates of the local and distant stations to determine the line of bearing.
Magnetic Conversion: Apply the G-M angle to convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth for use with a lensatic compass.
Physical Alignment: Align the antenna's boom or main radiating element perpendicular to or in line with the azimuth, depending on the specific antenna type (e.g., Dipole vs. Yagi).

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a reconnaissance team. You are tasked with establishing a point-to-point HF link with the Combat Operations Center (COC) located 50 miles away at Grid 12S VF 1234 5678. You are currently at Grid 12S VF 9876 5432.
steps: Identify the appropriate antenna type (Directional) for the distance and mission.
Calculate the grid azimuth from your position to the COC.
Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth using the local G-M angle.
Use a lensatic compass to identify the line of bearing.
Physically orient the antenna system so the main radiation lobe is aligned within +/- 3 degrees of the calculated azimuth.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the identification of radiation patterns and the precise calculation of azimuths. By mastering these skills, you ensure that the energy produced by your radio is focused where it is needed most.
conclusion.closingStatement: Precision in orientation is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Do not let a lack of attention to detail be the reason your message fails to get through.

tlo.condition: Given a tactical radio, an antenna system, and the location of a distant station.
tlo.behavior: Demonstrate antenna orientation for maximum signal strength.
tlo.standard: Achieving the highest possible signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio and establishing a reliable communications circuit by aligning the radiation pattern and adjusting take-off angles per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Orientation is a performance-based task where the Marine must execute physical adjustments to equipment based on azimuth and propagation variables.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and various antenna radiation pattern diagrams.
elos.behavior: Identify the radiation patterns for omnidirectional and directional antennas.
elos.standard: Correctly matching the pattern to the antenna type to ensure understanding of signal directionality per Chapter 2, Section I.
elos.justification: Knowledge of radiation patterns is a prerequisite for physical orientation of the antenna.

elos.condition: Given a lensatic compass and the grid coordinates of a distant station.
elos.behavior: Calculate the azimuth for antenna orientation.
elos.standard: Determining the correct line of bearing within +/- 3 degrees to facilitate maximum signal transfer per Chapter 2, Section IV.
elos.justification: Calculating the azimuth is a necessary skill step before the physical demonstration of orientation.

introduction.gainAttention: Many operators believe the antenna is just the wire or the whip they see above ground. In reality, for many tactical antennas, the ground beneath your feet is the 'other half' of the antenna system. If you have a poor ground, you have a broken antenna. Without proper grounding, your radio's efficiency can drop by over 50%, wasting battery life and killing your range.
introduction.overview: This lesson explains the theory of grounded antennas, the impact of soil conductivity, and the practical steps for installing grounding stakes and counterpoise systems to maximize radiation efficiency.
objectives: Describe the theory of grounded antennas and the impact of Earth conductivity (ELO-130).
Install a counterpoise system for a tactical antenna (ELO-131).
Perform the installation of an antenna grounding system (TLO-050).

mainPoints.title: Grounded Antenna Theory
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 2, Section II, the Earth acts as a reflecting surface for radio waves. A grounded antenna uses the Earth to create a 'mirror image' of the radiating element.
subPoints: Circuit Completion: The ground system provides a low-resistance path to complete the RF circuit.
Earth Conductivity: Moist, loamy soil provides excellent conductivity, while dry, sandy, or rocky soil provides poor conductivity, requiring artificial ground enhancements.
Safety: Proper grounding also protects equipment and personnel from lightning strikes and static buildup.

mainPoints.title: Grounding Methods and Counterpoises
mainPoints.content: When the natural Earth conductivity is insufficient, operators must use artificial means to improve the ground connection.
subPoints: Ground Stakes: Driven into the Earth to reach moist soil; multiple stakes can be connected in parallel to reduce resistance.
Counterpoise: A network of wires (radials) balanced above the ground. It is used when a true Earth ground is impossible to achieve (e.g., on top of a building or in extremely rocky soil).
Installation: Radials should be spread out like spokes on a wheel, extending from the base of the antenna.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are setting up an HF antenna in a desert environment where the soil is extremely dry and sandy. The radio is struggling to tune, and signal reports are weak. You must install a counterpoise system to establish a reliable circuit.
steps: Inspect the antenna base and identify the grounding terminal.
Unroll the counterpoise radial wires from the kit.
Lay out the radials in a symmetrical pattern around the antenna base, ensuring they are fully extended.
Secure the radials to the ground using stakes or weights to prevent movement.
Connect the central hub of the counterpoise to the radio's ground terminal using the shortest possible lead to minimize resistance.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed how the Earth completes the antenna circuit and how to compensate for poor soil using counterpoise systems. A well-grounded antenna is an efficient antenna.
conclusion.closingStatement: Never settle for a marginal ground. Taking the extra ten minutes to properly install your grounding system can be the difference between mission success and total communication blackout.

tlo.condition: Given a radio set, an antenna, and grounding materials (ground stakes, wire, or counterpoise kit).
tlo.behavior: Perform the installation of an antenna grounding system.
tlo.standard: Improving antenna efficiency and radiation characteristics by selecting the appropriate grounding method and ensuring low resistance to Earth per MCRP 3-40.3C Section II.
tlo.justification: This is a procedural task involving the physical assessment of soil and the installation of hardware to meet technical performance standards.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Describe the theory of grounded antennas and the impact of Earth conductivity on radiation.
elos.standard: Explaining how a ground system acts as a reflecting surface to complete the circuit per Chapter 2, Section II.
elos.justification: Understanding the 'why' of grounding is essential for selecting the correct method (stake vs. counterpoise) in the field.

elos.condition: Given a radio set and a counterpoise kit.
elos.behavior: Install a counterpoise system for a tactical antenna.
elos.standard: Ensuring all radial wires are extended and properly connected to the antenna base to provide an artificial ground per Chapter 2, Section II.
elos.justification: A component skill of the overall grounding TLO, specifically addressing environments where ground stakes are ineffective.

title: Frequency Band Analysis and Propagation Modes

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are a Radio Operator in a mountainous region. Your unit is 50 miles away, separated by a massive ridgeline. You try to key the handset on your VHF radio, but all you get is static. Understanding the electromagnetic spectrum isn't just for scientists—it's the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence. Today, we learn how to choose the right frequency to 'punch through' the terrain.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the characteristics of the HF, VHF, and UHF frequency bands and the two primary modes of radio wave propagation: Ground Wave and Sky Wave.
objectives: ELO-132: State the frequency ranges and characteristics for the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
ELO-133: Differentiate between Ground Wave and Sky Wave propagation modes.
ELO-134: Select the optimal frequency band for a specific communication path.

mainPoints.title: The Military Radio Frequency Spectrum
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Figure 1-1, tactical radios operate within three primary bands, each with distinct boundaries and behaviors.
subPoints: High Frequency (HF): 3 MHz to 30 MHz. Capable of long-range communication via sky wave.
Very High Frequency (VHF): 30 MHz to 300 MHz. Standard for FM tactical communications; primarily Line of Sight (LOS).
Ultra High Frequency (UHF): 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Used for LOS, ground-to-air, and satellite communications (SATCOM).

mainPoints.title: Propagation Fundamentals
mainPoints.content: Radio waves travel from the transmitter to the receiver in two primary ways depending on frequency and antenna type.
subPoints: Ground Wave: Follows the curvature of the Earth. Best at lower frequencies; affected by terrain and soil conductivity.
Sky Wave: Radiates upward to the ionosphere and is reflected back to Earth. Enables 'over-the-horizon' communication.
Skip Zone: The area between the end of the ground wave and the point where the first sky wave returns to Earth where no signal is received.

mainPoints.title: Frequency Selection Criteria
mainPoints.content: Selecting the correct band requires balancing distance, terrain, and atmospheric conditions per MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1.
subPoints: Short range (0-30 miles): VHF/UHF Ground Wave is typically preferred.
Medium to Long range (30-1500+ miles): HF Sky Wave is required.
Obstructions: If a mountain blocks LOS, HF Sky Wave or NVIS must be utilized regardless of short distance.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are assigned to a reconnaissance team 85 miles from the Combat Operations Center (COC). You have a PRC-150 (HF) and a PRC-117G (VHF/UHF). There is a mountain range between you and the COC.
steps: Identify the distance to the distant station (85 miles).
Consult MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1 to determine if VHF Ground Wave can cover 85 miles over mountainous terrain.
Determine the propagation mode required to clear the mountain (Sky Wave).
Select the appropriate frequency band (HF) and justify based on the 'skip' requirements.

conclusion.summary: We have defined the MHz boundaries for HF, VHF, and UHF bands and analyzed how Ground Waves and Sky Waves behave. Selecting the right band is the first step in establishing a reliable communication link.
conclusion.closingStatement: The mission depends on your ability to analyze the environment and select the right tool for the job. Don't let the terrain dictate your success; let your knowledge of propagation ensure the message gets through.

tlo.condition: Given a mission requirement, distance to the distant station, and MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1 (Frequency Range Characteristics).
tlo.behavior: Analyze frequency bands and propagation modes for a communication path.
tlo.standard: To select the appropriate frequency (HF, VHF, or UHF) and propagation mode (Ground Wave or Sky Wave) that maintains a continuous link based on distance and terrain obstructions per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The task requires the Marine to evaluate multiple variables (distance, terrain, and frequency characteristics) and differentiate between propagation modes to determine the optimal solution for a specific mission requirement.

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: State the frequency ranges and characteristics for the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
elos.standard: Accurately identifying the megahertz (MHz) boundaries for each band per Chapter 1, Figure 1-1.
elos.justification: Fundamental knowledge required before analyzing which band is appropriate for a specific distance.

elos.condition: Given a communication scenario involving varying distances and atmospheric conditions.
elos.behavior: Differentiate between Ground Wave and Sky Wave propagation modes.
elos.standard: Explaining the limitations of each mode regarding distance and the 'skip zone' per Chapter 1, Propagation Fundamentals.
elos.justification: Analysis of propagation modes is critical for determining if a link will be successful over a given distance.

elos.condition: Given a mission distance and MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1.
elos.behavior: Select the optimal frequency band for a specific communication path.
elos.standard: Choosing the band that provides the most reliable link based on the distance to the distant station per the Frequency Range Characteristics table.
elos.justification: This is the application of the analysis required in the TLO, moving from theory to decision-making.
