introduction.gainAttention: You are in a 'skip zone'—too far for ground wave to reach, but too close for a standard sky wave to 'skip' back down to you. You are effectively in a communications black hole. NVIS is the technique that allows us to fire a radio wave straight up and have it drop back down like a mortar round, filling that gap and ensuring 100% connectivity in the toughest terrain.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the definition of NVIS, the critical relationship between frequency and the ionosphere, and the specific antennas required for NVIS operations.
objectives: ELO-135: Define Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
ELO-136: Explain the relationship between the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and NVIS propagation.
ELO-137: Identify NVIS-capable antennas.

mainPoints.title: NVIS Theory and Definition
mainPoints.content: NVIS is a technique using high-angle radiation to provide regional radio coverage (0-300 miles) per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 4.
subPoints: Radiation Angle: Uses take-off angles of 60 to 90 degrees.
Coverage: Eliminates the skip zone, providing 'umbrella' coverage rather than a directional beam.
Tactical Advantage: Allows communication from deep valleys or behind dense vegetation.

mainPoints.title: Frequency Selection and the MUF
mainPoints.content: Success in NVIS depends entirely on selecting a frequency that the ionosphere will reflect at a steep angle.
subPoints: Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF): The highest frequency that will be reflected back to Earth. Frequencies above the MUF will pass through the ionosphere into space.
Critical Frequency: For NVIS, the operating frequency must be below the MUF (typically between 2 and 12 MHz).
Diurnal Changes: The MUF changes based on the time of day (higher during the day, lower at night).

mainPoints.title: NVIS Antennas
mainPoints.content: Standard vertical whip antennas are poor for NVIS because they radiate energy toward the horizon, not upward.
subPoints: AS-2259/GR: The primary tactical NVIS antenna, featuring crossed dipoles.
Half-Wave Dipole: When mounted at low heights (1/8 to 1/4 wavelength above ground), it directs energy vertically.
Field Expedients: Bending a vehicle whip antenna horizontally (NVIS 'slap' or 'tie-down') can facilitate high-angle radiation.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your platoon is located in a deep ravine. You must establish an HF link with a unit 40 miles away. You have a PRC-150, a 10-foot whip, and a wire antenna kit.
steps: Determine the MUF for the current time of day using provided signal data.
Select an operating frequency approximately 10-20% below the MUF.
Configure the wire antenna as a horizontal half-wave dipole at a height of approximately 15-20 feet to maximize vertical radiation.
Verify the radio's internal coupler achieves a tune, ensuring the high-angle radiation path is established.

conclusion.summary: NVIS is a vital HF technique that uses high-angle radiation and frequencies below the MUF to provide regional coverage and overcome terrain masking.
conclusion.closingStatement: Mastering NVIS means you are never truly 'cut off' by the terrain. By understanding the ionosphere and proper antenna height, you can maintain the link when every other system fails.

tlo.condition: Given an HF radio set, a wire antenna, and a requirement to communicate within a skip zone.
tlo.behavior: Demonstrate antenna configuration for Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
tlo.standard: Ensuring the antenna height is adjusted to achieve a high angle of incidence and a frequency is selected below the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) to establish communication within the skip zone per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This is a procedural application of theory where the Marine must execute specific physical adjustments and settings to achieve a technical result in a field environment.

elos.condition: Given a student handout and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Define Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
elos.standard: Accurately describing the use of high-angle radiation to provide communication in the skip zone per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the propagation method is a prerequisite for physical antenna configuration.

elos.condition: Given a scenario involving frequency selection for HF communications.
elos.behavior: Explain the relationship between the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and NVIS propagation.
elos.standard: Ensuring the selected frequency is below the MUF to allow for ionospheric reflection back to the skip zone per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding frequency constraints is critical for the 'frequency selection' portion of the TLO standard.

elos.condition: Given a list of HF antennas and technical specifications.
elos.behavior: Identify NVIS-capable antennas.
elos.standard: Selecting antennas such as the AS-2259/GR or half-wave dipoles at specific heights that support high-angle radiation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The Marine must be able to select the correct equipment before demonstrating configuration.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a hide site with a perfect line of sight to your distant end, yet your radio is overheating and your signal is barely breaking squelch. You are literally wasting your transmitter's power by turning it into heat in the dirt. Proper grounding isn't just a safety check; it is the difference between a clear transmission and a fried circuit card.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the critical requirements for grounding tactical antenna systems, including the purpose of grounding, identification of necessary hardware, and the impact of soil resistance on radio performance.
objectives: TLO-053: Perform grounding of an antenna system.
ELO-138: State the purpose of grounding an antenna system.
ELO-139: Identify grounding hardware components.
ELO-140: Describe the effects of ground resistance on radio performance.

mainPoints.title: Purpose and Principles of Grounding
mainPoints.content: Grounding provides a low-impedance path to the earth, which is essential for the efficient radiation of electromagnetic energy.
subPoints: Minimizing ground resistance ensures that the maximum amount of RF energy is radiated rather than lost.
Prevents transmitter power dissipation as heat, which protects internal components from damage (MCRP 3-40.3C, 2-19).
Ensures operator safety by preventing chassis electrification.

mainPoints.title: Grounding Hardware and Installation
mainPoints.content: Standard USMC tactical radio kits include specific components designed to establish an effective ground.
subPoints: Grounding Stake: The primary interface with the earth.
Mallet: Used to drive the stake into the soil.
Grounding Strap/Wire: Connects the radio or antenna base to the stake.
Standard: The stake must be driven approximately one meter into the earth to reach consistent moisture levels and minimize resistance (MCRP 3-40.3C, 2-20).

mainPoints.title: Soil Conditions and Resistance
mainPoints.content: The effectiveness of a ground is highly dependent on the environment.
subPoints: Dry, sandy soil has high resistance, leading to significant energy loss.
Moist, loamy soil provides the best conductivity for tactical grounding.
Poor grounding leads to reduced signal strength and a higher probability of 'dead spots' in the communication link.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with establishing a VHF retransmission site on a dry ridgeline. You must ground the OE-254 antenna system to ensure maximum range and equipment longevity.
steps: Identify the grounding stake, strap, and mallet from the SL-3 kit.
Select a location for the stake as close to the antenna base as possible.
Drive the grounding stake into the earth to a depth of approximately one meter.
Clean the contact points on the stake and the antenna base.
Securely attach the grounding strap between the antenna base and the stake.
Verify the connection is tight and free of debris.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the necessity of grounding to prevent heat dissipation and minimize resistance, the hardware required, and the standard of driving stakes to a one-meter depth.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who neglects the ground is an operator who neglects the mission. Ensure your ground is deep and your connections are tight.

tlo.condition: Given a tactical radio, antenna, grounding stake, and mallet in a field environment.
tlo.behavior: Perform grounding of an antenna system.
tlo.standard: Ensuring the grounding stake is driven approximately one meter into the earth to minimize ground resistance and prevent transmitter power dissipation as heat per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This is a fundamental skill-based task requiring the execution of a standard procedure to meet a technical safety and performance requirement.

elos.condition: Given a student handout and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: State the purpose of grounding an antenna system.
elos.standard: Including the requirement to minimize ground resistance and prevent transmitter power dissipation as heat per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Foundational knowledge of why grounding is performed ensures procedural compliance.

elos.condition: Given a tactical radio and grounding components.
elos.behavior: Identify grounding hardware components.
elos.standard: Correcting identifying the grounding stake, mallet, and grounding strap/wire per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Component identification is a prerequisite for the performance of the task.

elos.condition: Given a description of various soil conditions and grounding requirements.
elos.behavior: Describe the effects of ground resistance on radio performance.
elos.standard: Explaining how poor grounding leads to energy loss and reduced signal strength per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding the 'why' behind the 1-meter depth standard supports proper field implementation.

introduction.gainAttention: In a modern tactical environment, the airwaves are crowded. From the hum of a generator to the buzz of overhead power lines, manmade noise can render a million-dollar radio system useless. As a communicator, you must know how to fight through the noise to get the message across.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying manmade noise sources and utilizing antenna polarization and placement to mitigate interference and improve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
objectives: TLO-054: Troubleshoot manmade noise interference.
ELO-141: Identify common sources of manmade noise.
ELO-142: Explain the impact of antenna polarization on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
ELO-143: Differentiate between horizontal and vertical polarization for noise mitigation.

mainPoints.title: Sources of Manmade Noise
mainPoints.content: Manmade noise is often the primary limiting factor for VHF and UHF communications in urban or developed areas.
subPoints: Power lines and transformers (constant hum/buzz).
Vehicle engines and generators (ignition noise).
Electronic devices, computers, and fluorescent lighting (broadband interference).
Other tactical radios in close proximity (cosite interference).

mainPoints.title: Polarization and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)
mainPoints.content: SNR is the ratio of the desired signal strength to the background noise level. Improving SNR is the goal of all troubleshooting.
subPoints: Matching polarization between the transmitter and receiver maximizes signal reception.
Changing polarization can 'reject' interfering signals if the noise source is polarized differently than the desired signal (MCRP 3-40.3C, 2-6).

mainPoints.title: Mitigation Strategies
mainPoints.content: When interference occurs, the operator has several tactical options to restore communications.
subPoints: Reorienting antenna polarization: Switching from vertical to horizontal can often drop the noise floor significantly.
Relocation: Moving the antenna just a few meters away from a noise source (like a generator) can improve SNR.
Narrowband antennas: Utilizing antennas that only accept a specific frequency range to reject out-of-band interference.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is operating near a civilian power substation. Your VHF net is experiencing heavy static, making voice comms unreadable. You are using a vertical whip antenna.
steps: Identify the likely source of interference (power lines).
Monitor the current signal-to-noise ratio on the radio display.
Reorient the antenna from vertical to horizontal polarization.
Coordinate with the distant end to ensure they also switch to horizontal polarization.
Evaluate the change in audio clarity and SNR.
If noise persists, relocate the antenna system to a position where terrain masks the noise source.

conclusion.summary: We have identified manmade noise sources and learned how to use antenna polarization and siting to improve the signal-to-noise ratio.
conclusion.closingStatement: Do not accept a noisy net as 'just the way it is.' Use your knowledge of polarization and siting to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.

tlo.condition: Given a tactical radio system experiencing interference from manmade noise sources.
tlo.behavior: Troubleshoot manmade noise interference.
tlo.standard: By reorienting antenna polarization, relocating equipment, or utilizing narrowband antennas to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and reject interfering signals per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Troubleshooting requires the Marine to diagnose the cause of a system failure (interference) and select the most effective mitigation strategy based on the specific environment.

elos.condition: Given a list of interference sources in a tactical environment.
elos.behavior: Identify common sources of manmade noise.
elos.standard: Categorizing sources such as power lines, engines, and electronic devices per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Troubleshooting begins with identifying the likely source of the problem.

elos.condition: Given a tactical radio system and interference scenario.
elos.behavior: Explain the impact of antenna polarization on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
elos.standard: Describing how matching or changing polarization can reject unwanted signals or improve desired signal reception per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding polarization is a key component of the troubleshooting standard in the TLO.

elos.condition: Given two different antenna configurations and a specific manmade noise source.
elos.behavior: Differentiate between horizontal and vertical polarization for noise mitigation.
elos.standard: Determining which polarization is less susceptible to specific types of manmade interference per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: This matches the cognitive level of the TLO and requires the Marine to analyze the environment to select a solution.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are deployed to a desert environment with extremely dry, sandy soil. You set up your vertical whip antenna, but your signal is weak and your radio is overheating due to high SWR. In this scenario, the earth is a poor conductor, and your antenna system is incomplete. Without a solid ground, your radio cannot push the signal out. Today, we will learn how to 'create' that ground where nature didn't provide one.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the theory, calculation, and construction of an artificial ground, known as a counterpoise, to ensure maximum radiation efficiency in poor soil conditions.
objectives: TLO-055: Construct an artificial ground (counterpoise).
ELO-144: Define the purpose and function of a counterpoise.
ELO-145: Calculate the required length for counterpoise radials.

mainPoints.title: Purpose and Function of a Counterpoise
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Section II, a counterpoise is a substitute for an earth ground. It is used when high resistance soil (sand, rock, or dry earth) prevents an effective ground connection.
subPoints: Acts as an artificial capacitance to ground.
Facilitates the flow of antenna current by providing a low-impedance return path.
Essential for vertical whip or monopole antennas to complete the electrical circuit.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Radial Length
mainPoints.content: To ensure resonance and maximum current flow, counterpoise radials must be cut to specific lengths based on the operating frequency.
subPoints: Standard calculation is based on a quarter-wavelength of the operating frequency.
Formula: 234 / Frequency (in MHz) = Length in feet.
Precision is critical: Radials must be within +/- 2 inches of the calculated length to maintain resonance.

mainPoints.title: Construction and Deployment
mainPoints.content: The physical layout of the counterpoise determines its effectiveness in minimizing impedance.
subPoints: Radials should be deployed at the antenna feed point, extending outward like spokes on a wheel.
Use conductive material such as copper wire or tactical WD-1/TT wire.
Ensure radials are elevated slightly or laid flat on the surface, depending on the specific antenna requirements.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are operating an HF radio at 7.5 MHz in a rocky environment. You must construct a counterpoise for your vertical whip antenna to establish communications with the COC.
steps: Identify the operating frequency (7.5 MHz).
Calculate the required radial length (234 / 7.5 = 31.2 feet).
Measure and cut four radials to 31 feet 2 inches.
Connect the radials to the antenna base (ground side of the mount).
Deploy radials in a 360-degree pattern around the antenna base.
Verify the connection is secure and provides a continuous electrical path.

conclusion.summary: We have defined the counterpoise as an artificial ground, calculated radial lengths to within 2 inches of resonance, and discussed the physical construction of the system.
conclusion.closingStatement: A Marine's ability to adapt to the environment is what wins battles. When the ground fails you, the counterpoise ensures your message still gets through.

tlo.condition: Given a vertical whip or monopole antenna, conductive material, and a tactical radio in an area with poor soil conductivity.
tlo.behavior: Construct an artificial ground (counterpoise).
tlo.standard: To provide an artificial ground that minimizes impedance and ensures maximum current flow for radiation by deploying radials or mesh at the antenna feed point per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The Marine must apply technical knowledge to build a physical component (the counterpoise) that enables the radio system to function effectively in a non-ideal environment.

errors: Verb "Construct" is a Level 6 verb, but Level 3 was specified. Approved verbs for Level 3: Demonstrate, Perform, Calculate, Apply, Execute, Implement, Use

elos.condition: Given MCRP 3-40.3C and a scenario involving poor soil conductivity.
elos.behavior: Define the purpose and function of a counterpoise.
elos.standard: Ensuring the definition includes the creation of an artificial capacitance to ground to facilitate current flow per MCRP 3-40.3C, Section II.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the theoretical purpose of a counterpoise is a prerequisite for its physical construction.

elos.condition: Given a specific operating frequency and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Calculate the required length for counterpoise radials.
elos.standard: To within +/- 2 inches of the length required for the specific frequency to ensure resonance per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The Marine must be able to determine the physical dimensions of the materials before construction can begin.

introduction.gainAttention: The most powerful radio and the most efficient antenna are useless if the connection between them is flawed. A loose connector or the wrong type of cable can cause up to 90% of your signal to be lost as heat before it ever reaches the antenna. Mastering transmission lines ensures your voice reaches the objective.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying transmission line types, understanding the role of baluns, and performing proper installation and weatherproofing of antenna interfaces.
objectives: TLO-056: Perform the installation of antenna transmission lines.
ELO-146: Identify types of transmission lines and their characteristics.
ELO-147: Explain the function of a balun in the transmission circuit.
ELO-148: Connect transmission line interfaces to the radio and antenna.

mainPoints.title: Types of Transmission Lines
mainPoints.content: MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 3 identifies three primary types of lines used in tactical environments.
subPoints: Coaxial Cable: Most common; shielded to prevent interference; 50-ohm impedance (e.g., RG-213).
Twin-Lead: Parallel conductors; lower loss than coax but susceptible to nearby metal objects.
Open-Wire: Two parallel wires with air insulation; highest efficiency for long-range HF.

mainPoints.title: The Function of a Balun
mainPoints.content: A 'Balun' (Balanced to Unbalanced) is a critical component when mixing different types of equipment.
subPoints: Matches an unbalanced line (coax) to a balanced antenna (dipole).
Prevents 'line radiation' where the cable itself becomes part of the antenna.
Maintains the intended radiation pattern of the antenna system.

mainPoints.title: Installation Standards
mainPoints.content: Proper physical connection is the final step in ensuring system integrity.
subPoints: All connectors must be hand-tight; do not use pliers which can damage threads.
Weatherproofing (using electrical tape or sealant) is required for long-term installations to prevent moisture ingress.
Ensure no sharp bends in the cable, which can change the impedance and cause signal loss.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with setting up a half-wave dipole antenna using a standard tactical transceiver and coaxial cable.
steps: Select the appropriate coaxial cable for the transceiver.
Identify the balun and attach it to the center of the dipole antenna.
Connect the coaxial cable to the unbalanced side of the balun.
Route the cable to the transceiver, avoiding sharp 90-degree bends.
Connect the cable to the radio's antenna port, ensuring it is hand-tight.
Apply weatherproofing tape to the outdoor balun-to-cable connection.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the characteristics of coax and wire lines, explained how baluns maintain radiation patterns, and practiced the standards for secure, weatherproof connections.
conclusion.closingStatement: Attention to detail in your connections is the difference between a clear transmission and total radio silence. Treat your transmission lines with the same care as your weapon system.

tlo.condition: Given a transceiver, antenna, transmission line, and necessary connectors/baluns.
tlo.behavior: Perform the installation of antenna transmission lines.
tlo.standard: To connect the transceiver to the antenna while minimizing energy loss and matching impedance per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires the physical execution of technical procedures to connect hardware components. Level 3 (Apply) is appropriate as the Marine must apply knowledge of connectors and impedance matching to a real-world equipment setup.

elos.behavior: Identify types of transmission lines and their characteristics.
elos.standard: Correcting identifying coaxial, twin-lead, and open-wire lines and their respective impedance properties per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 3.
elos.justification: Identification of the correct transmission line is necessary to ensure impedance matching during installation.

elos.behavior: Explain the function of a balun in the transmission circuit.
elos.standard: Describing how the balun maintains the radiation pattern and prevents line radiation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding the role of the balun is critical for troubleshooting and proper installation of balanced antenna systems.

elos.behavior: Connect transmission line interfaces to the radio and antenna.
elos.standard: Ensuring all connections are hand-tight, weatherproofed if required, and provide a continuous electrical path per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: This is the primary physical skill required to achieve the TLO of performing installation.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley with 2,000-foot ridgelines on all sides. Your standard whip antenna can't clear the terrain, and your distant station is only 50 miles away—too close for traditional skywave but too far for ground wave. This is the 'skip zone.' The AS-2259/GR is your solution, using Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to 'bounce' your signal off the ionosphere and straight back down, effectively turning the sky into your repeater.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the theory of NVIS propagation, the identification of AS-2259/GR components, and the step-by-step assembly of the antenna system to establish reliable HF communications in restrictive terrain.
objectives: TLO-057: Demonstrate the employment of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
ELO-149: Explain the concept of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
ELO-150: Identify all components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
ELO-151: Assemble the AS-2259/GR antenna mast and radiating elements.

mainPoints.title: NVIS Propagation Theory
mainPoints.content: NVIS is a technique used to provide reliable communications over a range of 0 to 300 miles. It utilizes a high take-off angle (near 90 degrees) to direct the signal to the ionosphere, where it is reflected back to Earth at a similar angle.
subPoints: Overcomes terrain obstructions like mountains or dense vegetation.
Eliminates the 'skip zone' where ground waves die out and skywaves have not yet returned.
Requires frequencies usually between 2 and 12 MHz depending on atmospheric conditions.

mainPoints.title: AS-2259/GR Component Identification
mainPoints.content: The AS-2259/GR is a tactical, man-portable antenna kit designed specifically for NVIS. Operators must ensure all components are present and serviceable before deployment.
subPoints: Base Matching Unit: Provides the interface between the radio and the antenna.
Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that provide the vertical structure.
Radiating Elements: Four wire elements that serve as both the electrical antenna and the guy wires.
Carrying Bag: Used for transport and storage of all kit components.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Safety Procedures
mainPoints.content: Assembly must follow a specific sequence to ensure structural integrity and operator safety. The antenna is typically 15 feet tall when fully assembled.
subPoints: Site Selection: Choose a level area free of overhead power lines.
Base Setup: Secure the base matching unit and begin interlocking mast sections.
Element Deployment: Extend the four radiating elements at 90-degree intervals.
Safety: Ensure no personnel are touching the antenna during transmission due to RF burn hazards.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a mountain patrol base. You are tasked with establishing an HF link back to the Combat Operations Center (COC) located 45 miles away. Terrain prevents line-of-sight. You must deploy the AS-2259/GR to facilitate NVIS communications.
steps: Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit to ensure all components are serviceable.
Select a suitable site and clear debris.
Assemble the mast sections and attach the base matching unit.
Deploy and stake the four radiating elements at 90-degree intervals.
Connect the RF cable to the HF radio and perform a built-in test (BIT).
Establish a voice check with the distant station.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the fundamentals of NVIS propagation, identified the critical components of the AS-2259/GR, and practiced the assembly of the system. Understanding NVIS is the difference between being 'blacked out' by terrain and maintaining critical C2.
conclusion.closingStatement: The AS-2259/GR is a force multiplier in mountainous or jungle environments. Master its assembly, and you ensure your unit's voice is always heard, regardless of the terrain.

elos.justification: The AS-2259/GR is specifically designed for NVIS; the operator must understand the propagation theory to employ it effectively.

elos.justification: Accountability and serviceability of components are required before assembly can occur.

introduction.gainAttention: Your standard vehicle whip antenna is rated for about 15-30 miles under ideal conditions. But what happens when the convoy moves 40 miles out? To maintain the net, you need height and gain. The OE-254 antenna extends your VHF range significantly, ensuring that distance doesn't become a barrier to mission success.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the OE-254 antenna system, covering component identification and the technical procedures for erecting the mast safely to support VHF line-of-sight communications.
objectives: TLO-058: Demonstrate the employment of an OE-254 antenna.
ELO-152: Identify the components of an OE-254 antenna kit.
ELO-153: Perform the assembly and erection of the OE-254 antenna.

mainPoints.title: OE-254 System Components
mainPoints.content: The OE-254 is a broadband, omnidirectional antenna system operating in the 30-88 MHz range. It does not require tuning, making it ideal for frequency-hopping nets.
subPoints: Feedcone and Radiating Elements: The 'top' of the antenna that handles the signal.
Mast Sections: 11 tubular sections used to reach a height of approximately 30 feet.
Guy Wires and Stakes: Used to stabilize the mast against wind and gravity.
Base Stake: The foundation point for the mast assembly.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Erection Procedures
mainPoints.content: Erecting a 30-foot mast requires coordination and adherence to safety standards to prevent equipment damage or injury.
subPoints: Ground Assembly: The feedcone and elements are assembled on the ground before the mast is raised.
Guy Wire Spacing: Guy wires must be secured at 120-degree intervals to provide equal tension.
Verticality: The mast must be perfectly vertical to ensure omnidirectional coverage and structural stability.
Cable Management: Ensure the coaxial cable is not kinked or pinched during the lift.

practicalApplication.scenario: The Platoon is establishing a static Observation Post (OP). You are required to increase the range of the VHF net to reach the Company HQ. You have been provided an OE-254 kit and must erect it within 15 minutes.
steps: Layout all components and verify serviceability per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Assemble the feedcone and attach the three upper radiating elements.
Connect the coaxial cable to the feedcone.
Assemble mast sections and attach guy wires to the guy rings.
Erect the antenna using the 'walk-up' or 'vertical' method as a team.
Secure guy wires to stakes at 120-degree intervals and tension the lines.
Connect to the VHF radio and verify signal strength.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the components of the OE-254 and demonstrated the proper techniques for its assembly and erection. This antenna is the standard for extending VHF range in the Marine Corps.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio is only as good as its antenna. By mastering the OE-254, you provide your commander with the extended reach necessary for modern distributed operations.

tlo.standard: By assembling and erecting the antenna to establish VHF line-of-sight (LOS) communications per MCRP 6-22D.

elos.justification: Knowledge of the specific hardware is a prerequisite for physical assembly and employment.

elos.behavior: Perform the assembly and erection of the OE-254 antenna.
elos.standard: Ensuring the mast is vertical, guy wires are secured at 120-degree intervals, and the feedcone is properly seated per MCRP 3-40.3C.

title: Planning the Siting of an Antenna Farm

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine your unit is established in a hide site, but your radio signature is so concentrated and poorly managed that it glows like a beacon on enemy electronic warfare displays. A poorly planned antenna farm doesn't just cause signal interference; it provides the enemy with the exact coordinates of your Command Post (CP). Proper siting is the difference between mission success and being targeted by indirect fire before the first SITREP is even sent.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the tactical, technical, and doctrinal requirements for siting an antenna farm. We will discuss how to balance the need for signal radiation with the requirement for concealment and how to calculate the necessary separation between antennas to prevent co-site interference.
objectives: ELO-154: Identify tactical, technical, and doctrinal siting considerations for an antenna farm.
ELO-155: Determine the required separation distances between antennas.
ELO-156: Analyze terrain for the placement of an antenna farm.

mainPoints.title: Siting Considerations
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8, siting must balance three primary categories of considerations to ensure survivability and connectivity.
subPoints: Tactical: Focus on concealment from ground and air observation, use of natural cover, and physical security of the site.
Doctrinal: Placement relative to the Command Post (Main, Tactical, or Rear) and accessibility for maintenance personnel.
Technical: Avoiding man-made noise sources (generators, power lines) and ensuring the ground conductivity supports the frequency bands in use.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Separation and Layout
mainPoints.content: To minimize co-site interference, antennas must be separated based on their frequency and power output. This prevents 'de-sensing' receivers and ensures clear communication.
subPoints: Vertical Separation: Placing antennas at different heights to reduce coupling.
Horizontal Separation: Maintaining physical distance between antennas operating in the same frequency band.
Frequency Separation: Ensuring assigned frequencies are not too close to each other (typically 10% separation for VHF).

mainPoints.title: Terrain Analysis for CIS
mainPoints.content: Terrain selection is driven by the wave propagation characteristics of the equipment being used.
subPoints: Line of Sight (LOS): VHF and UHF systems require high ground with clear paths to distant stations.
Masking: Using hills or vegetation to shield the antenna farm from enemy direction-finding (DF) while maintaining a path for friendly signals.
HF NVIS: Requires relatively flat areas without overhead obstructions to allow for high-angle radiation.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the CIS Chief for an infantry battalion. You have been provided a 1:50,000 scale map and a list of 12 radio nets (4 HF, 6 VHF, 2 UHF). You must select a site for the antenna farm that is within 300 meters of the CP but remains concealed from a known enemy observation post on a nearby ridge.
steps: Identify potential high ground for VHF/UHF LOS requirements.
Evaluate vegetation and depressions for tactical concealment.
Sketch an antenna farm layout showing at least 15 meters of separation between VHF antennas.
Identify power line hazards or man-made noise sources on the map to avoid.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the critical factors in siting an antenna farm, including the tactical need for concealment, the technical requirement for antenna separation, and the analysis of terrain to support LOS and NVIS propagation.
conclusion.closingStatement: A professional CIS plan is invisible to the enemy but crystal clear to the commander. Master these siting principles to keep your unit connected and alive.

tlo.condition: Given a tactical scenario, unit location, and CIS requirements.
tlo.behavior: Plan the siting of an antenna farm.
tlo.standard: Accounting for tactical, technical, and doctrinal considerations per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: Siting an antenna farm requires the Marine to synthesize multiple complex variables, including terrain analysis, electromagnetic interference, and tactical security, to create a functional layout. This falls under Level 6 (Create).

elos.behavior: Identify tactical, technical, and doctrinal siting considerations for an antenna farm.
elos.standard: Including factors such as concealment, interference, and frequency separation per Chapter 8.
elos.justification: Planning requires a foundational knowledge of the constraints and requirements defined in doctrine.

elos.condition: Given a list of radio systems and frequencies.
elos.behavior: Determine the required separation distances between antennas.
elos.standard: To minimize co-site interference and optimize signal radiation per the antenna farm layout principles in MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Calculation of separation is a technical application necessary for the overall site plan.

title: Construction of a Half-Wave Dipole Antenna

introduction.gainAttention: You are 300 miles from the nearest relay, and your standard vehicle whip antenna cannot break through the atmospheric noise. You have a spool of wire, some insulators, and a radio. In the next hour, you will learn how to turn those raw materials into a high-gain antenna that can reach across the battlespace using the principles of resonance.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the mathematical and practical steps to construct a field-expedient half-wave dipole antenna. We will calculate the length based on frequency, assemble the components, and verify the antenna's performance using VSWR.
objectives: ELO-157: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-158: Assemble the components of a field-expedient dipole.
ELO-159: Verify the resonance of the antenna.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Length Calculation
mainPoints.content: The physical length of an antenna must correspond to the wavelength of the assigned frequency to achieve resonance.
subPoints: The standard formula for a half-wave dipole in feet is: 468 divided by the frequency in MHz.
Example: For a frequency of 10 MHz, the total length is 46.8 feet.
Each 'leg' of the dipole is half of the total length (23.4 feet).

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Construction
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly ensures the antenna is durable and electrically sound.
subPoints: Wire: Use copper or WD-1/TT field wire.
Insulators: Use glass, plastic, or dry wood to prevent the signal from grounding out at the ends.
Feed Line: The coaxial cable must be attached at the center, with the center conductor to one leg and the shield to the other.

mainPoints.title: Verification of Resonance
mainPoints.content: Once constructed, the antenna must be tested to ensure it is efficiently radiating energy rather than reflecting it back into the radio.
subPoints: Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) measures this efficiency.
A ratio of 1:1 is perfect; 3:1 is the maximum acceptable limit for most tactical radios.
High VSWR indicates the antenna is the wrong length or has a poor connection, which can damage the radio's power amplifier.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team is assigned a primary HF frequency of 7.5 MHz. You must construct a half-wave dipole antenna using the provided field kit and establish a link with the distant station.
steps: Calculate the total length of the antenna (468 / 7.5 = 62.4 feet).
Measure and cut two lengths of wire, each 31.2 feet long.
Attach the wires to the center insulator and connect the coaxial feed line.
Attach end insulators and hoist the antenna into the air using para-cord.
Connect the radio and perform a VSWR check to ensure a reading of 3:1 or less.

conclusion.summary: You now know how to calculate the length of a dipole, assemble it from field-expedient materials, and verify that it is tuned to your operating frequency.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ability to build an antenna from scratch is the hallmark of a proficient radio operator. When the standard equipment fails, your knowledge of antenna fundamentals ensures the message still gets through.

tlo.condition: Given an HF radio, antenna wire, insulators, coaxial cable, and an assigned frequency.
tlo.behavior: Construct a half-wave dipole antenna.
tlo.standard: By calculating the required length and assembling the antenna to support HF communications at the assigned frequency per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: Constructing a field-expedient antenna requires the Marine to formulate a solution from raw materials based on mathematical calculations. This synthesis of theory and physical production is classified as Level 6 (Create).

elos.behavior: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
elos.standard: Using the standard formula (468 / Frequency in MHz) to determine the length in feet within a 1% margin of error.
elos.justification: Accurate calculation is the technical prerequisite for constructing a resonant antenna.

elos.condition: Given antenna wire, insulators, and a center-feed mechanism.
elos.behavior: Assemble the components of a field-expedient dipole.
elos.standard: Ensuring the wire is cut to the calculated length, insulators are properly tied, and the coaxial feed line is securely attached per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Physical assembly of the components is the application step of the construction process.

elos.behavior: Verify the resonance of the antenna.
elos.standard: By checking the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) to ensure it is within acceptable operating limits (typically 3:1 or less) for the radio system.
elos.justification: Verification ensures the constructed product meets the technical standard for communication.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a dense urban environment or a deep mountain valley. You have a clear mission, but a massive concrete structure or a granite cliff face is standing directly between you and your distant station, completely severing your Line of Sight (LOS). In the VHF and UHF bands, we are taught that LOS is king, but when the king falls, the reflected wave becomes your best friend. Understanding how to 'bounce' your signal off the environment can be the difference between mission success and total comms blackout.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the technical principles of reflected wave propagation and the practical application of using environmental surfaces to maintain VHF/UHF communications when direct line-of-sight is obstructed.
objectives: TLO-061: Demonstrate communications using reflected waves.
ELO-160: Identify the principles of reflected wave propagation.
ELO-161: Describe the characteristics of suitable reflecting surfaces for VHF/UHF signals.

mainPoints.title: Principles of Reflected Wave Propagation
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 1, radio waves behave similarly to light waves when they encounter a surface. When a VHF/UHF wave hits a reflecting surface, it creates an incident wave and a reflected wave.
subPoints: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
Reflection occurs when the surface is large compared to the wavelength of the signal.
VHF/UHF waves are particularly susceptible to reflection due to their shorter wavelengths.

mainPoints.title: Characteristics of Suitable Reflecting Surfaces
mainPoints.content: Not all surfaces are created equal. To effectively bounce a signal, the operator must identify surfaces that minimize absorption and maximize reflection.
subPoints: Conductivity: Metallic surfaces (water towers, hangars) are the most efficient reflectors.
Density: Solid rock faces and concrete buildings provide high reflectivity compared to vegetation.
Surface Smoothness: The surface must be relatively smooth in relation to the wavelength to avoid scattering (diffraction).
Size: The surface must be several wavelengths wide and tall to act as an effective mirror for the signal.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Orientation for Reflected Waves
mainPoints.content: To use a reflected wave, the operator must deviate from standard 'pointing' procedures.
subPoints: Direct the antenna toward the reflecting object rather than the distant station.
Coordinate with the receiving station to also orient their antenna toward the same reflecting point.
Maintain proper polarization (usually vertical for tactical VHF) to ensure signal consistency.

practicalApplication.scenario: The unit is positioned behind a large hill that blocks direct LOS to the Combat Operations Center (COC). A large metal warehouse is visible to the North, which has a clear view of both your position and the COC.
steps: Identify the warehouse as the primary reflecting surface based on material and location.
Calculate the approximate angle required to hit the surface so the reflection angle points toward the COC.
Orient the VHF whip or directional antenna toward the warehouse.
Attempt to establish contact and make small adjustments to the antenna azimuth to peak the signal strength.

conclusion.summary: We have covered how VHF/UHF signals can be reflected off man-made and natural structures to overcome LOS obstructions. We identified that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection and that dense, conductive surfaces make the best reflectors.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the modern battlespace, you won't always have a clear line of sight. Master the reflected wave, and you ensure that terrain never dictates your ability to communicate.

tlo.condition: Given a VHF/UHF radio and a scenario where direct Line of Sight (LOS) is obstructed by terrain or structures,
tlo.behavior: demonstrate communications using reflected waves,
tlo.standard: by directing antennas toward a reflecting object to achieve practical communications per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: Level 3 (Apply) is appropriate because the Marine must apply the principles of wave propagation and reflection to a specific physical environment to achieve a functional result.

elos.behavior: identify the principles of reflected wave propagation,
elos.standard: defining the relationship between the incident wave and the reflecting surface per Chapter 1.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the underlying physics of wave reflection is a prerequisite for practical application.

elos.condition: Given a tactical scenario and various terrain features,
elos.behavior: describe the characteristics of suitable reflecting surfaces for VHF/UHF signals,
elos.standard: ensuring the surfaces identified are capable of reflecting signals to a distant station per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The Marine must be able to comprehend which environmental features (buildings, mountains) are viable for the technique.

title: HF Antenna Selection for Sky Wave Propagation

introduction.gainAttention: You are tasked with establishing a high-frequency (HF) circuit to a unit 200 miles away. You have a radio, a wire kit, and a ticking clock. If you choose an antenna with a take-off angle that is too low, your signal will skip right over the target. If it's too high, it might not have the range. In HF communications, your antenna is your most critical piece of software—select the wrong one, and you are just talking to yourself.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the relationship between take-off angles, circuit distances, and the selection of HF antennas using MCRP 3-40.3C standardized data.
objectives: TLO-062: Determine the appropriate HF antenna for sky wave propagation.
ELO-162: Explain the relationship between take-off angle and circuit distance.
ELO-163: Interpret antenna selection data from Table 4-1.
ELO-164: Compare antenna characteristics regarding gain and directivity.

mainPoints.title: Take-Off Angle and Circuit Distance
mainPoints.content: The take-off angle is the angle above the horizon at which an antenna radiates the majority of its energy. This angle determines where the signal will return to earth after reflecting off the ionosphere.
subPoints: High Take-Off Angles (60-90 degrees): Used for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to cover short ranges (0-300 miles) and overcome terrain masking.
Low Take-Off Angles (less than 30 degrees): Used for long-distance communications (300+ miles) to maximize skip distance.
The height of the antenna above ground directly influences the take-off angle.

mainPoints.title: Interpreting Table 4-1 (Antenna Selection)
mainPoints.content: MCRP 3-40.3C Table 4-1 provides a standardized matrix for selecting antennas based on distance and time of day.
subPoints: Distance Categories: Short (0-300 miles), Medium (300-1000 miles), Long (1000+ miles).
Time of Day: Ionospheric layers change between day and night, requiring different frequency and antenna considerations.
Antenna Recommendations: Identifies specific types like the AS-2259, Dipole, or Inverted Vee based on these variables.

mainPoints.title: Comparing Gain and Directivity
mainPoints.content: Different antennas provide different levels of gain (signal strength) and directivity (concentration of energy).
subPoints: Omnidirectional: Best for nets with stations in multiple directions (e.g., Vertical Whip).
Bidirectional: Concentrates energy in two directions (e.g., Half-Wave Dipole).
Directional: Maximum gain toward a specific station (e.g., Sloping Vee or Rhombic).
Gain vs. Complexity: Higher gain antennas often require more space and setup time.

practicalApplication.scenario: Mission: Establish a 150-mile HF circuit during daylight hours. You have a standard wire antenna kit and an AS-2259/GR. Terrain is heavily wooded.
steps: Consult MCRP 3-40.3C Table 4-1 for the 0-300 mile range.
Identify that a high take-off angle (NVIS) is required for this distance.
Compare the AS-2259 (NVIS specific) against a Horizontal Dipole.
Select the AS-2259/GR or a Dipole at a height of 1/4 wavelength or less to ensure the required take-off angle.
Justify the selection based on the need to clear the surrounding vegetation and hit the 150-mile target.

conclusion.summary: We have analyzed how take-off angles dictate the skip distance of an HF signal and how to use Table 4-1 to select the right antenna for the mission. We also compared gain and directivity to ensure the signal reaches the intended recipient.
conclusion.closingStatement: HF is an art backed by science. By mastering antenna selection, you turn the ionosphere into a tool rather than an obstacle.

tlo.behavior: determine the appropriate HF antenna for sky wave propagation,
tlo.standard: ensuring the selection meets the required take-off angle and coverage requirements for the specified distance and time of day per Table 4-1.
tlo.justification: Level 5 (Evaluate) is required because the Marine must judge multiple variables (distance, time, and site constraints) against doctrinal criteria to select the most effective solution.

elos.behavior: explain the relationship between take-off angle and circuit distance,
elos.standard: detailing how the angle of radiation affects the skip distance in sky wave propagation per Chapter 2.
elos.justification: Understanding the geometry of sky wave propagation is essential before evaluating specific antenna types.

introduction.gainAttention: You are operating in a dense jungle environment and your standard vehicle whip antenna has been sheared off by heavy vegetation. You are out of range for your manpack's standard antenna, and a CASEVAC request needs to be transmitted immediately. In this moment, your ability to turn a roll of WD-1/TT wire and some plastic spoons into a functional antenna is the only thing that will get that bird in the air. Field expediency is not just a 'nice to have' skill; it is a survival requirement for the Marine communicator.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of constructing field-expedient antennas using MCRP 3-40.3C. We will focus on identifying necessary components, calculating precise lengths for specific frequencies, and applying proper insulation techniques to ensure signal radiation.
objectives: TLO-063: Construct a field-expedient antenna.
ELO-165: Calculate the physical length of a wire antenna.
ELO-166: Identify the components required for a field-expedient antenna.
ELO-167: Apply proper insulation and support techniques.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Components and Materials
mainPoints.content: A field-expedient antenna requires three primary components to function effectively: the radiator, the transmission line, and insulators.
subPoints: Radiator: The active element (usually wire) that emits the radio frequency energy.
Transmission Line: The medium (coaxial cable or twin-lead) that carries energy from the radio to the antenna.
Insulators: Non-conductive materials (plastic, glass, or dry wood) used to prevent the signal from grounding into supports like trees or poles.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Antenna Length
mainPoints.content: To achieve resonance, the antenna must be cut to a specific length based on the assigned frequency. For a half-wave dipole, the standard formula is used to ensure maximum power transfer.
subPoints: Formula: Length in feet = 468 / Frequency in MHz.
Example: For a frequency of 14.2 MHz, the total length is approximately 33 feet (16.5 feet per element).
Accuracy: Calculations must be accurate to within 1 inch to maintain a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

mainPoints.title: Insulation and Support Techniques
mainPoints.content: Proper mounting is critical. An antenna that touches a wet tree limb or the ground will short out, causing the radio to lose power or sustain damage.
subPoints: Height: Antennas should be mounted as high as possible to achieve the required radiation pattern and clear obstacles.
Isolation: Use field-expedient insulators (buttons, plastic scraps, or dry wood) at the ends of the radiator to separate it from the support ropes.
Orientation: Ensure the antenna is oriented (broadside) toward the receiving station for maximum signal strength.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a temporary patrol base. You are assigned a frequency of 35.50 MHz (VHF). You must construct a center-fed half-wave dipole using a field antenna kit and available trees for support.
steps: Calculate the total length of the radiator using the formula (468 / 35.5).
Measure and cut two equal lengths of wire (each representing 1/4 wavelength).
Identify and inspect insulators for cracks or conductivity.
Attach the radiator wires to the center insulator and the transmission line.
Secure the ends of the radiator to support ropes using insulators.
Hoist the antenna into the trees, ensuring it does not touch branches or the ground.
Connect to the radio and perform a radio check.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the identification of antenna components, the mathematical calculation of antenna length based on frequency, and the physical techniques required to insulate and support a field-expedient antenna.
conclusion.closingStatement: The difference between a successful mission and a communications failure often comes down to the operator's technical proficiency. Master these calculations and construction techniques now so you can employ them when the tactical situation is at its worst.

title: Troubleshooting and Field Repair of Antenna Systems

introduction.gainAttention: In the heat of an engagement, antennas are often the first things to break. Shrapnel, high winds, and vehicle movement can easily snap a whip or sever a wire. If you cannot repair your antenna in the field, you are effectively out of the fight. A Marine who can troubleshoot and perform a Western Union splice under pressure is an invaluable asset to any maneuver element.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying common antenna failures and performing field-expedient repairs to restore electrical continuity and structural integrity to antenna systems per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-064: Troubleshoot antenna components for field repair.
ELO-168: Identify common types of damage to whip, wire, and mast components.
ELO-169: Describe field repair techniques for wire and whip antennas.
ELO-170: Perform a western union splice on antenna wire.

mainPoints.title: Identifying Antenna System Damage
mainPoints.content: Troubleshooting begins with a visual inspection of the entire system from the radio connector to the tip of the antenna.
subPoints: Whip Antennas: Look for cracks at the base, snapped sections, or corrosion at the joints.
Wire Antennas: Check for frayed insulation, severed conductors, or grounded wires.
Masts and Guys: Inspect for bent sections, frayed guy lines, or loose tensioners that affect stability.

mainPoints.title: Field Repair Principles
mainPoints.content: The goal of any field repair is to restore two things: electrical continuity and mechanical strength.
subPoints: Electrical Continuity: The signal must have a clear, low-resistance path to travel. Use solder or tight mechanical splices.
Mechanical Strength: The repair must be able to withstand the tension of being hoisted or the vibration of a moving vehicle.
Weatherproofing: Use electrical tape or heat shrink to prevent moisture from corroding the repair site.

mainPoints.title: The Western Union Splice
mainPoints.content: The Western Union splice is the standard military method for joining two pieces of antenna wire because it provides excellent conductivity and will not pull apart under tension.
subPoints: Preparation: Strip approximately 4-6 inches of insulation from both ends of the wire.
The Twist: Cross the wires and wrap each end tightly around the standing part of the opposite wire (at least 5-7 turns).
Finishing: Ensure the wraps are tight and close together to maximize surface contact.

practicalApplication.scenario: During a movement to contact, a low-hanging branch has severed the wire antenna used for your long-range HF net. You must troubleshoot the system, identify the break, and perform a permanent field repair to restore communications.
steps: Perform a visual inspection of the antenna system to locate the break.
Retrieve the severed ends of the antenna wire.
Strip the insulation from the wire ends using a multi-tool or knife.
Execute a Western Union splice, ensuring at least five tight wraps on each side.
Test the mechanical strength of the splice by applying moderate tension.
Seal the splice with electrical tape to prevent corrosion.
Re-hoist the antenna and verify electrical continuity with a radio check.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed how to identify damage across various antenna types, the principles of maintaining continuity and strength, and the specific steps to perform a Western Union splice.
conclusion.closingStatement: Equipment will fail, but the mission cannot. Your ability to troubleshoot and repair your gear ensures that the Commander's intent is always heard, regardless of the conditions on the ground.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes environment where every word of a SITREP matters, but your million-dollar radio system is failing because of a five-dollar connector. You can have the best radio and the perfect antenna, but if the transmission line between them is poorly installed, your signal will dissipate as heat before it ever leaves the wire. Today, we ensure that power reaches the air.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the selection, characteristics, and installation of transmission lines, focusing on impedance matching, minimizing SWR, and proper physical connection techniques per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-065: Implement transmission line installation.
ELO-171: Identify the characteristics of coaxial and twin-lead transmission lines.
ELO-172: Explain the effects of attenuation and Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) on radio performance.
ELO-173: Connect transmission lines using appropriate connectors or baluns.

mainPoints.title: Transmission Line Characteristics
mainPoints.content: Transmission lines are the vital link between the transceiver and the antenna. Understanding their electrical properties is essential for system efficiency.
subPoints: Coaxial Cable: Most common in the Marine Corps (e.g., RG-213, RG-58). Consists of a center conductor, dielectric insulator, shield, and outer jacket. Standard impedance is typically 50 ohms.
Twin-Lead: Consists of two parallel conductors. It has higher impedance (typically 300 ohms) and lower loss than coax but is more susceptible to interference and environmental factors.
Impedance Matching: The characteristic impedance of the line must match the radio and the antenna to ensure maximum power transfer.

mainPoints.title: Attenuation and Standing Wave Ratio (SWR)
mainPoints.content: Improper installation leads to signal degradation and potential hardware failure.
subPoints: Attenuation: The gradual loss of signal strength as it travels through the line, measured in decibels (dB). Caused by resistance in the wire and dielectric losses.
SWR: A measure of how much power is reflected back to the transmitter. High SWR (above 3:1) indicates a mismatch, reducing radiated power and potentially damaging the radio's final power amplifier.
Power Loss: Energy not radiated is converted to heat within the transmission line or the radio.

mainPoints.title: Installation and Connection Techniques
mainPoints.content: Physical security and weatherproofing are the primary defenses against signal leakage and line degradation.
subPoints: Connectors: Use of BNC, N-type, or PL-259 connectors. Ensure they are tight and free of corrosion.
Baluns: Used when connecting a balanced antenna (like a dipole) to an unbalanced line (coax) to maintain the radiation pattern and prevent line radiation.
Weather-Sealing: Use of silicone tape or electrical sealant on outdoor connections to prevent moisture ingress, which causes rapid attenuation and cable rot.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with setting up a temporary base station. You have been provided with an HF radio, a dipole antenna, and a roll of RG-213 coaxial cable. You must prepare the line and connect the system for immediate operation.
steps: Select the correct transmission line (coax) for the 50-ohm radio output.
Inspect connectors for physical damage or shorts.
Connect the coax to the antenna using a 1:1 balun to ensure a balanced feed.
Secure all connections with weather-sealing tape.
Route the cable to avoid sharp bends or proximity to power lines.
Perform a radio check and monitor the SWR meter to ensure a reading below 1.5:1.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the differences between coaxial and twin-lead lines, the critical nature of impedance matching to prevent high SWR, and the technical requirements for physical installation.
conclusion.closingStatement: A Marine's ability to communicate is only as reliable as the cable connecting their gear. Master these connections, and you ensure the message gets through every time.

title: Construction of Field-Expedient Vertical Half-Rhombic Antennas

introduction.gainAttention: You are operating in a valley and need to hit a distant station 400 miles away, but your standard whip antenna is failing to clear the ridgeline. By using a few hundred feet of wire and a single resistor, you can build a directional 'powerhouse' that focuses your signal exactly where it needs to go. This is the Vertical Half-Rhombic.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the technical procedures for calculating, aligning, and constructing a field-expedient vertical half-rhombic antenna to achieve directional gain in the HF band.
objectives: TLO-066: Construct a field-expedient vertical half-rhombic antenna.
ELO-174: Calculate the required length for a half-rhombic antenna wire.
ELO-175: Align the antenna's major axis toward the distant station.
ELO-176: Install a terminating resistor at the end of the antenna wire.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Theory and Calculation
mainPoints.content: The vertical half-rhombic is a long-wire antenna that uses the ground to complete its electrical circuit, creating a directional radiation pattern.
subPoints: Wavelength Calculation: Use the formula (492 / Frequency in MHz) to find the half-wavelength in feet.
Leg Length: For a half-rhombic, each leg should typically be at least one full wavelength for effective gain.
Height Requirements: The center support (mast) must be high enough to maintain the required angle for the desired take-off angle.

mainPoints.title: Orientation and Alignment
mainPoints.content: Because the half-rhombic is highly directional, precise alignment is mandatory for successful communication.
subPoints: Major Axis: The line running from the feed point through the mast to the termination point.
Compass Calibration: Use a lensatic compass to determine the azimuth to the distant station.
Tolerance: The antenna must be aligned within 5 degrees of the target azimuth to ensure the main lobe of the radiation pattern covers the receiving station.

mainPoints.title: Termination and Grounding
mainPoints.content: The terminating resistor is what differentiates a directional antenna from a bi-directional one.
subPoints: Resistor Value: A non-inductive resistor of 500-600 ohms is required.
Function: The resistor absorbs the energy that would otherwise reflect back, making the antenna 'non-resonant' and unidirectional.
Grounding: The resistor must be connected to a high-quality ground (ground rod or counterpoise) at the far end of the antenna to complete the circuit.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a patrol base and requires long-haul HF communications to a higher headquarters located at an azimuth of 045 degrees. You are provided with a spool of WD-1/TT wire, a 600-ohm resistor, and a 30-foot mast.
steps: Calculate the wire length based on the assigned frequency of 7.5 MHz.
Measure and cut the wire to the calculated length (+/- 1 inch).
Use a lensatic compass to stake out the 045-degree azimuth line.
Erect the center mast and attach the wire, ensuring it forms the 'V' shape in the vertical plane.
Install the 600-ohm resistor at the distant end of the wire.
Drive a ground rod and attach the other end of the resistor to it.
Connect the feed point to the radio and verify the directional orientation.

conclusion.summary: We have practiced the mathematical calculation of antenna legs, the use of the lensatic compass for directional alignment, and the installation of the terminating resistor to ensure unidirectional gain.
conclusion.closingStatement: The vertical half-rhombic is one of the most effective field-expedient tools in a communicator's arsenal. When the terrain is against you, use the physics of the half-rhombic to win the frequency.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes environment where every second counts. You have a clear line of sight to your distant station, your batteries are fresh, and your frequency is correct, yet your signal is barely readable. You rotate your antenna 90 degrees, and suddenly the signal is crystal clear. That simple adjustment is the power of understanding antenna polarization.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of antenna polarization, the specific characteristics of vertical and horizontal fields, and how to orient antennas to achieve maximum signal strength per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-067: Demonstrate antenna orientation for polarization.
ELO-177: Define antenna polarization.
ELO-178: Describe the advantages of vertical and horizontal polarization.

mainPoints.title: Defining Antenna Polarization
mainPoints.content: Polarization is the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) as it leaves the antenna in relation to the earth's surface. It is a critical factor in antenna-to-antenna communication.
subPoints: The electric field determines the polarization.
If the electric field is parallel to the earth, it is horizontally polarized.
If the electric field is perpendicular to the earth, it is vertically polarized.
For maximum signal transfer, both the transmitting and receiving antennas must have the same polarization.

mainPoints.title: Vertical Polarization Characteristics
mainPoints.content: Vertical polarization is widely used in tactical environments, particularly with whip antennas and mobile communications.
subPoints: Advantage: Provides omnidirectional (360-degree) coverage.
Advantage: More effective for ground wave propagation over long distances.
Disadvantage: More susceptible to manmade noise, which is often vertically polarized.

mainPoints.title: Horizontal Polarization Characteristics
mainPoints.content: Horizontal polarization is frequently used in high frequency (HF) sky wave communications and fixed-site installations.
subPoints: Advantage: Less susceptible to manmade interference (e.g., vehicle ignitions).
Advantage: Effective for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to communicate over obstacles.
Requirement: Requires more space and support structures (masts/trees) than vertical whips.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with establishing a VHF link between two stationary command posts separated by 15 kilometers of rolling terrain. You have been issued two OE-254 antenna systems.
steps: Identify the polarization of the distant station's antenna.
Assemble the OE-254 antenna system according to technical manuals.
Orient the antenna elements to match the polarization of the distant station (Vertical for standard VHF tactical nets).
Conduct a radio check to verify signal strength.
Rotate the antenna 90 degrees to observe the 'cross-polarization' effect and the resulting signal degradation.

conclusion.summary: We have defined antenna polarization as the orientation of the electric field relative to the earth. We compared vertical polarization, ideal for mobile ground waves, with horizontal polarization, which excels in reducing manmade noise and supporting sky wave propagation.
conclusion.closingStatement: Mastering antenna orientation ensures that you maximize your equipment's potential, ensuring the MAGTF maintains the critical comms link required for mission success.

introduction.gainAttention: In a modern tactical environment, the enemy isn't the only thing trying to jam your signal. Your own generators, vehicles, and even poorly shielded power lines can create a 'wall of noise' that renders your multi-million dollar radio system useless. Knowing how to fight through this manmade noise is a requirement for every radio operator.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying manmade noise sources, understanding their impact on the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and applying mitigation techniques to restore reliable communications.
objectives: TLO-068: Troubleshoot manmade noise interference.
ELO-179: Identify common sources of manmade noise.
ELO-180: Explain the impact of noise on the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).
ELO-181: Determine mitigation techniques for noise reduction.

mainPoints.title: Sources of Manmade Noise
mainPoints.content: Manmade noise is caused by the discharge of electrical energy. It is most prevalent in urban areas or near industrial/military hubs.
subPoints: Power lines and transformers (arcing or corona discharge).
Vehicle ignition systems and alternators.
Electric motors and generators.
Computers, switching power supplies, and other digital electronic equipment.

mainPoints.title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)
mainPoints.content: The SNR is the relationship between the strength of the desired signal and the level of background noise (the noise floor).
subPoints: A high SNR means the signal is much stronger than the noise, resulting in clear audio/data.
A low SNR occurs when the noise floor rises, 'masking' the signal and making it unreadable.
Increasing transmitter power is one way to improve SNR, but reducing the noise floor at the receiver is often more effective.

mainPoints.title: Mitigation and Troubleshooting Techniques
mainPoints.content: When interference is detected, operators must systematically apply techniques to reduce the noise floor.
subPoints: Re-siting: Move the antenna away from the noise source (e.g., move 50 meters away from a generator).
Polarization Change: If the noise is vertically polarized (common for power lines), switching to horizontal polarization can significantly reduce interference.
Grounding: Ensure the radio and antenna system are properly grounded to drain off stray electromagnetic energy.
Physical Shielding: Use terrain or buildings to block the path between the noise source and the antenna.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your radio team is co-located with a logistics hub. You are experiencing heavy static on your HF net, coinciding with the operation of a large mobile generator 10 meters from your antenna.
steps: Monitor the radio and identify the specific type of interference (pulsing vs. constant hum).
Measure the signal quality with the generator running versus when it is momentarily shut down.
Calculate the approximate SNR based on the radio's signal strength indicator.
Relocate the antenna to a distance at least 30-50 meters from the generator and power lines.
Verify the improvement in SNR and conduct a radio check with the distant station.

conclusion.summary: We have identified that manmade noise from vehicles and power lines can severely degrade our Signal-to-Noise Ratio. By understanding how the noise floor masks our signals, we can apply mitigation techniques like re-siting, grounding, and polarization shifts.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who can troubleshoot noise is an asset to any unit. Don't just accept a bad signal—find the source, mitigate the noise, and get the message through.

tlo.standard: reducing interference to achieve a reliable signal-to-noise ratio that allows for clear communication per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The Marine must analyze the environment, identify the specific source of interference, and differentiate between various mitigation techniques to solve the problem.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are part of a Quick Reaction Force (QRF) inserted into a deep valley. Your mission depends on maintaining a link with the Combat Operations Center (COC) 150 miles away. You have an HF radio, but if you simply throw up a standard whip antenna, your signal will likely be absorbed by the canyon walls or shoot straight into space and never return. Selecting the right antenna isn't just a technical task; it is the difference between a successful extraction and being cut off from support.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the critical factors in selecting the correct antenna for tactical communications, focusing on the relationship between frequency bands, range requirements, and antenna radiation patterns as defined in MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-069: Given a mission requirement, an assigned frequency (HF, VHF, or UHF), and a specified range, apply antenna selection criteria by selecting an antenna configuration that supports the assigned frequency band and range requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
ELO-182: Given a list of frequencies, identify military radio frequency bands by classifying frequencies into HF, VHF, and UHF categories per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 1.

ELO-183: Given various antenna types (e.g., Dipole, Whip, OE-254), describe antenna radiation patterns and range capabilities by matching antenna characteristics to mission distance requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.

mainPoints.title: Military Radio Frequency Bands
mainPoints.content: The electromagnetic spectrum is divided into bands that dictate how radio waves behave and what equipment is required.
subPoints: High Frequency (HF): 3 to 30 MHz. Used for long-range communication via sky wave propagation.
Very High Frequency (VHF): 30 to 300 MHz. The primary band for MAGTF tactical ground communications, generally limited to line-of-sight.
Ultrahigh Frequency (UHF): 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Used for ground-to-air, satellite communications (SATCOM), and short-range line-of-sight.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Radiation Patterns and Range
mainPoints.content: Different antennas distribute energy in specific ways, which determines their effective range and application.
subPoints: Omnidirectional (Whip): Radiates energy equally in all directions (360 degrees). Best for mobile operations and short-range VHF/UHF.
Bidirectional (Dipole): Radiates energy in two main directions. Ideal for established HF links at medium ranges.
Directional (OE-254/Log Periodic): Concentrates energy in a specific direction to increase range and reduce interference/detection.

mainPoints.title: Selection Criteria for Mission Success
mainPoints.content: To select the right antenna, the operator must balance the assigned frequency, the distance to the receiving station, and the tactical environment.
subPoints: Short Range (0-30 miles): Typically VHF/UHF using whip or OE-254 antennas.
Medium to Long Range (30-300+ miles): Typically HF using NVIS (Near Vertical Incidence Skywave) or long-wire configurations.
Terrain Considerations: High ground is essential for VHF/UHF line-of-sight, while HF can overcome terrain obstacles using sky wave propagation.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a reconnaissance team. You are assigned a frequency of 4.500 MHz (HF) and must establish a link with a base 120 miles away located behind a mountain range. You have a manpack radio, a 10-foot whip antenna, and a field-expedient wire kit.
steps: Identify the frequency band (HF).
Determine the propagation requirement (Sky wave/NVIS required due to distance and terrain).
Evaluate the available antennas (Whip vs. Wire).
Select the wire antenna and configure it as a Half-Wave Dipole to support the HF sky wave requirement.
Verify the antenna length calculation based on the 4.500 MHz frequency.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the classification of HF, VHF, and UHF bands and how antenna types like the whip and dipole provide different radiation patterns to meet mission ranges. Understanding these criteria ensures the MAGTF maintains reliable command and control.
conclusion.closingStatement: The most powerful radio in the Marine Corps is useless if the energy never reaches the target. Master your antenna selection, and you master the airwaves.
