introduction.gainAttention: Have you ever had a radio check come back 'weak but readable' even though you were only a mile away from the other station? You might have had the best antenna and the right frequency, but if your antenna was standing straight up while the receiving antenna was laying flat, you were losing up to 95% of your signal strength. This is the 'cross-polarization' trap, and it is a common mistake that can jeopardize a mission.
introduction.overview: This lesson defines antenna polarization and provides the criteria for selecting vertical or horizontal orientation based on the frequency band and the intended mode of propagation (ground wave vs. sky wave).
objectives: TLO-070: Given a tactical radio, a frequency, and a mission requirement, apply antenna polarization selection by matching the polarization (vertical, horizontal, or circular) to the frequency band and transmission mode per MCRP 3-40.3C.
ELO-184: Given a list of antenna types and MCRP 3-40.3C, define antenna polarization by identifying the physical orientation of the radiated electric field per MCRP 3-40.3C, page 2-6.
ELO-185: Given a tactical scenario involving ground wave and sky wave propagation, describe the advantages of vertical and horizontal polarization per MCRP 3-40.3C, pages 2-9 and 2-10.
ELO-186: Given various frequency bands (HF, VHF, UHF) and MCRP 3-40.3C, identify polarization requirements for various frequencies per MCRP 3-40.3C, page 2-8.

mainPoints.title: Defining Polarization
mainPoints.content: Polarization is the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) as it leaves the antenna.
subPoints: Vertical Polarization: The electric field is perpendicular to the Earth's surface (e.g., a standard whip antenna).
Horizontal Polarization: The electric field is parallel to the Earth's surface (e.g., a horizontal dipole).
Circular Polarization: The electric field rotates as it propagates; primarily used in SATCOM to overcome atmospheric rotation.

mainPoints.title: Advantages of Polarization Types
mainPoints.content: The choice of polarization affects how the signal interacts with the ground and the atmosphere.
subPoints: Vertical Advantages: Best for ground wave communication (VHF). It is easier to employ on mobile platforms and provides omnidirectional coverage.
Horizontal Advantages: Best for HF sky wave (NVIS). It is less susceptible to man-made interference and provides better performance when communicating over long distances via the ionosphere.

mainPoints.title: Matching Polarization to Frequency and Mode
mainPoints.content: To ensure maximum signal transfer, the transmitting and receiving antennas must use the same polarization.
subPoints: VHF/UHF Ground-to-Ground: Use Vertical polarization for standard tactical nets.
HF Sky Wave: Use Horizontal polarization to maximize reflection off the ionosphere.
SATCOM: Use Circular polarization to ensure the signal can be received regardless of the satellite's orientation.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are setting up a base station for an HF NVIS net to communicate with units 50-100 miles away. You are also monitoring a VHF convoy net on a separate radio.
steps: Identify the propagation mode for the HF net (Sky wave/NVIS).
Identify the propagation mode for the VHF net (Ground wave).
Orient the HF Dipole antenna horizontally to support sky wave propagation.
Orient the VHF whip antenna vertically to support ground wave communication with the convoy.
Ensure all stations in the net are informed of the polarization to ensure matching.

conclusion.summary: Polarization is the physical orientation of the radio wave's electric field. We have learned that vertical polarization is the standard for VHF ground wave, while horizontal polarization is the preferred choice for HF sky wave operations.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the field, 'close enough' doesn't work for polarization. Match your orientation to your mission requirements to ensure your signal is heard loud and clear.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a hide site, trying to send a critical SITREP. You have a perfect line of sight, but your signal is being drowned out by enemy jamming or local interference. Simply having a powerful radio isn't enough; if your antenna is pointed the wrong way, you are shouting into the wind while the enemy's noise fills your ears. Mastering antenna orientation is the difference between a clear transmission and total radio silence.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the principles of orienting directional antennas to maximize signal strength and minimize interference. We will define antenna azimuth, explore the relationship between orientation and signal-to-noise ratio, and practice calculating the correct azimuth for distant stations.
objectives: ELO-187: Define antenna azimuth
ELO-188: Explain the relationship between antenna orientation and signal-to-noise ratio
ELO-189: Determine the required azimuth for antenna orientation

mainPoints.title: Antenna Azimuth Fundamentals
mainPoints.content: Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from a north base line (true or magnetic north) to the direction of the antenna's radiation pattern. For a horizontal half-wave antenna, the maximum radiation occurs broadside to the wire.
subPoints: Reference North: Always specify if using True North or Magnetic North based on your map and compass.
Radiation Pattern: Directional antennas do not radiate equally in all directions; the azimuth identifies the 'lobe' of maximum energy.
MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-26.

mainPoints.title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Nulls
mainPoints.content: Proper orientation does two things simultaneously: it places the distant station in the antenna's maximum radiation lobe and places known interference sources in the antenna's 'nulls' (areas of minimum radiation).
subPoints: SNR Maximization: Increasing the desired signal while decreasing background noise or jamming.
Null Placement: By rotating the antenna, an operator can 'dial out' interference coming from a specific direction.
MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-27.

mainPoints.title: Calculating and Determining Azimuth
mainPoints.content: To communicate effectively, the operator must determine the exact direction to the distant station using map coordinates and then translate that to a physical heading for the antenna.
subPoints: Map Work: Use the protractor to find the grid azimuth between your location and the distant station.
Conversion: Apply the G-M angle to convert grid azimuth to magnetic azimuth for use with a lensatic compass.
Tolerance: Standards require calculation within +/- 5 degrees for effective HF/VHF directional links.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are located at Grid 12S VF 1234 5678. You must establish a link with a distant station at Grid 12S VF 2234 6678. An enemy direction-finding unit is known to be operating 90 degrees offset from your intended path.
steps: Identify your location and the distant station location on the map.
Calculate the grid azimuth to the distant station using a protractor.
Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth.
Identify the 'null' points of your horizontal half-wave antenna.
Physically orient the antenna wire so the broadside (maximum radiation) faces the distant station azimuth.
Verify the orientation using a lensatic compass.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the definition of azimuth, the importance of SNR in marginal communication environments, and the technical steps to calculate antenna headings. Proper orientation ensures your signal reaches the target while minimizing the impact of interference.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the fleet, you won't always have the luxury of a perfect environment. Your ability to orient your antenna precisely is what will keep the command's common operational picture updated when the spectrum gets crowded.

introduction.gainAttention: Every radio operator knows that an antenna needs to be 'up,' but many forget that for many systems, the ground is just as important as the wire in the air. Without a proper ground, you are essentially operating with only half of an antenna system. A poor ground leads to ground losses, reduced range, and potential safety hazards for the operator.
introduction.overview: This lesson explains the theory behind grounded antennas, the various types of grounding systems available to Marines, and how to select the best method based on the terrain you encounter in the field.
objectives: ELO-190: Explain grounded antenna theory
ELO-191: Identify types of antenna grounds
ELO-192: Select the appropriate grounding method

mainPoints.title: Grounded Antenna Theory
mainPoints.content: For many antenna types, the earth acts as a reflecting surface. A grounded antenna uses the earth as the other half of the circuit (the 'image' antenna). The efficiency of this reflection depends entirely on the soil's conductivity.
subPoints: Image Theory: The ground creates a virtual reflection of the antenna, completing the radiation pattern.
Conductivity: High conductivity (moist soil) improves reflection; low conductivity (sand/rock) absorbs energy, causing 'ground loss.'
MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-19.

mainPoints.title: Types of Antenna Grounds
mainPoints.content: There are three primary ways to establish a ground in the field: ground rods, counterpoises, and ground screens.
subPoints: Ground Rods: Metal stakes driven into the earth to reach moist soil.
Counterpoise: A network of wires used when the earth itself is a poor conductor; it acts as an artificial ground.
Ground Screen: A mesh or radial system used to provide a highly reflective surface directly under the antenna.
MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Pages 2-20 through 2-23.

mainPoints.title: Environmental Selection Criteria
mainPoints.content: The choice of grounding method is dictated by the terrain. You must adapt your grounding strategy to the soil conditions to maintain signal integrity.
subPoints: Moist/Loam Soil: Standard ground rods are usually sufficient.
Sandy/Dry Soil: Requires a counterpoise or ground screen because the soil cannot conduct electricity effectively.
Rocky Terrain: Ground rods cannot be driven; a counterpoise is mandatory for safety and performance.
MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-20.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit has moved into a desert environment characterized by high sand content and extremely low soil moisture. You are tasked with setting up a grounded vertical antenna for long-haul HF communications.
steps: Assess the soil condition (dry sand).
Determine that a standard ground rod will be insufficient due to low conductivity.
Select the counterpoise method as the appropriate grounding solution.
Lay out the counterpoise radials in a star pattern centered at the antenna base.
Connect the counterpoise to the radio's ground terminal.
Ensure all connections are tight and free of corrosion.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed how the earth completes the antenna circuit, the different hardware used for grounding, and how to adapt your grounding technique to sandy, rocky, or moist environments.
conclusion.closingStatement: A Marine who understands grounding is a Marine who can communicate from anywhere. Don't let poor soil conditions be the reason your message doesn't get through.

tlo.justification: Level 3 (Apply) is selected as this task involves the practical execution of a technical procedure to ensure equipment functionality.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine your unit is pinned down in a 'dead space' where your standard vehicle whip antenna cannot reach the Combat Operations Center. You have the radio, but the terrain is winning. In this moment, your ability to transform a few feet of copper wire and a handful of insulators into a high-performance antenna is the only thing that will get the Quick Reaction Force to your position. Field-expedient antenna construction is not just a technical skill; it is a survival skill for the tactical communicator.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for calculating antenna length and the physical construction of field-expedient wire antennas to optimize signal strength in marginal environments.
objectives: TLO-073: Implement tactical single-channel radio (SCR) antennas.
ELO-193: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-194: Construct a field-expedient wire antenna.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Antenna Length for Resonance
mainPoints.content: To ensure maximum power transfer, an antenna must be resonant at the operating frequency. For a half-wave dipole, the physical length is determined by the speed of light and the effects of end-capacitance in wire.
subPoints: Standard Formula: Length in feet = 468 / Frequency in MHz.
The resulting length represents the total span from end to end.
For a center-fed dipole, this length must be divided by two for each element (234 / Freq).
Accuracy Requirement: The cut must be within +/- 2% of the calculated value to maintain an acceptable Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

mainPoints.title: Field-Expedient Construction Techniques
mainPoints.content: When standard antennas are damaged or insufficient, Marines must use available materials to construct functional radiators per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 6.
subPoints: Materials: WD-1/TT field wire, insulators (buttons, plastic, or dry wood), and support structures (trees, masts).
Inverted Vee Configuration: A center-fed dipole where the center is elevated and the ends are sloped toward the ground, providing a mix of horizontal and vertical polarization.
Sloping Vee: A directional antenna requiring two wires sloped from a central mast toward the direction of the receiving station.
Safety: Ensure antennas are not placed near power lines and that the 'hot' elements are insulated from the ground and support structures.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team is tasked with establishing a reliable VHF net with a station 15 miles away over moderately rolling terrain. You are assigned a frequency of 50.50 MHz. You have a spool of WD-1/TT, two insulators, and a 20-foot mast.
steps: Calculate the total length of a half-wave dipole for 50.50 MHz using the 468/F formula.
Measure and cut two equal lengths of wire (each representing 1/4 wave).
Attach the wires to a center insulator and connect the transmission line (coax or balanced line).
Erect the antenna in an Inverted Vee configuration using the provided mast.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength improvement over the standard whip.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the mathematical requirements for antenna resonance and the physical steps to construct field-expedient wire antennas. By applying the 468/F formula and utilizing configurations like the Inverted Vee, you can overcome the limitations of standard-issue equipment.
conclusion.closingStatement: The difference between a marginal net and a reliable net is the Marine who knows how to adapt their equipment to the environment. Master these calculations and construction techniques to ensure the message always gets through.

introduction.gainAttention: Why does a radio work perfectly at noon but fail at midnight? Why can you hear a station 500 miles away but not the one 50 miles away? Radio waves are not magic; they follow the laws of physics. As a communicator, you must understand how to manipulate these waves using the right antenna characteristics to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.
introduction.overview: This lesson analyzes how radio waves interact with the environment and how to select antenna characteristics—such as gain, directivity, and take-off angle—to ensure successful communication circuits.
objectives: TLO-074: Analyze antenna characteristics for a radio communications circuit.
ELO-195: Explain the factors affecting radio wave propagation.
ELO-196: Compare antenna gain and directivity characteristics.
ELO-197: Determine the appropriate take-off angle for HF communications.

mainPoints.title: Radio Wave Propagation Factors
mainPoints.content: Radio waves interact with the Earth's atmosphere and terrain in three primary ways: reflection, diffraction, and refraction.
subPoints: Reflection: Waves 'bouncing' off the ground, buildings, or the ionosphere.
Diffraction: The 'bending' of waves over the top of obstacles like hills or mountains, allowing for communication in the 'shadow' of the obstacle.
Refraction: The bending of waves as they pass through different medium densities, such as the layers of the ionosphere in HF skywave propagation.

mainPoints.title: Gain and Directivity
mainPoints.content: Antennas do not create power; they concentrate it. Understanding how to focus this energy is critical for long-range or low-power operations.
subPoints: Omni-directional: Radiates energy equally in all directions (e.g., vertical whip). Best for mobile units and nets with stations in multiple directions.
Directional: Concentrates energy into a specific beam (e.g., Yagi, Sloping Vee). Increases 'Gain' in the desired direction while reducing interference from other directions.
Signal-to-Noise (S/N) Ratio: The goal of selecting a directional antenna is to maximize the signal at the receiver while minimizing background noise.

mainPoints.title: HF Take-Off Angles and NVIS
mainPoints.content: In HF communications, the angle at which the wave leaves the antenna (take-off angle) determines where the signal will return to Earth.
subPoints: Low Take-Off Angle: (Below 30 degrees) Used for long-distance skywave (DX) communications.
High Take-Off Angle: (60-90 degrees) Used for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS).
NVIS Benefits: Eliminates the 'skip zone' (the area where ground waves end but skywaves haven't returned yet), providing reliable comms over obstacles in a 0-300 mile range.
Antenna Height: To achieve NVIS, a dipole must be placed low to the ground (typically 1/8 to 1/4 wavelength high).

practicalApplication.scenario: You are established in a deep valley. Your distant station is 75 miles away, on the other side of a mountain range. You are using HF. Standard skywave is 'skipping' over them, and ground wave is blocked by the mountain.
steps: Identify the propagation requirement: Determine if this requires Ground Wave, Long-Range Skywave, or NVIS.
Select the appropriate take-off angle: Choose between low-angle (long distance) or high-angle (NVIS).
Select the antenna configuration: Determine the height of a half-wave dipole above ground to produce a 60-90 degree take-off angle.
Analyze the polarization: Determine if vertical or horizontal polarization is more effective for the chosen propagation path per MCRP 3-40.3C.

conclusion.summary: We have analyzed how reflection, diffraction, and refraction impact your signal. We compared omni-directional and directional antennas and identified how take-off angles, specifically NVIS, can be used to overcome terrain masking.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who simply 'turns it on' is a user; an operator who analyzes the propagation path and selects the perfect antenna is a professional. Use these principles to ensure the MAGTF maintains command and control in any environment.

tlo.behavior: Analyze antenna characteristics for a radio communications circuit.

tlo.justification: Level 4 (Analyze) is necessary because the Marine must differentiate between multiple variables (frequency, range, and propagation path) to determine the optimal antenna selection.

elos.justification: Understanding propagation fundamentals is necessary before a Marine can analyze which antenna characteristics will best mitigate path loss.

elos.standard: Differentiate between omni-directional and directional patterns to determine the most effective signal concentration for the intended receiver per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 2.
elos.justification: Analysis requires the ability to compare different technical specifications to find the optimal solution for a specific communication circuit.

elos.justification: Determining the take-off angle is a critical analytical step in matching antenna characteristics to the propagation path.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-intensity conflict where the commander needs immediate fire support. You have the radio, the frequency, and the coordinates, but if you cannot physically establish a link between your transmitter and the receiver, that mission fails. The radio link is the fundamental bridge of the MAGTF; without it, command and control ceases to exist.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the identification of radio link components, the physical connection of transmission lines, and the verification of signal integrity through radio checks.
objectives: Identify the components of a radio link (ELO-198)
Connect transmission lines to the radio and antenna (ELO-199)
Perform a radio signal check (ELO-200)

mainPoints.title: The Radio Communication Circuit
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 1, a complete radio communication circuit consists of six essential elements that must work in unison to facilitate information exchange.
subPoints: Transmitter: Generates the radio frequency (RF) signal.
Transmission Line: Transports the signal from the transmitter to the antenna.
Transmitting Antenna: Radiates the signal into space.
Propagation Path: The medium through which the signal travels.
Receiving Antenna: Intercepts the radiated signal.
Receiver: Demodulates the signal back into useful information.

mainPoints.title: Physical Connections and Impedance Matching
mainPoints.content: The physical connection between the radio and the antenna is the most common point of failure. Operators must ensure maximum power transfer by minimizing energy loss.
subPoints: Secure all connectors to prevent signal leakage or intermittent loss.
Use weather-proofing (e.g., electrical tape or sealant) for semi-permanent installations.
Utilize baluns (balanced-to-unbalanced) or adapters to match impedance and prevent standing waves.
Avoid sharp bends in coaxial cables which can cause signal attenuation.

mainPoints.title: Signal Verification (The Radio Check)
mainPoints.content: Once the physical link is established, the operator must verify the quality of the circuit using standardized reporting formats.
subPoints: Signal Strength: Rated from 1 (weak) to 5 (loud).
Readability: Rated from 1 (unreadable) to 5 (clear).
Standard response: 'Loud and Clear' indicates a fully functional link.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with setting up a VHF manpack radio station at a Forward Operating Base (FOB). You are provided with a PRC-117G, a whip antenna, and a 10-foot coaxial cable.
steps: Identify all components of the radio link provided in the kit.
Inspect the coaxial cable and connectors for damage.
Connect the transmission line to the radio's RF port and the base of the antenna.
Ensure the antenna is vertically polarized and clear of immediate obstructions.
Power on the system and perform a radio check with the distant station.
Report signal strength and readability to the instructor.

introduction.gainAttention: MCRP 3-40.3C states that the antenna is the one factor an operator has the most control over. By understanding how radio waves interact with the Earth and the atmosphere, you can turn a 'no-comm' situation into a reliable link, regardless of the distance or terrain.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the characteristics of ground wave and sky wave propagation, the impact of the atmosphere on signals, and how to select the correct mode for your mission.
objectives: Identify the characteristics of ground wave and sky wave propagation (ELO-201)
Explain the impact of the Earth's atmosphere on radio wave propagation (ELO-202)
Select the appropriate propagation mode (ground or sky wave) (ELO-203)

mainPoints.title: Types of Propagation
mainPoints.content: Radio waves travel from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna via different paths depending on frequency and antenna type.
subPoints: Ground Waves: Comprised of surface waves (following the Earth's curvature) and space waves (line-of-sight). Best for short-range VHF/UHF.
Sky Waves: Radiated upward and reflected back to Earth by the ionosphere. Essential for long-range HF communications.
Surface Waves: Affected by the conductivity of the Earth's surface; better over water than dry land.

mainPoints.title: Atmospheric Effects
mainPoints.content: The Earth's atmosphere is not a vacuum; it actively changes the direction and strength of radio signals.
subPoints: Troposphere: The lowest layer; causes refraction and can lead to 'ducting' in certain weather conditions.
Ionosphere: Contains layers (D, E, F1, F2) that change density based on time of day and solar activity. This layer reflects HF waves back to Earth.
Refraction vs. Reflection: Refraction is the bending of waves; reflection is the 'bouncing' of waves off an atmospheric layer.

mainPoints.title: Selecting the Propagation Mode
mainPoints.content: Selection depends on the distance to the distant station and the assigned frequency band.
subPoints: Short range (0-30 miles): Utilize ground wave propagation with VHF/UHF frequencies.
Medium to Long range (30-2500+ miles): Utilize sky wave propagation with HF frequencies.
NVIS (Near Vertical Incidence Skywave): A specific sky wave technique for communicating over obstacles (mountains) at short ranges (0-300 miles).

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is operating in a mountainous region. You need to establish a link with a unit 150 miles away located on the other side of a 10,000-foot ridgeline. You have both HF and VHF assets available.
steps: Analyze the distance (150 miles) and the terrain (mountainous obstruction).
Determine why ground wave (line-of-sight) will fail in this scenario.
Select the appropriate propagation mode (Sky Wave/NVIS).
Identify the atmospheric layer (Ionosphere) required to reflect the signal.
Select the appropriate frequency band (HF) to achieve the reflection.

conclusion.summary: We have analyzed the differences between ground and sky wave propagation, how the ionosphere enables long-distance comms, and how to select the mode based on mission parameters.
conclusion.closingStatement: Understanding the environment is just as important as understanding the hardware. Use the atmosphere to your advantage to maintain the link.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine establishing a Command Post in a valley to hide from the enemy, only to realize your radio operators cannot reach the higher headquarters because of terrain masking, or worse, your own radios are interfering with each other so much that no one can hear a clear transmission. The success of the MAGTF depends on our ability to communicate; that communication starts with where and how we plant our antennas.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the critical factors for selecting and organizing an antenna farm, including tactical, technical, and doctrinal considerations, noise analysis, and internal layout principles to ensure maximum signal propagation.
objectives: TLO-077: Determine a site for an antenna farm.
ELO-204: List tactical, technical, and doctrinal siting considerations for an antenna farm.
ELO-205: Analyze potential sources of man-made and natural noise.
ELO-206: Plan the internal arrangement of antennas within the farm.

mainPoints.title: Siting Considerations
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8, selecting a site requires balancing three primary categories of constraints to ensure the antenna farm supports the Command Post (CP) effectively.
subPoints: Tactical: Focus on security, concealment from enemy observation, and protection from electronic warfare.
Technical: Focus on ground conductivity, elevation for line-of-sight, and avoiding obstructions like dense vegetation or buildings.
Doctrinal: Proximity to the CP (usually within 1 kilometer) and accessibility for maintenance personnel.

mainPoints.title: Noise and Interference Analysis
mainPoints.content: Operators must identify and mitigate interference that can degrade signal quality. Noise is categorized into natural and man-made sources.
subPoints: Natural Noise: Atmospheric interference (lightning) and galactic noise, as well as terrain masking (mountains/hills).
Man-made Noise: Power lines, generators, electric motors, and other electronic equipment in the vicinity.
Mitigation: Siting antennas away from high-traffic roads and power grids to reduce the noise floor.

mainPoints.title: Internal Arrangement and Layout
mainPoints.content: Proper layout within the farm prevents co-site interference, where one transmitter 'swamps' a nearby receiver.
subPoints: Separation: Maintain maximum physical distance between antennas, especially those operating in the same frequency band.
Polarization: Use consistent polarization (vertical or horizontal) for the intended link, but consider cross-polarization to reduce interference between local antennas.
Frequency Banding: Grouping antennas by band (HF, VHF, UHF) to manage cable runs and power requirements.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Radio Chief for a Battalion Landing Team. You have been given a 1:50,000 scale map and a list of 12 radio nets (4 HF, 6 VHF, 2 UHF). You must select a site within 800 meters of the planned CP location.
steps: Identify three potential sites on the map based on elevation and accessibility.
Conduct a site survey to identify man-made noise sources (e.g., nearby power lines).
Draft a site diagram showing the placement of each antenna.
Verify that separation distances meet the requirements to prevent co-site interference.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the tactical and technical requirements for siting an antenna farm, how to identify noise sources, and the principles of internal layout to ensure clear communications.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio is only as good as its antenna, and an antenna is only as good as its location. Master these siting principles to ensure the Commander's intent is always heard.

introduction.gainAttention: In the heat of a fire mission, a radio operator realizes they cannot reach the supporting artillery battery because they selected a VHF radio for a 60-mile shot over a mountain range. This is a failure of basic signal theory. Understanding which frequency band to use for specific distances is the difference between a successful mission and a catastrophic silence.
introduction.overview: This lesson provides the criteria for selecting the correct frequency band and equipment based on mission range and environmental constraints, following the standards in MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-078: Apply frequency band and equipment selection criteria.
ELO-207: State the frequency ranges and distance capabilities for HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
ELO-208: Describe the relationship between antenna length, polarization, and frequency.
ELO-209: Select the specific antenna type and radio set required.

mainPoints.title: Frequency Band Capabilities
mainPoints.content: Radio waves behave differently based on their frequency. MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1 defines the standard planning ranges.
subPoints: High Frequency (HF): 3-30 MHz. Ground wave (0-50 miles); Sky wave (100-8000 miles). Used for long-range comms.
Very High Frequency (VHF): 30-300 MHz. Range 0-30 miles. Primary band for tactical maneuver units.
Ultra High Frequency (UHF): 300 MHz-3 GHz. Range 0-50 miles (Line of Sight) or global via SATCOM.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Fundamentals: Length and Polarization
mainPoints.content: The physical characteristics of an antenna must match the frequency and the desired path of the signal.
subPoints: Antenna Length: There is an inverse relationship between frequency and length; as frequency increases, the required antenna length decreases.
Polarization: Vertical polarization is standard for mobile/whip antennas; horizontal polarization is often used for HF sky wave to reduce ground loss.
Resonance: An antenna must be 'cut' or adjusted to the specific frequency to ensure maximum power transfer.

mainPoints.title: Equipment Selection Criteria
mainPoints.content: Selecting the right radio and antenna depends on the mission's distance, terrain, and mobility requirements.
subPoints: Short Range (Tactical): VHF manpack (e.g., PRC-117G) with a whip antenna.
Long Range (Beyond Line of Sight): HF radio (e.g., PRC-150) with a NVIS or Dipole antenna.
Satellite: UHF/SHF dedicated terminals for over-the-horizon requirements.

practicalApplication.scenario: A reconnaissance team is inserting 450 miles away from the ship. They must maintain a constant voice link. You must select the frequency band, the radio set, and the antenna type for this mission.
steps: Identify the range requirement (450 miles).
Consult Table 1-1 to determine the correct band (HF Sky wave).
Select the appropriate radio (PRC-150).
Calculate the required antenna length for the assigned frequency using the formula in Chapter 2.
Determine the best polarization for the environment.

conclusion.summary: We have reviewed the planning ranges for HF, VHF, and UHF, the relationship between frequency and antenna physical properties, and the selection process for mission-specific equipment.
conclusion.closingStatement: Selecting the right tool for the job is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Use MCRP 3-40.3C as your guide to ensure the MAGTF stays connected across any distance.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a Combat Operations Center (COC) during a high-tempo operation. The Commander needs to transmit a critical FRAGO, but every time the VHF radio keys up, the HF receiver screams with static, and the data link drops. This isn't a hardware failure; it's a planning failure. Improper antenna placement creates 'cosite interference' that can blind a unit as effectively as enemy electronic warfare. Today, we will learn how to plan an antenna farm that ensures clear, uninterrupted communications.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the critical factors for selecting a site and laying out multiple antennas in a tactical environment to minimize interference and maximize signal integrity.
objectives: TLO-079: Plan an antenna farm layout.
ELO-210: Identify site selection considerations for an antenna farm.
ELO-211: Explain antenna farm layout principles regarding polarization and separation.
ELO-212: Determine required antenna spacing and placement.

mainPoints.title: Site Selection Considerations
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8, site selection must balance tactical requirements with technical necessity.
subPoints: Tactical Considerations: Mission requirements, security, cover, concealment, and accessibility.
Technical Considerations: Soil conductivity (moist loam is best), distance from man-made noise sources (power lines, generators), and terrain obstacles (clear line-of-sight for VHF/UHF).
Command Post Types: Distinguish between Tactical, Main, and Rear command post footprints.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Farm Layout Principles
mainPoints.content: The goal of layout planning is to minimize Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) and cosite interference through physical and frequency separation.
subPoints: Polarization: Use different polarizations (vertical vs. horizontal) to provide up to 20dB of isolation between antennas.
Frequency Band Separation: Group antennas by frequency band (HF, VHF, UHF) to prevent cross-band harmonic interference.
Directionality: Point directional antennas away from sensitive receivers.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Spacing and Placement
mainPoints.content: Specific distance requirements must be maintained to ensure electromagnetic compatibility (EMC).
subPoints: Horizontal Separation: The physical distance between antenna masts to prevent near-field coupling.
Vertical Separation: Placing antennas at different heights on a single mast or terrain feature to reduce interference.
Power and Signal Line Routing: Ensure power cables and signal lines do not run parallel for long distances to prevent induction noise.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Radio Chief for a Battalion Landing Team. You have been provided a 100m x 100m plot for a Main Command Post. You must layout three VHF OE-254s, two HF dipoles, and one SATCOM antenna.
steps: Analyze the terrain for highest points and soil quality.
Identify man-made noise sources (e.g., the generator pit).
Plot antenna positions on a site map ensuring maximum horizontal separation.
Assign polarizations to minimize interference between adjacent nets.
Brief the layout to the instructor, justifying placement based on MCRP 3-40.3C standards.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the tactical and technical considerations for site selection, the principles of polarization and separation, and the specific requirements for antenna spacing.
conclusion.closingStatement: A well-planned antenna farm is the backbone of reliable C2. By applying these principles, you ensure that the Commander's voice is heard when it matters most.

introduction.gainAttention: Standard whip antennas have a 'skip zone'—an area too far for ground waves but too close for standard skywaves. If your unit is 50 miles away behind a mountain range, a standard antenna will fail you. The AS-2259/GR is designed specifically to solve this problem by shooting the signal straight up to bounce off the ionosphere and come straight back down, like a tactical 'satellite' made of air. This is Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS).
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the components, theory, and assembly of the AS-2259/GR antenna for NVIS communications.
objectives: TLO-080: Perform AS-2259/GR antenna employment.
ELO-213: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna.
ELO-214: Describe Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation characteristics.
ELO-215: Assemble the AS-2259/GR antenna.

mainPoints.title: NVIS Propagation Theory
mainPoints.content: NVIS uses high take-off angles (60-90 degrees) to provide reliable communications over obstacles and into deep valleys.
subPoints: Range: Typically effective from 0 to 300 miles.
Frequency: Generally operates between 2 and 12 MHz.
Terrain Independence: Because the signal travels vertically, it is not blocked by mountains or dense vegetation.

mainPoints.title: AS-2259/GR Components
mainPoints.content: The AS-2259/GR is a tactical, collapsible antenna kit designed for rapid deployment.
subPoints: Mast Sections: Seven fiberglass sections that provide the vertical structure.
Radiators: Two crossed-dipole wire assemblies that also act as guy wires.
Base and Top Cap: The interface for the coaxial cable and the termination point for the radiators.
Stakes and Carrying Bag: Essential for securing the antenna and transport.

mainPoints.title: Assembly and Erection Procedures
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly ensures the antenna remains vertical and the radiators are correctly tensioned for resonance.
subPoints: Site Leveling: Ensure the base is on flat ground.
Sequential Assembly: Adding mast sections while maintaining control of the radiator wires.
Tensioning: Using the guy stakes to ensure the mast is perfectly vertical and the wires are taut.
Connection: Attaching the RG-213 or similar coaxial cable to the radio's HF coupler.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team must establish an HF NVIS link with a higher headquarters located 75 miles away. You have been issued an AS-2259/GR kit and an HF radio set.
steps: Inventory all AS-2259/GR components.
Select a clear 60-foot diameter circle for the antenna footprint.
Assemble the mast sections and top cap.
Erect the antenna, securing the radiator wires to the stakes at 90-degree intervals.
Connect the antenna to the radio and perform a successful radio check.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the unique NVIS capabilities of the AS-2259/GR, identified its components, and practiced the steps for assembly.
conclusion.closingStatement: Mastering the AS-2259/GR gives you the ability to communicate in the most restrictive terrain on earth. When the mountains block your path, NVIS goes over them.

title: Construction of Field-Expedient Half-Wave Dipole Antennas

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a contested environment where your primary whip antenna has been damaged by shrapnel or vegetation. Without a replacement, your unit is isolated. However, with a spool of copper wire and some basic insulators, you can construct a half-wave dipole that not only restores communications but likely outperforms your original antenna in signal strength and reliability. Mastering the dipole is the difference between being 'off the air' and maintaining the common operational picture.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mathematical calculation, material selection, and physical construction of a field-expedient half-wave dipole antenna using standard and improvised materials found in a tactical environment.
objectives: TLO-081: Construct a field-expedient half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-216: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-217: Identify suitable materials for antenna radiators and insulators.
ELO-218: Demonstrate wire splicing and insulator attachment techniques.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Length Calculation
mainPoints.content: The physical length of an antenna must correspond to the electrical wavelength of the assigned frequency to achieve resonance. For a half-wave dipole, we use the standard formula derived from the speed of light and the 'end effect' of wire.
subPoints: The formula is: Length in feet = 468 / Frequency in MHz.
This total length is then divided by two to determine the length of each individual leg (element) of the dipole.
Calculations must be accurate to within 1 inch to ensure a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

mainPoints.title: Material Selection and Properties
mainPoints.content: Field-expedient antennas require an understanding of conductivity and dielectric properties to ensure signal radiation rather than absorption.
subPoints: Radiators: Copper wire is preferred for high conductivity; WD-1/TT (slash wire) can be used but requires stripping and twisting of strands.
Insulators: Used to prevent the signal from grounding out through support structures. Suitable materials include plastic, glass, or dry wood.
Feed Lines: Coaxial cable (RG-213) or twin-lead must be used to connect the radio to the center of the antenna.

mainPoints.title: Construction and Splicing Techniques
mainPoints.content: Mechanical strength is just as important as electrical continuity. If a splice fails, the link fails.
subPoints: Use the Western Union splice for wire-to-wire connections to ensure maximum tensile strength.
Insulators must be secured using knots that do not slip, such as the bowline or two half-hitches.
The center insulator (feed point) must be weather-sealed if possible to prevent moisture from entering the coaxial cable.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your team is assigned a frequency of 7.5 MHz for a long-range HF shot. You have a spool of copper wire, two plastic insulators, and a length of RG-58 coax. You must calculate the lengths and construct the antenna for immediate deployment.
steps: Calculate total length: 468 / 7.5 = 62.4 feet.
Divide by two for each leg: 31.2 feet (31 feet, 2.4 inches).
Measure and cut two lengths of wire to the calculated dimension.
Attach the wires to the center insulator and connect the coax center conductor to one leg and the shield to the other.
Attach end insulators and secure the antenna to support structures (trees or masts).

conclusion.summary: We have covered the critical formula for antenna resonance (468/f), the selection of conductive and non-conductive materials, and the physical assembly of the dipole.
conclusion.closingStatement: A Marine's ability to build an antenna from scratch is a hallmark of technical proficiency. Ensure your calculations are precise; in the world of HF communications, an inch of wire can be the difference between a clear voice and total silence.

introduction.gainAttention: Have you ever noticed your radio chassis getting hot or receiving a 'RF burn' when you touch the handset? This is a clear indicator of a poor ground. An antenna is only half of a system; the Earth itself acts as the other half. Without a proper ground, your radiated power is wasted, and your equipment is at risk. Today we fix that.
introduction.overview: This lesson details the types of grounding systems, methods for improving conductivity in poor soil, and the physical installation of ground rods and leads per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-082: Implement an antenna ground system.
ELO-219: Identify the three primary types of ground systems.
ELO-220: Describe methods for improving soil conductivity.
ELO-221: Install a ground rod and lead.

mainPoints.title: Types of Ground Systems
mainPoints.content: Depending on the frequency and the antenna type, different grounding methods are required to provide an effective reflecting surface.
subPoints: Earth Ground: A direct connection to the soil using rods or pipes.
Counterpoise: A network of wires elevated above the ground, used when the earth itself is too resistive.
Ground Screen: A mesh of wires placed directly on the ground surface to reduce ground resistance.

mainPoints.title: Improving Soil Conductivity
mainPoints.content: In environments like deserts (sand) or mountains (rock), the soil does not naturally conduct electricity well. We must 'treat' the soil to improve performance.
subPoints: Chemical Treatment: Adding salt water or magnesium sulfate to the area around the ground rod.
Multiple Rods: Connecting several ground rods in parallel to increase the surface area contact with the earth.
Deep Driving: Driving rods deeper into the water table where conductivity is naturally higher.

mainPoints.title: Installation and Bonding
mainPoints.content: The connection between the radio and the ground must be as short and direct as possible to minimize impedance.
subPoints: Ground rods should be driven at least 6-8 feet into the earth if possible.
The ground lead (wire) must be securely bonded to the radio's ground lug or chassis.
Ensure all connections are free of paint, rust, or corrosion to maintain electrical continuity.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are setting up a base station in a dry, sandy environment. The radio is showing high reflected power. You must install a grounding system and treat the soil to ensure the link is established.
steps: Identify the grounding lug on the radio chassis.
Drive a standard ground rod into the earth at a 90-degree angle.
Prepare a saline solution (salt and water) and saturate the soil around the rod.
Connect a heavy-gauge ground lead from the rod to the radio using a grounding clamp.
Test the system for a reduction in reflected power or RF interference.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the three types of grounds (earth, counterpoise, screen), how to use salt water to fix poor soil conductivity, and the proper installation of ground rods.
conclusion.closingStatement: A solid ground is the foundation of every successful radio site. It protects your equipment, protects your Marines, and ensures your signal reaches its destination. Never consider an antenna 'installed' until the ground is verified.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a remote patrol base, and your only link to the Combat Operations Center is a field-expedient wire antenna. A sudden mortar strike or even a fallen branch snaps that wire. Without a spare antenna, your unit is isolated. Knowing how to restore that electrical connection isn't just a technical skill—it is a survival requirement for maintaining Command and Control (C2).
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the identification of antenna damage, the execution of the Western Union splice for field repair, and the verification of electrical continuity to ensure the antenna is mission-ready.
objectives: TLO-083: Given a damaged wire antenna, splicing materials, and hand tools, perform field repair of wire antennas, restoring electrical continuity to support mission requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
ELO-222: Identify types of antenna wire damage including breaks, insulation wear, and connector corrosion.
ELO-223: Demonstrate a Western Union splice ensuring the splice is mechanically secure and provides metal-to-metal contact.
ELO-224: Verify electrical continuity confirming the circuit is closed and the antenna is capable of radiating energy.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Damage Assessment
mainPoints.content: Before repairs can begin, the operator must conduct a thorough visual and physical inspection of the antenna system.
subPoints: Identify physical breaks in the copper or copper-clad steel conductor.
Inspect for insulation wear or 'nicks' that could cause grounding against wet vegetation or masts.
Check for connector corrosion (oxidation) which increases resistance and degrades signal quality.
Reference MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 6, Section: Wire Antennas.

mainPoints.title: The Western Union Splice
mainPoints.content: The Western Union splice is the standard military field repair for wire conductors because it provides maximum mechanical strength and excellent electrical conductivity.
subPoints: Strip approximately 4-6 inches of insulation from both ends of the broken wire.
Cross the wires and wrap each end tightly around the standing part of the opposite wire (at least 5-7 turns).
Ensure the wraps are tight and provide 'metal-to-metal' contact without gaps.
Apply electrical tape to protect the splice from further oxidation and environmental wear.

mainPoints.title: Verification of Continuity
mainPoints.content: A repair is not complete until the electrical path is verified. A visually 'good' splice may still fail electrically.
subPoints: Use a multimeter set to the Ohms (Ω) or Continuity setting to check for a closed circuit.
If a multimeter is unavailable, perform a radio check and monitor the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR).
Confirm the antenna is capable of radiating energy without arcing at the repair point.

practicalApplication.scenario: During a field exercise, your HF dipole antenna has been severed in two places due to vehicle movement. You are provided with a multi-tool and electrical tape.
steps: Locate the two break points in the antenna wire.
Strip the insulation back 5 inches on all four severed ends.
Execute two Western Union splices to rejoin the antenna segments.
Verify the mechanical strength by applying a moderate tug to the wire.
Use a multimeter to confirm continuity from the connector to the end of the wire.

conclusion.summary: We have covered how to identify antenna damage, the specific steps to perform a Western Union splice, and how to verify that your repair will actually support radio communications.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the fleet, you won't always have a brand-new antenna in the SL-3 kit. Your ability to repair what you have ensures the MAGTF remains connected and lethal.

tlo.standard: restoring electrical continuity to support mission requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The Marine must execute a specific set of mechanical skills (splicing and sealing) to restore a system to its operational state.

title: Integration of Baluns in Antenna Systems

introduction.gainAttention: Have you ever noticed excessive noise on your HF nets or a radio that gets 'hot' to the touch during transmission? This is often caused by an impedance mismatch or an unbalanced feed line trying to drive a balanced antenna. By using a balun, you can eliminate this 'stray' RF and significantly improve your signal-to-noise ratio.
introduction.overview: This lesson explains the differences between balanced and unbalanced circuits, how to identify a balun, and the proper procedure for integrating a balun into a dipole antenna system.
objectives: TLO-084: Given a balanced antenna, an unbalanced transmitter output, and a balun, execute the integration of a balun into an antenna system per MCRP 3-40.3C.
ELO-225: Differentiate between balanced and unbalanced circuits.
ELO-226: Identify the physical components of a balun.
ELO-227: Connect a balun to the antenna system.

mainPoints.title: Balanced vs. Unbalanced Circuits
mainPoints.content: Understanding the electrical characteristics of your components is critical for efficient power transfer.
subPoints: Unbalanced Circuits: Typically coaxial cable (RG-213/RG-58) where one conductor is grounded (the shield).
Balanced Circuits: Typically dipole antennas or twin-lead wire where both sides have equal impedance to ground.
The Balun (Balanced-to-Unbalanced) acts as a transformer to bridge these two different circuit types.
Reference MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 3, Section: Baluns.

mainPoints.title: Balun Identification and Components
mainPoints.content: Operators must be able to distinguish baluns from standard insulators or center-feeds.
subPoints: Housing: Weatherproof casing containing the toroidal transformer.
Unbalanced Port: Usually an SO-239 (UHF) connector for the coaxial feed line.
Balanced Terminals: Two wing-nuts or eyelets for attaching antenna wire elements.
Ratio Markings: Look for 1:1 or 4:1 markings indicating the impedance transformation ratio.

mainPoints.title: Integration Procedures
mainPoints.content: Proper connection ensures the balun functions correctly and prevents damage to the radio's final power amplifier.
subPoints: Mount the balun at the center point of the antenna (e.g., the apex of a dipole).
Connect the coaxial feed line to the unbalanced SO-239 connector.
Attach the two antenna wire elements to the balanced terminal lugs.
Ensure all connections are finger-tight and weather-sealed if the installation is long-term.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with setting up a 40-meter horizontal dipole using a spool of WD-1/TT wire and a standard 50-ohm coaxial cable. You must integrate a 1:1 balun to ensure system efficiency.
steps: Identify the 1:1 balun from the provided antenna kit.
Connect the PL-259 connector of the coaxial cable to the base of the balun.
Attach the left and right legs of the dipole wire to the balanced terminals on the sides of the balun.
Secure the wires using the provided wing-nuts.
Hoist the antenna and perform a VSWR check to ensure the integration was successful.

conclusion.summary: We have defined balanced and unbalanced circuits, identified the components of a balun, and demonstrated how to connect one to a field antenna.
conclusion.closingStatement: A balun is the 'handshake' between your radio and the atmosphere. Mastering its use ensures your signal goes to the receiver, not back into your radio as heat.

tlo.behavior: execute the integration of a balun into an antenna system
tlo.standard: transforming energy between balanced and unbalanced circuits to reduce noise and improve signal quality per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task involves the practical application of hardware components into a circuit to achieve a specific technical outcome.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes tactical environment, attempting to establish a critical link for a Call for Fire. You have a functional radio and a clear line of sight, but your signal is unreadable. The difference between a successful mission and a communications failure often comes down to a simple 90-degree physical adjustment of your antenna. Understanding polarization is the difference between a 'broken' radio and a lethal Marine.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of antenna polarization, the specific advantages of vertical and horizontal orientations, and how to select the correct polarization based on frequency bands and communication modes as outlined in MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: ELO-228: Define antenna polarization
ELO-229: Describe the advantages of vertical and horizontal polarization
ELO-230: Differentiate polarization requirements by frequency band

mainPoints.title: Fundamentals of Polarization
mainPoints.content: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric field (E-field) with respect to the Earth's surface.
subPoints: Vertical Polarization: The electric lines of force are perpendicular to the Earth's surface.
Horizontal Polarization: The electric lines of force are parallel to the Earth's surface.
Circular Polarization: The E-field rotates as it propagates (commonly used in SATCOM).

mainPoints.title: Advantages of Polarization Types
mainPoints.content: The choice of polarization impacts signal strength based on the environment and noise levels.
subPoints: Vertical Advantages: Easier to use with mobile/manpack whips; provides better ground wave propagation; requires less physical space.

Horizontal Advantages: Less susceptible to manmade noise (which is usually vertically polarized); better for sky wave propagation in HF; less likely to be detected by enemy direction-finding equipment in certain terrains.

mainPoints.title: Frequency Band Requirements
mainPoints.content: Polarization must be matched between the transmitting and receiving stations to minimize 'polarization loss.'
subPoints: HF Band: Uses both vertical (ground wave) and horizontal (sky wave/NVIS) depending on the mission.
VHF/UHF Bands: Predominantly use vertical polarization for line-of-sight and tactical FM communications.
Requirement: If the transmitting antenna is vertical, the receiving antenna must be vertical to ensure maximum signal transfer.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Radio Supervisor for a platoon-sized patrol. You are tasked with establishing a VHF link to the COC (Line of Sight) and an HF link to the Rear (Sky Wave).
steps: Identify the correct polarization for the VHF whip antenna to maximize ground wave reach.
Orient the HF Dipole antenna horizontally to support sky wave propagation for long-distance comms.
Inspect the antenna farm to ensure all antennas are oriented correctly to match the receiving stations' polarization.

conclusion.summary: We have defined polarization as the orientation of the E-field, identified the tactical advantages of vertical and horizontal orientations, and determined how to apply these concepts across HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
conclusion.closingStatement: Proper antenna orientation is a basic but vital skill. Never assume a weak signal is a hardware failure until you have verified that your polarization matches your net.

tlo.condition: Given a mission requirement, a tactical radio, and a specific frequency band (LF, MF, HF, VHF, or UHF).
tlo.behavior: analyze antenna polarization requirements
tlo.standard: ensuring transmitting and receiving antennas are oriented to provide the strongest possible signal and minimize loss per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: The Marine must evaluate multiple variables including frequency band and propagation mode (Ground vs. Sky wave) to determine the correct orientation, which requires breaking down the environmental factors to understand their relationship to signal strength.

elos.standard: identifying the orientation of the electric field with respect to the Earth's surface per Chapter 2, Section I.
elos.justification: Foundational knowledge of the term is required before analysis of requirements can occur.

elos.behavior: describe the advantages of vertical and horizontal polarization
elos.standard: detailing ground wave characteristics and manmade noise suppression for each per Chapter 2, Section I.
elos.justification: Understanding the pros/cons of each polarization type is a prerequisite for selecting the correct orientation in a mission.

introduction.gainAttention: Have you ever noticed that your HF radio works perfectly at 1200, but by 2000 the signal has completely vanished? You didn't change your settings, and the radio isn't broken. The atmosphere itself has changed. As a Marine communicator, you must understand the 'invisible' terrain of the ionosphere to maintain command and control.
introduction.overview: This lesson details the structure of the ionosphere, how regular variations like the time of day affect your signal, and how to diagnose irregular disturbances that can crash your HF nets.
objectives: ELO-231: Describe the layers of the ionosphere
ELO-232: Explain regular ionospheric variations
ELO-233: Diagnose irregular ionospheric disturbances

mainPoints.title: Layers of the Ionosphere
mainPoints.content: The ionosphere consists of several layers of ionized gas that refract HF radio waves back to Earth.
subPoints: D Layer: Lowest layer (37-57 miles); absorbs HF signals; disappears at night.
E Layer: Middle layer (62-93 miles); aids in medium-range daytime comms.
F Layer: Highest and most important for long-range comms; splits into F1 and F2 during the day and merges at night.

mainPoints.title: Regular Variations
mainPoints.content: Ionization levels change predictably based on the sun's activity.
subPoints: Daily: Ionization is highest at noon and lowest at night, requiring frequency changes (higher frequencies by day, lower by night).
Seasonal: The sun's angle changes ionization levels throughout the year.
Solar Cycle: An 11-year cycle of sunspot activity that dictates long-term HF propagation quality.

mainPoints.title: Irregular Disturbances
mainPoints.content: Unpredictable events can cause immediate and total communication blackouts.
subPoints: Sudden Ionospheric Disturbance (SID): Caused by solar flares; results in immediate absorption of HF signals on the sunlit side of Earth.
Ionospheric Storms: Caused by solar particle radiation; can last several days and causes erratic signal fading and increased noise.

practicalApplication.scenario: During a 24-hour training exercise, your HF net experiences a total signal loss at 1400 local time immediately following a reported solar flare. Later, at 0200, the signal becomes weak and 'watery.'
steps: Identify the 1400 blackout as a Sudden Ionospheric Disturbance (SID).
Determine the appropriate layer (F2) to target for long-range comms during the day.
Adjust the frequency downward for the 0200 link to account for the lower ionization levels at night.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the D, E, and F layers of the ionosphere, the predictable daily and seasonal changes in propagation, and the irregular disturbances like SIDs that can disrupt our mission.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ionosphere is a dynamic environment. A Marine who can predict its changes is a Marine who can always get the message through.

tlo.condition: Given a High Frequency (HF) radio net and observed signal degradation or loss.
tlo.behavior: Analyze ionospheric effects on communications.
tlo.standard: Identifying the specific ionospheric variation affecting the circuit and determining the impact on the communication link per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: The task requires the Marine to break down observed signal behavior (degradation/loss) into specific causes such as SID, Ionospheric Storms, or Sporadic E to understand the relationship between atmospheric conditions and circuit performance. This requires analysis of variables rather than simple recall or application.

elos.behavior: describe the layers of the ionosphere
elos.standard: identifying the D, E, and F (F1/F2) layers and their relative altitudes per Chapter 1.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the ionospheric structure is required to analyze how it affects radio waves.

elos.behavior: explain regular ionospheric variations
elos.standard: accounting for daily, seasonal, and solar cycle changes that impact HF propagation per Chapter 1.
elos.justification: Operators must understand predictable variations to distinguish them from irregular disturbances during analysis.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley in a remote AO, hundreds of miles from the nearest relay or satellite footprint. Your mission depends on getting a SITREP to the COC. Without a satellite, your only lifeline is the sky—specifically, the ability to bounce a signal off the ionosphere and land it exactly on your target. Mastering sky wave propagation is the difference between mission success and total isolation.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mechanics of sky wave propagation, including the terminology of skip zones, the determination of the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF), and the calculation of antenna take-off angles required for long-distance HF communication.
objectives: ELO-234: Define sky wave propagation terms (skip distance, skip zone, and multi-hop transmission).
ELO-235: Determine the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF).
ELO-236: Calculate the required take-off angle.

mainPoints.title: Sky Wave Propagation Terminology
mainPoints.content: Understanding the geometry of a sky wave path is essential for establishing a link. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 1, we must distinguish between where the signal goes and where it is lost.
subPoints: Skip Distance: The distance from the transmitter to the point where the sky wave first returns to Earth.
Skip Zone: The 'dead space' between the end of the ground wave's reach and the beginning of the first sky wave's return.
Multi-hop: When a signal reflects off the ionosphere, bounces off the Earth, and reflects off the ionosphere again to reach extreme distances.

mainPoints.title: Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF)
mainPoints.content: The MUF is the highest frequency that will be returned to Earth for a given distance. If you exceed the MUF, your signal passes through the ionosphere into space.
subPoints: Frequency must be high enough to overcome D-layer absorption.
Frequency must be low enough (below the MUF) to ensure refraction back to Earth.
The Frequency of Optimum Transmission (FOT) is generally 85% of the MUF.

mainPoints.title: Take-off Angle and Antenna Geometry
mainPoints.content: The angle at which the signal leaves the antenna (take-off angle) determines where it will land. This is controlled by antenna type and height above ground.
subPoints: Lower take-off angles (closer to the horizon) result in longer skip distances.
Higher take-off angles are used for shorter distances (NVIS).
Adjusting antenna height relative to wavelength (λ) is the primary method for field-tuning the take-off angle.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with establishing a link to a station 800 miles away. You are provided with a propagation chart and a 150-foot wire for a half-wave dipole.
steps: Identify the skip distance required (800 miles).
Consult the propagation diagram to find the MUF for the current time of day.
Select an operating frequency (FOT) approximately 15% below the MUF.
Calculate the required take-off angle for an 800-mile skip.
Determine the necessary antenna height to achieve that take-off angle per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 2.

conclusion.summary: We have defined the critical terms of sky wave propagation, identified how to determine the MUF to prevent signal loss into space, and explained how to manipulate take-off angles to hit a specific target distance.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ionosphere is a constantly shifting medium. By mastering these calculations, you ensure that your signal reaches its destination regardless of the distance or terrain.

tlo.behavior: Execute sky wave transmission paths.
tlo.standard: Determining the necessary frequency and angle of incidence to ensure the signal reflects off the ionosphere to the target skip distance per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: This is a procedural task involving the application of technical calculations (critical angle, ionization density) to a specific operational requirement. The Marine must use information in a concrete situation to achieve a specific outcome.

elos.standard: including skip distance, skip zone, and multi-hop transmission per Chapter 1.
