title: Frequency Selection for Sky Wave Propagation

introduction.gainAttention: The sun is the most powerful signal jammer—and the most powerful repeater—in the MAGTF. It creates the very layers we use to communicate over the horizon, but it also creates the layers that swallow our signals whole. If you don't understand the ionosphere, you are just guessing with your frequency dial.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the structure of the ionosphere and how solar activity dictates frequency selection. We will examine the D, E, and F layers and the concepts of Critical Frequency and MUF.
objectives: ELO-237: Identify the layers of the ionosphere (D, E, and F).
ELO-238: Explain the concepts of Critical Frequency and Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF).

mainPoints.title: Layers of the Ionosphere
mainPoints.content: The ionosphere is divided into distinct layers based on ionization density, each affecting HF waves differently per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 1.
subPoints: D-Layer: The lowest layer; exists only during daylight. It primarily absorbs low-frequency energy.
E-Layer: The middle layer; helps with medium-distance skip and disappears mostly at night.
F-Layer: The highest and most important layer for long-haul comms. It splits into F1 and F2 during the day and merges at night.

mainPoints.title: Critical Frequency and Solar Effects
mainPoints.content: Critical frequency is the highest frequency that will be returned to Earth when transmitted vertically. It is the baseline for all sky wave planning.
subPoints: Higher solar activity (sunspots/daylight) increases ionization, raising the critical frequency.
At night, ionization levels drop, requiring the use of lower frequencies.
If the operating frequency is above the critical frequency and the angle is too steep, the wave will not return.

practicalApplication.scenario: It is 1200 local time. You are experiencing high signal attenuation on your lower HF frequencies. You must transition your net to a more effective frequency based on the current state of the ionosphere.
steps: Identify the current dominant ionospheric layer (D-layer absorption is high at noon).
Determine if the current frequency is being absorbed by the D-layer or passing through the F-layer.
Explain why a higher frequency (closer to the MUF) is required during peak daylight to 'punch through' the D-layer.
Select a new frequency that remains below the Critical Frequency for the F2 layer.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the D, E, and F layers of the atmosphere and their roles in absorption and refraction. We also covered how solar radiation dictates the Critical Frequency and MUF.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator who understands the ionosphere can 'see' the path their signal takes. Use this knowledge to stay ahead of the solar cycle and maintain the link.

tlo.condition: Given a mission requirement, a high frequency (HF) radio, and current ionospheric conditions.
tlo.behavior: Apply frequency selection for sky wave propagation.
tlo.standard: Selecting a frequency that is below the critical frequency and above the absorption level of the D-layer to ensure reflection back to Earth, in accordance with MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: The Marine must use known ionospheric data and mission requirements to select a specific frequency. This is a direct application of technical knowledge to a task to ensure signal reflection.

elos.condition: Given a diagram of the Earth's atmosphere and MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.behavior: Identify the layers of the ionosphere (D, E, and F).
elos.standard: Correctly identifying each layer and its primary effect on HF radio waves (absorption vs. refraction) per Chapter 1 of the reference.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the ionospheric structure is a fundamental prerequisite for understanding sky wave propagation and frequency selection.

elos.condition: Given a scenario involving varying times of day and solar activity.
elos.behavior: Explain the concepts of Critical Frequency and Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF).
elos.standard: Describing how solar radiation levels dictate the highest frequency that will be returned to Earth rather than passing into space, in accordance with MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding the theoretical limits of frequency selection is necessary before a Marine can apply selection techniques in the field.

title: HF Antenna Height and Take-Off Angle Management

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley in the Hindu Kush. You have a clear line of sight to the sky, but your signal is being blocked by 2,000-foot ridgelines. You try to increase power, but it does nothing. By simply lowering your antenna closer to the ground, you can change the physics of your signal, bouncing it off the ionosphere to drop straight down on your target—overcoming the terrain that just defeated your standard setup.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the critical relationship between antenna height and the take-off angle of radio waves. We will discuss how to manipulate antenna height to achieve Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) for short-range communication and low-angle radiation for long-range skip.
objectives: TLO-089: Demonstrate antenna height adjustment for signal coverage.
ELO-239: Describe the effect of antenna height on the take-off angle.
ELO-240: Calculate the optimal antenna height in wavelengths.

mainPoints.title: The Relationship Between Height and Take-Off Angle
mainPoints.content: The height of an antenna above the ground directly determines the angle at which the radio wave leaves the antenna (the take-off angle). Ground reflections interact with the primary wave to either reinforce or cancel the signal at specific angles.
subPoints: Lowering an antenna (relative to wavelength) increases the take-off angle, directing energy upward.
Raising an antenna (relative to wavelength) decreases the take-off angle, directing energy toward the horizon.
Take-off angle is the primary factor in determining the 'skip distance' or the area where the signal returns to Earth.

mainPoints.title: Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS)
mainPoints.content: NVIS is a technique used for high-angle radiation (60 to 90 degrees) to provide reliable communications over short distances (0-300 miles), effectively eliminating the skip zone.
subPoints: To achieve NVIS, the antenna is typically placed at a height of 1/8 to 1/4 wavelength above the ground.
This configuration is ideal for mountainous terrain or heavily forested areas where line-of-sight is impossible.
MCRP 3-40.3C identifies the AS-2259/GR as a primary NVIS antenna, but horizontal dipoles can be adjusted for the same effect.

mainPoints.title: Long-Range Propagation and Wavelength Calculation
mainPoints.content: For long-distance communications (beyond 300 miles), a low take-off angle is required to ensure the signal travels further before hitting the ionosphere.
subPoints: Optimal height for long-range skip is generally 1/4 to 1/2 wavelength above the ground.
Calculation Formula: Wavelength in feet = 984 / Frequency in MHz. Antenna height is then determined by dividing that wavelength by the desired fraction (e.g., 1/2).
Failure to maintain proper height can result in the signal 'skipping' over the intended receiving station.

practicalApplication.scenario: The unit is established in a patrol base surrounded by high terrain. You are ordered to establish a high-frequency (HF) link to a Combat Operations Center (COC) located 45 miles away. You have a 5 MHz frequency assigned and a field-expedient wire dipole.
steps: Calculate the wavelength for 5 MHz (984 / 5 = 196.8 feet).
Determine the NVIS height requirement (1/4 wavelength = approx 49 feet; 1/8 wavelength = approx 24 feet).
Adjust the dipole height to approximately 25 feet to maximize high-angle radiation.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength and clarity over the ridgelines.

conclusion.summary: We have covered how antenna height dictates the take-off angle, the specific requirements for NVIS versus long-range propagation, and the mathematical methods for determining optimal height based on frequency.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the HF world, height is not just about 'getting higher' for better line-of-sight; it is about controlling the geometry of the skywave. Master these adjustments, and you can communicate from anywhere to everywhere.

tlo.condition: Given a tactical radio, a field-expedient or standard antenna, and a specified communication range requirement.
tlo.behavior: Demonstrate antenna height adjustment for signal coverage.
tlo.standard: Controlling the angle of incidence to either achieve Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) for short-range or low-angle radiation for long-range, ensuring the skip zone does not interfere with the target area per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: This is a physical, hands-on task where the Marine applies principles of antenna theory to achieve a specific signal pattern. It requires the execution of physical adjustments based on theoretical requirements.

elos.condition: Given a requirement for Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) communications.
elos.behavior: Describe the effect of antenna height on the take-off angle.
elos.standard: Explaining how lowering an antenna's height relative to the ground increases the radiation angle for short-range coverage per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The Marine must comprehend the inverse relationship between antenna height and take-off angle to achieve specific range requirements.

elos.condition: Given a specific HF frequency and a requirement for long-range communications.
elos.behavior: Calculate the optimal antenna height in wavelengths.
elos.standard: Determining the height (typically 1/4 to 1/2 wavelength) required to produce a low-angle radiation pattern for long-distance skip per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Application of mathematical formulas for wavelength is a component skill required to physically adjust antenna height for signal coverage.

introduction.gainAttention: You are mid-transmission on a critical MEDEVAC request when your net is suddenly overwhelmed by a rhythmic, buzzing interference. Is the enemy jamming you? Is it a solar flare? Or is it the poorly shielded generator the engineers just parked ten feet from your antenna? If you can't tell the difference, you can't fix the link, and the mission fails.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying the causes of HF signal degradation, differentiating between types of noise, and analyzing when to change frequencies or antenna configurations to maintain the link.
objectives: TLO-090: Troubleshoot HF signal degradation.
ELO-241: Differentiate between natural noise and man-made noise.
ELO-242: Analyze the requirement for a frequency or antenna change.

mainPoints.title: Identifying Noise Sources
mainPoints.content: Noise is any undesired electrical energy that interferes with the received signal. It is categorized by its origin: natural or man-made.
subPoints: Natural Noise: Includes atmospheric static (lightning/thunderstorms) and cosmic noise. Atmospheric noise is most prevalent below 30 MHz.
Man-made Noise: Produced by power lines, electric motors, generators, and electronic devices. It is characterized by rhythmic pulses or constant hums.
Differentiating: Natural noise is usually random and 'crackling,' while man-made noise often follows a pattern or increases in proximity to industrial equipment.

mainPoints.title: Signal Fading and Multipath Propagation
mainPoints.content: Fading is the variation in signal strength at the receiver. It can be caused by the ionosphere changing density or by multipath propagation.
subPoints: Multipath Fading: Occurs when the same signal reaches the antenna via different paths (e.g., one skip vs. two skips), causing the waves to interfere with each other.
Selective Fading: Affects only certain frequencies within a sideband, causing voice distortion.
Skip Zone Issues: If a station is in the 'dead space' between the end of the ground wave and the first skywave return, communication will be impossible regardless of power.

mainPoints.title: Corrective Actions and Management
mainPoints.content: Once the cause of degradation is identified, the operator must apply the correct technical solution.
subPoints: Frequency Change: If atmospheric noise or ionospheric fading occurs, move to a frequency further from the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) or closer to the Lowest Usable Frequency (LUF).
Antenna Management: If man-made noise is the issue, re-orient the antenna (polarization change) or move the antenna further from the noise source.
NVIS Transition: If the receiver is in a skip zone, lower the antenna height to transition to NVIS coverage.

practicalApplication.scenario: During a night-time HF net, your signal strength drops from a 4-by-4 to a 2-by-1. You hear a constant, high-pitched whine in the background. A nearby unit has just started their vehicle's engine to charge batteries.
steps: Identify the noise as man-made based on the rhythmic whine and timing of the vehicle start.
Attempt to mitigate by re-orienting the antenna's null point toward the noise source.
If noise persists, analyze the frequency: check if a shift to a higher frequency in the HF band reduces the man-made interference level.
Document the interference and the successful corrective action in the radio log.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the characteristics of natural versus man-made noise, the mechanics of fading, and the decision-making process for frequency and antenna management.
conclusion.closingStatement: A Radio Operator is a technician, not just a button-pusher. By understanding the environment and the equipment, you ensure that the Marine on the ground always has a voice.

tlo.condition: Operating an HF radio net and experiencing irregular signal variations or fading.
tlo.behavior: Troubleshoot HF signal degradation.
tlo.standard: Identifying the cause of signal degradation and applying appropriate frequency or antenna management techniques to maintain the communication link per MCRP 6-22D.
tlo.justification: Troubleshooting requires diagnosing a problem by differentiating between various potential causes (regular vs. irregular variations) and determining the correct solution. This involves analyzing the system state to find a resolution.

warnings: Condition should typically start with "Given..." or include "when" to describe circumstances.

elos.condition: Given an HF circuit experiencing interference.
elos.behavior: Differentiate between natural noise and man-made noise.
elos.standard: Identifying the characteristics of atmospheric static versus industrial or electronic interference to determine the likely source of degradation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Troubleshooting requires the ability to analyze the environment and distinguish between different types of signal inhibitors.

elos.condition: Given a scenario where a signal is fading due to multipath propagation.
elos.behavior: Analyze the requirement for a frequency or antenna change.
elos.standard: Determining if the degradation is caused by the skip zone or ionospheric changes and selecting the appropriate corrective action per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: This higher-level cognitive task is the core of troubleshooting, requiring the Marine to evaluate symptoms and choose a technical solution.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are part of a reconnaissance team deep behind enemy lines. You have a critical intelligence report to transmit, but your directional antenna is off by just 15 degrees. To you, it looks 'close enough,' but to the receiving station 50 miles away, your signal is nonexistent. In the world of directional antennas, 'close' is the difference between mission success and total communication blackout.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for orienting directional antennas, including the calculation of magnetic declination and the identification of antenna radiation patterns to ensure maximum signal gain.
objectives: ELO-243: Define the terms azimuth and magnetic declination.
ELO-244: Calculate the true azimuth from a magnetic heading.
ELO-245: Identify the main radiation lobe of the antenna.
TLO-091: Demonstrate the orientation of the antenna within +/- 10 degrees.

mainPoints.title: Navigation Fundamentals for Radio Operators
mainPoints.content: To accurately point an antenna, an operator must understand the relationship between the map and the ground. Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from a north base line. Because a compass points to Magnetic North and maps are based on True North, operators must apply Magnetic Declination.
subPoints: Azimuth: A direction expressed as a horizontal angle measured from north.
Magnetic Declination: The angular difference between true north and magnetic north.
LARS Rule: Left Add, Right Subtract (when converting from magnetic to grid/true depending on local declination diagram).

mainPoints.title: Antenna Radiation Patterns and Gain
mainPoints.content: Directional antennas do not radiate energy equally in all directions. They concentrate energy into 'lobes.' The Main Lobe (or major lobe) is the area containing the maximum radiation. To achieve the 'Gain' specified in technical manuals, this main lobe must be centered on the receiving station.
subPoints: Main Lobe: The direction of maximum sensitivity or power discharge.
Gain: The increase in signal strength achieved by focusing energy in a specific direction.
Directivity: The ability of an antenna to concentrate energy in a narrow beam.

mainPoints.title: Orientation Procedures
mainPoints.content: Orientation is the physical process of aligning the antenna's boom or wire elements with the calculated true azimuth. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, a directional antenna must be aligned within +/- 10 degrees of the target path to ensure the receiving station is within the half-power beamwidth of the main lobe.
subPoints: Step 1: Determine the target's true azimuth from the map.
Step 2: Convert true azimuth to magnetic azimuth using the local declination.
Step 3: Use a compass to find the magnetic heading on the ground.
Step 4: Physically rotate the antenna until the main radiation lobe is centered on that heading.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are tasked with establishing a point-to-point HF link with a distant station located at a true azimuth of 045 degrees. The local magnetic declination is 10 degrees East.
steps: Calculate the magnetic azimuth (045 - 10 = 035 degrees).
Identify the main radiation lobe of the provided directional antenna (e.g., the direction the 'arrow' or boom points).
Use the M2 compass to identify the 035-degree magnetic heading.
Rotate and secure the antenna so it is aligned within 10 degrees of the target azimuth.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the definitions of azimuth and declination, the math required to convert headings, and the physical alignment of the antenna's main lobe.
conclusion.closingStatement: Precision in antenna orientation is a force multiplier. By mastering these calculations and alignment techniques, you ensure that every watt of power your radio produces is delivered exactly where it needs to go.

tlo.condition: Given a directional antenna, a magnetic compass, a map of magnetic declination, and a target azimuth for the radio path,
tlo.behavior: demonstrate the orientation of the antenna,
tlo.standard: ensuring the antenna is aligned to the true azimuth of the radio path within +/- 10 degrees to achieve maximum signal strength per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task requires the physical application of tools and mathematical adjustment for declination to achieve a specific physical alignment, which aligns with Level 3 (Apply).

elos.behavior: define the terms azimuth and magnetic declination,
elos.standard: matching the definitions provided in the publication glossary.
elos.justification: Knowledge of basic terminology is a prerequisite for performing antenna orientation.

warnings: Standard should include measurable criteria (time limits, accuracy percentages) or reference authoritative sources (per MCRP..., IAW TM...).

elos.justification: The Marine must be able to convert magnetic readings to true azimuths before orienting the antenna.

elos.behavior: identify the main radiation lobe of the antenna,
elos.standard: ensuring the direction of maximum gain is correctly determined for alignment.
elos.justification: Identifying the physical orientation of the radiation pattern is necessary for proper alignment.

introduction.gainAttention: You're in the middle of a heavy rainstorm, tucked into a tree line, and your once-clear voice circuit has turned into a wall of static. You can hear the distant end, but they can't hear you. Replacing the radio isn't the answer—understanding the environment and the physics of your antenna is. As a Marine communicator, you must be a problem solver, not just an operator.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying sources of interference and performing technical adjustments to antennas to restore marginal communication circuits.
objectives: ELO-246: Describe the difference between natural and manmade noise.
ELO-247: Adjust the antenna polarization.
ELO-248: Re-site the antenna to minimize signal absorption.
TLO-092: Troubleshoot the communication circuit to restore operational standards.

mainPoints.title: Identifying Noise and Interference
mainPoints.content: Noise is any unwanted electrical energy that interferes with the desired signal. It is categorized into two primary types: Natural and Manmade.
subPoints: Natural Noise: Includes atmospheric static (lightning) and galactic noise (solar activity).
Manmade Noise: Produced by power lines, generators, vehicle ignitions, and other electronic devices.
Troubleshooting Tip: If noise decreases when the antenna is disconnected, the noise is being 'picked up' from the environment.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Polarization
mainPoints.content: Polarization is the orientation of the electric field of the radio wave. For maximum signal transfer, the transmitting and receiving antennas must have the same polarization.
subPoints: Vertical Polarization: The antenna element is perpendicular to the Earth. Better for ground-wave communication.
Horizontal Polarization: The antenna element is parallel to the Earth. Often used in HF NVIS to reduce manmade noise.
Adjustment: If a signal is weak, rotating a whip from vertical to horizontal (if the distant end did the same) can often clear the circuit.

mainPoints.title: Siting and Environmental Factors
mainPoints.content: The physical location of an antenna significantly impacts performance. In vegetated areas, high-frequency signals (VHF/UHF) are absorbed by leaves and branches. Multipath interference occurs when signals reflect off objects and arrive at the receiver at different times.
subPoints: Vegetation: Move antennas to clearings or above the tree line to reduce absorption.
Multipath: Characterized by 'picket fencing' or rapid fading. Moving the antenna even a few feet can often find a 'hot spot' where reflections reinforce the signal.

practicalApplication.scenario: A VHF circuit is experiencing heavy fading and 'picket fencing' while operating from a dense jungle environment near a running generator.
steps: Identify the generator as a source of manmade noise and move the antenna away from the power source.
Check the distant end's polarization; if they are using a horizontal wire, adjust your antenna from vertical to horizontal.
Move the antenna to a nearby clearing to reduce signal absorption from wet vegetation.
Perform a radio check to verify signal strength (SINAD) has improved.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the types of noise, the importance of matching polarization, and how to re-site antennas to avoid environmental absorption.
conclusion.closingStatement: A radio operator's value is proven when things go wrong. By systematically troubleshooting noise and siting issues, you ensure the MAGTF maintains the ability to command and control in any environment.

tlo.condition: Given a radio circuit experiencing marginal signal quality, necessary tools, and operational equipment,
tlo.behavior: troubleshoot the communication circuit,
tlo.standard: by performing systematic technical adjustments until signal strength is optimized or restored to operational standards per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: Troubleshooting requires the Marine to analyze the system components, identify the source of degradation, and determine the relationship between variables such as antenna height and location, fitting Level 4 (Analyze).

elos.condition: Given a list of communication interference scenarios,
elos.behavior: describe the difference between natural and manmade noise,
elos.standard: identifying at least two examples of each per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: Understanding the source of signal degradation is the first step in the troubleshooting process.

elos.condition: Given a radio circuit with poor signal quality and a field-expedient antenna,
elos.behavior: adjust the antenna polarization,
elos.standard: by switching between vertical and horizontal orientations to match the distant station's polarization.
elos.justification: Polarization mismatch is a common cause of marginal signals that can be corrected through technical adjustment.

warnings: Standard should include measurable criteria (time limits, accuracy percentages) or reference authoritative sources (per MCRP..., IAW TM...).
Verb "Adjust" is not in the standard Bloom's Taxonomy verb list. Consider using one of: Demonstrate, Perform, Calculate, Apply, Execute, Implement, Use

elos.condition: Given a radio circuit experiencing multipath interference in a vegetated area,
elos.behavior: re-site the antenna,
elos.standard: to a location that minimizes signal absorption and reflection per the guidelines in Chapter 5.
elos.justification: Siting is a critical troubleshooting step for restoring VHF/UHF line-of-sight communications.

warnings: Behavior should start with the action verb "Perform". Currently starts with "re-site".

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a hide site and your primary whip antenna is destroyed. You have a spool of WD-1/TT field wire and a radio, but if you cannot calculate the exact length needed for your operating frequency, your signal will never reach the extraction bird. Precision in antenna length is the difference between a successful CASEVAC and total radio silence.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mathematical principles required to calculate radio wavelengths and the physical length of antenna components to ensure maximum power transfer and system efficiency.
objectives: TLO-093: Calculate the required transmission line length to achieve maximum energy transfer.
ELO-249: Calculate the wavelength in meters using the (300 / Frequency in MHz) formula.
ELO-250: Determine the physical length of a half-wave dipole in feet using the (468 / Frequency in MHz) formula.
ELO-251: Explain the effect of impedance mismatch on energy transfer.

mainPoints.title: Wavelength and Frequency Relationship
mainPoints.content: Radio waves travel at the speed of light (300 million meters per second). The physical size of a radio wave is inversely proportional to its frequency.
subPoints: Formula: Wavelength (λ) = 300 / Frequency in MHz.
Higher frequencies result in shorter physical wavelengths.
Lower frequencies result in longer physical wavelengths.

mainPoints.title: Calculating Antenna Physical Length
mainPoints.content: For a half-wave dipole antenna, the electrical length is slightly shorter than the wavelength in free space due to the 'end effect.'
subPoints: Formula for half-wave dipole in feet: 468 / Frequency in MHz.
Example: For 7.0 MHz, the length is 468 / 7 = 66.8 feet.
Accurate cutting ensures the antenna is resonant at the desired frequency.

mainPoints.title: Impedance Mismatch and Reflected Energy
mainPoints.content: Impedance is the total opposition to current flow in a circuit. When the impedance of the radio, transmission line, and antenna do not match, energy is reflected back to the source.
subPoints: Reflected energy creates 'standing waves' on the transmission line.
High Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) reduces the signal strength sent into the atmosphere.
Extreme mismatch can cause heat buildup and damage the radio's final power amplifier.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are assigned to establish an HF link on 14.250 MHz using a field-expedient half-wave dipole.
steps: Calculate the full wavelength in meters for 14.250 MHz.
Calculate the total physical length of the wire antenna in feet using the 468 formula.
Divide the total length by two to determine the length of each dipole leg.
Measure and mark the wire for cutting.

conclusion.summary: We have covered how to calculate wavelength, determine the physical length of a half-wave dipole, and the critical importance of matching impedance to prevent reflected energy damage.
conclusion.closingStatement: The math is simple, but the impact is tactical. Master these calculations to ensure your voice is heard when the mission depends on it.

tlo.condition: Given a transceiver, a transmission line with mismatched impedance, a load antenna, and a single operating frequency,
tlo.behavior: calculate the required transmission line length,
tlo.standard: to achieve maximum energy transfer and minimize reflected energy by cutting the line to a specific half or quarter-wavelength per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: This task involves applying mathematical formulas to a specific frequency to determine a physical measurement required for technical implementation, fitting Level 3 (Apply).

elos.condition: Given a specific operating frequency,
elos.behavior: calculate the wavelength in meters,
elos.standard: using the formula (300 / Frequency in MHz) to achieve 100% accuracy.
elos.justification: Determining the wavelength is the foundational mathematical step for all antenna and line length calculations.

elos.condition: Given a calculated wavelength and a requirement for a half-wave dipole,
elos.behavior: determine the physical length of the antenna wire in feet,
elos.standard: using the formula (468 / Frequency in MHz) per MCRP 3-40.3C.
elos.justification: The Marine must be able to convert electrical wavelength to physical wire length for practical application.

errors: Verb "Determine" is a Level 5 verb, but Level 3 was specified. Approved verbs for Level 3: Demonstrate, Perform, Calculate, Apply, Execute, Implement, Use

elos.behavior: explain the effect of impedance mismatch on energy transfer,
elos.standard: including the concepts of reflected energy and standing waves.
elos.justification: Understanding the 'why' behind cutting lines to specific lengths ensures the Marine understands the goal of optimization.

warnings: Standard should include measurable criteria (time limits, accuracy percentages) or reference authoritative sources (per MCRP..., IAW TM...).

introduction.gainAttention: A radio is just a box of electronics until it is integrated into a functional circuit. In the MAGTF, the Single Channel Radio (SCR) is the primary means of communication for maneuver units. If you cannot properly implement the circuit, you are effectively isolated from the fight.
introduction.overview: This lesson identifies the components of a tactical radio circuit and the procedures for establishing a reliable link with a high signal-to-noise ratio.
objectives: TLO-094: Implement a radio communications circuit providing the greatest signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio.
ELO-252: Identify the five components of a tactical radio communication circuit.
ELO-253: Explain the relationship between S/N ratio and link reliability.
ELO-254: Perform the physical connection of the radio communications circuit.

mainPoints.title: The Five Components of a Radio Circuit
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C page 1-5, every radio circuit consists of five essential elements.
subPoints: Transmitter: Generates the radio frequency signal.
Receiver: Processes the received signal back into useful information.
Transmission Lines: The medium (coax/wire) that carries energy from the radio to the antenna.
Antenna: Radiates the energy into space or intercepts it from space.
Propagation Medium: The space through which the radio wave travels (Earth's atmosphere).

mainPoints.title: Signal-to-Noise (S/N) Ratio
mainPoints.content: The reliability of a link is determined by how much stronger the desired signal is compared to the background noise.
subPoints: Noise can be natural (static, lightning) or man-made (engines, other radios).
Increasing S/N ratio is achieved by increasing transmitter power, using a higher-gain antenna, or moving away from noise sources.
A higher S/N ratio ensures information is available in a 'useful form' for the commander.

mainPoints.title: Physical System Integration
mainPoints.content: Proper assembly is critical to prevent signal loss and equipment damage.
subPoints: Ensure all connectors are clean and dry.
Tighten BNC/TNC connectors hand-tight; do not use pliers.
Route transmission lines away from power cables to avoid interference.

practicalApplication.scenario: Given a PRC-117G, an OE-254 antenna, and a 50-foot coax cable, establish a VHF link with a distant station 15km away.
steps: Identify and layout the five components of the circuit.
Assemble the OE-254 antenna according to the technical manual.
Connect the transmission line to the antenna and the radio's VHF port.
Power on the system and perform a radio check to verify S/N quality.
Adjust antenna placement if signal quality is marginal.

conclusion.summary: We have identified the five components of a radio circuit, the importance of the S/N ratio, and the physical steps to connect a tactical system.
conclusion.closingStatement: Effective communication is the backbone of Command and Control. By ensuring every connection is secure and every component is optimized, you ensure the MAGTF remains a lethal, coordinated force.

tlo.condition: Given a tactical Single Channel Radio (SCR), power supply, transmission lines, antennas, and a distant station,
tlo.behavior: implement a radio communications circuit,
tlo.standard: establishing a link that provides the greatest signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio and ensures information is available in a useful form per MCRP 3-40.3C.
tlo.justification: The Marine must execute a series of procedural steps (modulation, propagation, and demodulation) to achieve a functional end-state capability, which is a Level 3 (Apply) task.

elos.condition: Given a list of communications equipment and MCRP 3-40.3C,
elos.behavior: identify the components of a tactical radio communication circuit,
elos.standard: ensuring all five primary components (transmitter, receiver, transmission lines, antennas, and propagation medium) are correctly named per MCRP 3-40.3C page 1-5.
elos.justification: Knowledge of the basic components is a prerequisite for the physical implementation of a circuit.

elos.condition: Given a scenario involving signal interference,
elos.behavior: explain the relationship between signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio and link reliability,
elos.standard: describing how increasing signal strength or decreasing noise improves the useful form of information per MCRP 3-40.3C page 1-23.
elos.justification: Understanding the concept of S/N ratio is necessary to achieve the 'greatest S/N ratio' standard required by the TLO.

elos.condition: Given a tactical radio, antenna, and transmission line,
elos.behavior: perform the physical connection of the radio communications circuit,
elos.standard: ensuring all connections are secure and the system is configured for operation per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 3.
elos.justification: This is the component skill required to physically implement the circuit described in the TLO.

title: Frequency Band Selection and Terrain Analysis

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are a radio operator in a dense urban environment like Fallujah or a mountainous region like the Hindu Kush. You have a critical MEDEVAC request, but your signal is blocked by a concrete wall or a granite peak. Knowing which frequency band to select isn't just a technical skill—it is the difference between getting your message through and total communications silence when lives are on the line.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental characteristics of the HF, VHF, and UHF frequency bands and how to select the appropriate band based on mission range and terrain constraints per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-095: Apply frequency band selection criteria.
ELO-255: State the frequency ranges for the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
ELO-256: Describe the impact of Line of Sight (LOS) obstructions on VHF and UHF frequencies.
ELO-257: Select the appropriate frequency band (HF, VHF, or UHF) for a mission.

mainPoints.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Military Bands
mainPoints.content: The electromagnetic spectrum is divided into bands based on wavelength and frequency. For tactical communications, we focus on three primary bands.
subPoints: High Frequency (HF): 3 to 30 MHz. Used for long-range communications via skywave propagation.
Very High Frequency (VHF): 30 to 300 MHz. The primary band for tactical FM communications (SINCGARS).
Ultra High Frequency (UHF): 300 to 3,000 MHz. Used for short-range LOS, ground-to-air, and satellite communications (SATCOM).

mainPoints.title: Line of Sight (LOS) and Terrain Obstructions
mainPoints.content: VHF and UHF frequencies are primarily Line of Sight (LOS) dependent. Unlike HF, which can 'skip' off the ionosphere, VHF and UHF signals are easily blocked or degraded by physical objects.
subPoints: Diffraction: The ability of a wave to bend around an edge. Lower frequencies (VHF) diffract better than higher frequencies (UHF).
Path Loss: The reduction in power density of an electromagnetic wave as it propagates through space, exacerbated by jungle foliage or urban structures.
Terrain Impact: Mountains and buildings create 'shadow zones' where VHF/UHF signals cannot reach.

mainPoints.title: Selection Criteria for Mission Success
mainPoints.content: Selecting the right band requires balancing the required range against the terrain profile between the transmitter and receiver.
subPoints: Short Range/Clear LOS: Use UHF for high data rates or ground-to-air.
Tactical Range (0-30km)/Moderate Obstacles: Use VHF (FM) for standard maneuver elements.
Long Range (Beyond 30km)/Non-LOS: Use HF to overcome terrain via skywave or NVIS.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Radio Operator for a reconnaissance team inserted 65km away from the Combat Operations Center (COC). The terrain between you and the COC consists of a significant mountain range. You have an AN/PRC-150 (HF) and an AN/PRC-117G (VHF/UHF/SATCOM).
steps: Analyze the distance (65km) against the capabilities of VHF LOS.
Evaluate the terrain (Mountain range) and its effect on LOS frequencies.
Consult MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1 to determine the best band for non-LOS long range.

title: Ground Wave Propagation and Antenna Height

introduction.gainAttention: Have you ever noticed that your radio range increases significantly when you move from a dry, sandy desert to the coastline? Or why simply putting your antenna on a taller mast suddenly brings a distant station in 'loud and clear'? This isn't luck—it's the physics of ground wave propagation.
introduction.overview: This lesson explains the components of ground wave propagation, the impact of surface absorption, and the techniques used to extend range by adjusting antenna height per MCRP 3-40.3C.
objectives: TLO-096: Apply ground wave propagation factors.
ELO-258: Define the components of ground wave propagation.
ELO-259: Explain how surface absorption affects ground wave signal strength.
ELO-260: Demonstrate antenna height adjustment techniques.

mainPoints.title: Components of the Ground Wave
mainPoints.content: A ground wave is a radio wave that travels along the Earth's surface. It consists of three distinct components.
subPoints: Surface Wave: Travels along the surface of the Earth. It is the primary component for HF ground wave.
Direct Wave: Travels in a straight line from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna (LOS).
Ground-Reflected Wave: The portion of the wave that reflects off the ground before reaching the receiving antenna.

mainPoints.title: Surface Absorption and Conductivity
mainPoints.content: As a surface wave travels, it induces a current in the Earth, which robs the wave of energy. This is known as surface absorption.
subPoints: Conductivity: Better conductivity (e.g., salt water) allows the wave to travel further with less loss.
Dielectric Constant: The Earth's ability to store capacitive energy affects the velocity and attenuation of the wave.
Soil Types: Sea water is the best conductor; dry, sandy soil is the poorest, significantly reducing range.

mainPoints.title: Overcoming the Earth's Curvature
mainPoints.content: The 'Radio Horizon' is approximately 15% farther than the visual horizon. To extend the range of a VHF/UHF circuit, we must overcome the Earth's curvature.
subPoints: Antenna Height: Increasing the height of the antenna directly increases the distance to the radio horizon.
Formula: Range increases as the square root of the antenna height.
Practical Application: Using an OE-254 mast or elevating a whip antenna to a higher terrain feature.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is operating in a region with high soil resistance (dry rocky terrain). You are attempting to maintain a VHF link with a convoy 15km away, but the signal is intermittent due to a slight rise in the Earth's curvature between the two points.
steps: Identify the components of the ground wave currently in use (Direct and Surface).
Assess the impact of the dry soil on the surface wave (High absorption).
Calculate the necessary increase in antenna height to clear the intermediate terrain rise.
Deploy an elevated antenna (e.g., OE-254 or field-expedient mast).
Verify the link quality after the height adjustment.

conclusion.summary: We defined the surface, direct, and ground-reflected waves. We explored how soil conductivity affects signal absorption and demonstrated that increasing antenna height is the most effective way to extend the radio horizon.
conclusion.closingStatement: Understanding the ground you stand on is just as important as understanding the radio in your hand. Use the Earth to your advantage, and always seek the high ground for your antennas.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are part of a Deep Reconnaissance Platoon 500 miles behind enemy lines. Your satellite link is jammed, and your VHF radios are useless due to the curvature of the earth. Your only hope for extraction is a high-frequency radio signal that must bounce off the very edge of space to reach the Rear Area. This isn't science fiction; it's the science of sky wave propagation, and mastering it is the difference between being 'no comms' and getting your Marines home.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the mechanics of sky wave propagation, specifically focusing on the ionospheric layers, the relationship between frequency and atmospheric density, and the calculation of skip zones to ensure reliable long-distance communication.
objectives: Identify the layers of the ionosphere (D, E, F1, and F2) and their effects on radio wave propagation.
Explain the relationship between frequency selection and ionospheric density, specifically the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF).
Calculate the skip distance and skip zone for a sky wave signal.

mainPoints.title: Layers of the Ionosphere
mainPoints.content: The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere (30 to 250 miles above Earth) ionized by solar radiation. It consists of four distinct layers that affect HF signals.
subPoints: D Layer: The lowest layer (30-55 miles); exists only during daylight; primarily absorbs radio energy rather than refracting it.
E Layer: (55-90 miles); used for medium-range sky wave; density depends on the sun's angle.
F Layer: The most important for long-range comms. During the day, it splits into F1 (90-140 miles) and F2 (140-250 miles). At night, they merge into a single F layer.
F2 Layer: The highest and most dense layer, providing the longest skip distances.

mainPoints.title: Frequency Selection and Ionospheric Density
mainPoints.content: Successful sky wave propagation depends on matching the frequency to the current state of the ionosphere. If a frequency is too high, it passes through the ionosphere into space. If it is too low, it is absorbed by the D layer.
subPoints: Critical Frequency: The highest frequency that will be refracted back to Earth when transmitted vertically.
Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF): The highest frequency that will return to Earth at a specific angle for a specific distance. Operating just below the MUF provides the strongest signal.
Lowest Usable Frequency (LUF): The frequency below which the signal is lost to atmospheric noise or absorption.

mainPoints.title: Skip Distance and Skip Zones
mainPoints.content: Understanding where your signal 'lands' is critical for mission planning. The signal does not cover the entire distance between the transmitter and the receiver.
subPoints: Skip Distance: The distance from the transmitter to the point where the sky wave first returns to Earth.
Skip Zone: The 'dead space' between the end of the ground wave's reach and the beginning of the first sky wave's return. No signal is receivable in this zone.
Factors: Skip distance increases as the frequency increases or the angle of radiation (take-off angle) decreases.

practicalApplication.scenario: A Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU) is established at a base. A patrol is sent 300 miles away. The ground wave for the PRC-150 ends at 40 miles. The first sky wave return is calculated to begin at 250 miles based on the current MUF.
steps: Identify the skip distance (250 miles).
Identify the ground wave range (40 miles).
Calculate the skip zone (the area between 40 miles and 250 miles).
Determine if the patrol at 300 miles is in a 'comm-capable' area (Yes, they are beyond the skip distance).
Adjust frequency if the patrol moves into the 100-mile range to shorten the skip distance.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the four layers of the ionosphere, the critical importance of selecting a frequency below the MUF, and how to identify skip zones where communication is impossible.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ionosphere is constantly changing with the sun. A radio operator who understands these changes can maintain communications across continents, while one who doesn't will be left talking to static.

introduction.gainAttention: Why can you talk to a pilot 30,000 feet in the air using a UHF radio, but you can't talk to a squad on the other side of a single ridgeline using that same radio? The answer lies in the physics of the electromagnetic spectrum. Choosing the wrong frequency band isn't just a technical error; it's a tactical failure that can leave a unit isolated in the middle of a firelight.
introduction.overview: This lesson defines the HF, VHF, and UHF frequency bands and provides the criteria for selecting the optimal band based on mission range, terrain, and atmospheric conditions.
objectives: State the frequency ranges for the HF, VHF, and UHF bands per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Differentiate between the propagation characteristics of HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
Select the optimal frequency band for a specified mission range.

mainPoints.title: The Military Radio Spectrum
mainPoints.content: Tactical radios operate within specific segments of the electromagnetic spectrum, each with unique properties.
subPoints: High Frequency (HF): 3 to 30 MHz. Used for long-range 'over-the-horizon' communications.
Very High Frequency (VHF): 30 to 300 MHz. The primary band for MAGTF ground maneuver units (e.g., SINCGARS).
Ultra High Frequency (UHF): 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Used for line-of-sight (LOS), ground-to-air, and satellite communications.

mainPoints.title: Propagation Characteristics
mainPoints.content: The way a wave travels determines its utility in different environments.
subPoints: HF Propagation: Capable of both ground wave (short range) and sky wave (long range) via ionospheric refraction.
VHF Propagation: Primarily Line-of-Sight (LOS). It follows the curvature of the earth slightly but is easily blocked by dense vegetation and terrain.
UHF Propagation: Strictly Line-of-Sight. It does not follow the earth's curvature and is heavily impacted by physical obstacles, but it is ideal for penetrating the atmosphere for SATCOM.

mainPoints.title: Band Selection Criteria
mainPoints.content: Selection is based on the distance to the receiver and the obstacles in between.
subPoints: Short Range (0-10km): VHF or UHF is preferred for clarity and equipment portability.
Medium Range (10-40km): VHF (Ground Wave) is standard, provided terrain is relatively flat.
Long Range (50-8000 miles): HF is required to utilize sky wave refraction.
Air-to-Ground: UHF is the standard due to clear LOS and high data potential.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the Radio Supervisor for a convoy. You have three tasks: 1. Maintain comms with the lead vehicle 1km away. 2. Maintain comms with a Close Air Support (CAS) aircraft. 3. Maintain comms with the Rear Operations Center (ROC) 150 miles away.
steps: Select the band for the lead vehicle (VHF/UHF - Short range LOS).
Select the band for the CAS aircraft (UHF - Standard for aviation).
Select the band for the ROC (HF - Required for 150-mile sky wave).
Identify which link is most likely to be affected by a mountain range between the convoy and the ROC (The HF link, if the take-off angle is too low).

conclusion.summary: We have defined the HF, VHF, and UHF bands and analyzed how their propagation characteristics dictate their use in the field.
conclusion.closingStatement: The spectrum is a tool. Like any tool, you must pick the right one for the job. Use HF for the distance, VHF for the maneuver, and UHF for the sky.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in a deep valley, and your higher headquarters is only 50 miles away. Your VHF line-of-sight is blocked by terrain, and your standard HF skywave is overshooting them, landing 300 miles away in the 'skip zone.' You are effectively isolated. NVIS is the 'silver bullet' that allows us to bounce signals off the ionosphere at such a steep angle that they rain back down locally, filling that gap and ensuring the commander maintains C2 in restrictive terrain.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the principles of NVIS propagation, the specific antenna systems used to achieve it, and the technical adjustments required to eliminate the skip zone for short-range HF communications.
objectives: TLO-099: Demonstrate Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) antenna configuration
ELO-267: Describe the concept of Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation
ELO-268: Identify NVIS-capable antennas
ELO-269: Adjust the antenna height and orientation

mainPoints.title: NVIS Propagation Principles
mainPoints.content: NVIS is a technique that uses high-angle radiation to provide reliable signals at ranges from 0 to 300 miles, effectively eliminating the skip zone.
subPoints: Radiation is directed nearly vertically (60 to 90 degrees) toward the ionosphere.
Requires frequencies below the critical frequency (typically 2-12 MHz).
Eliminates the 'dead space' between the end of the ground wave and the start of the first skywave hop.

mainPoints.title: NVIS-Capable Antenna Systems
mainPoints.content: Not all antennas are suitable for NVIS. The goal is to maximize vertical radiation rather than horizontal distance.
subPoints: AS-2259/GR: The primary tactical NVIS antenna, consisting of two crossed dipoles.
Horizontal Dipole: Can be used for NVIS if mounted at the correct height.
Half-Wave Dipole: Most effective when placed close to the ground to force energy upward.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Configuration for NVIS
mainPoints.content: The critical factor for NVIS is the height of the antenna above the ground, which determines the take-off angle.
subPoints: Antenna height must be 1/4 wavelength or less from the ground (typically 10-30 feet).
Placing the antenna close to the ground uses the earth as a reflector to push the signal straight up.
Orientation: For NVIS, the horizontal orientation is less critical for directionality than it is for standard skywave, but height remains the primary variable.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a defilade position. You must establish a reliable HF link with a relay station 45 miles away. You have an HF radio and a wire antenna kit.
steps: Determine the operating frequency and calculate the 1/4 wavelength height.
Deploy a horizontal dipole antenna at a height not exceeding 1/4 wavelength from the ground.
Ensure the antenna is parallel to the ground to maximize the 60-90 degree take-off angle.
Perform a radio check to verify the elimination of the skip zone.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the theory of NVIS propagation, identified the AS-2259 and horizontal dipoles as NVIS-capable, and practiced configuring these antennas at low heights to achieve high-angle radiation.
conclusion.closingStatement: As a radio operator, your ability to manipulate the take-off angle of your signal is the difference between a failed mission and a successful C2 link. Master the NVIS configuration to ensure the MAGTF stays connected, regardless of terrain.

title: Components of a Radio Communication Link

introduction.gainAttention: When a radio link fails, an untrained operator stares at the screen and hopes it starts working. A Marine professional visualizes the entire circuit. By understanding the seven components of a radio link, you can systematically isolate a fault from the microphone in your hand to the antenna on a distant hill, ensuring the message always gets through.
introduction.overview: This lesson defines the radio communication circuit and identifies the seven essential components required for energy to travel from a transmitter to a receiver.
objectives: TLO-100: Identify the seven components of a radio communication link
ELO-270: Define the term 'radio communication circuit'
ELO-271: Label the seven components of a radio communication circuit
ELO-272: Describe the function of each component within the communication circuit

mainPoints.title: The Radio Communication Circuit
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C, a radio communication circuit consists of the equipment and path necessary to transmit information between two or more points.
subPoints: It is a closed-loop conceptual model for troubleshooting.
The circuit is only as strong as its weakest component.

mainPoints.title: The Seven Components
mainPoints.content: A complete tactical radio link is comprised of seven distinct parts that work in sequence.
subPoints: 1. Transmitter: Generates the radio frequency signal.
2. Transmission Line (TX): Routes the signal from the transmitter to the antenna.
3. Transmitting Antenna: Converts electrical energy into electromagnetic waves.
4. Propagation Path: The medium (atmosphere/space) through which the wave travels.
5. Receiving Antenna: Intercepts the electromagnetic wave and converts it back to electrical energy.
6. Transmission Line (RX): Routes the signal from the antenna to the receiver.
7. Receiver: Processes the signal back into an intelligible form (voice/data).

mainPoints.title: Component Functions and Integrity
mainPoints.content: Each component must be matched and functional to ensure system integrity.
subPoints: Transmission lines must have proper impedance matching to minimize energy loss.
Antennas must be resonant to the frequency generated by the transmitter.
The propagation path is the only component the operator cannot physically repair, but can adapt to by changing frequency or antenna type.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are provided with a non-functional HF radio setup and a diagram of a communication link. You must identify where the break in the circuit is located.
steps: Label the seven components on the provided technical diagram.
Trace the flow of energy from the transmitter to the propagation path.
Identify common failure points for each component (e.g., frayed transmission lines, mismatched antennas).
Explain how a failure in the 'Receiving Antenna' component affects the overall circuit.

conclusion.summary: We have defined the radio communication circuit and identified the seven components: transmitter, two transmission lines, two antennas, the propagation path, and the receiver.
conclusion.closingStatement: Understanding these seven components is the foundation of all CIS troubleshooting. If you know the path the energy takes, you will never be overwhelmed by a system failure.

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are operating a long-range HF patrol net 300 miles from the Combat Operations Center. You have a critical CASEVAC request, but your signal is fluttering and dropping into the noise floor. You cannot simply increase power without risking electronic detection. Understanding the 'why' behind signal fading is the difference between getting that message through and total mission failure.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the identification of signal fading causes, the differentiation of noise sources, and the practical mitigation techniques required to maintain HF communications in a contested environment.
objectives: TLO-101: Troubleshoot signal fading in HF communications.
ELO-273: Identify the causes of signal fading.
ELO-274: Differentiate between natural and manmade noise.
ELO-275: Demonstrate mitigation techniques for signal fading.

mainPoints.title: Causes of HF Signal Fading
mainPoints.content: Signal fading in the HF band is primarily driven by the interaction between radio waves and the ionosphere. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, operators must recognize two primary phenomena.
subPoints: Multipath Interference: Occurs when a signal takes multiple paths to the receiver (e.g., ground wave and sky wave arriving at different times), causing phase cancellation.
Absorption: The loss of energy as the radio wave passes through the ionospheric layers, particularly the D-layer during daylight hours.

mainPoints.title: Noise Identification
mainPoints.content: To troubleshoot a circuit, the operator must determine if the signal degradation is caused by the environment or local interference.
subPoints: Natural Noise: Includes atmospheric static (lightning) and cosmic noise. It is usually characterized by wide-band 'crackling' sounds.
Manmade Noise: Generated by power lines, generators, vehicle ignitions, and other electronic devices. This often presents as rhythmic humming or buzzing.

mainPoints.title: Mitigation Techniques
mainPoints.content: Once the cause is identified, the operator must take corrective action without relying on increased transmitter power, which increases the Electronic Signature.
subPoints: Frequency Selection: Shifting to a different frequency within the assigned ALE (Automatic Link Establishment) pool to avoid specific interference or absorption layers.
Antenna Orientation: Adjusting the physical polarization or direction of the antenna to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

practicalApplication.scenario: The student is provided an AN/PRC-150 set up for a skywave link. The instructor introduces a simulated manmade noise source (generator) and a fading signal. The student must identify the noise type and adjust the antenna orientation to restore the link.
steps: Monitor the received signal strength indicator (RSSI) on the radio.
Identify if the interference is rhythmic (manmade) or random (natural).
Relocate the antenna or adjust orientation to nullify the noise source.
Select an alternate frequency if signal fading persists due to ionospheric changes.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the mechanics of multipath interference and absorption, how to tell the difference between a generator and a thunderstorm on your net, and how to fix your signal through smart antenna employment.
conclusion.closingStatement: In the HF world, the smartest operator—not the loudest one—wins the fight. Use these techniques to keep your signature low and your signal clear.

title: Antenna Selection and Calculation for SCR Operations

introduction.gainAttention: A million-dollar radio is nothing more than a heavy paperweight if it is connected to a poorly selected or incorrectly sized antenna. In the Marine Corps, we don't just use what's in the bag; we build what the mission requires. Mastering antenna selection ensures your signal clears the trees and reaches the objective.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the characteristics of military frequency bands, the mathematical calculation of antenna lengths, and the impact of terrain on polarization.
objectives: TLO-102: Apply antenna selection criteria for Single-Channel Radio (SCR) operations.
ELO-276: Identify the characteristics of HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
ELO-277: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
ELO-278: Explain the impact of terrain on antenna polarization selection.

mainPoints.title: Frequency Band Characteristics
mainPoints.content: Tactical SCRs operate across three primary bands, each with unique propagation behaviors defined in MCRP 3-40.3C.
subPoints: HF (3-30 MHz): Supports long-range skywave and short-range groundwave; highly dependent on ionospheric conditions.
VHF (30-300 MHz): Primary band for MAGTF maneuver units; generally limited to Line of Sight (LOS).
UHF (300 MHz-3 GHz): Used for ground-to-air and SATCOM; strictly LOS and highly susceptible to atmospheric moisture.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Length Calculation
mainPoints.content: For an antenna to radiate efficiently, it must be resonant at the operating frequency. The most common field-expedient antenna is the half-wave dipole.
subPoints: The standard formula for a half-wave dipole in feet is: 468 / Frequency in MHz.
Example: For a frequency of 10 MHz, the total length is 46.8 feet (each leg is 23.4 feet).

mainPoints.title: Terrain and Polarization
mainPoints.content: The physical environment dictates how we orient our antennas.
subPoints: Vertical Polarization: Best for groundwave communication and mobile operations; less affected by ground reflections.
Horizontal Polarization: Preferred for skywave (NVIS) to bounce signals over obstacles like mountains or dense jungle canopy.
Jungle/Urban: Vertical polarization can suffer high 'clutter' loss; horizontal may be required to clear immediate vegetation.

practicalApplication.scenario: The unit is tasked to establish a VHF link in a heavily wooded area. The student is given a frequency of 50.00 MHz and must determine the antenna type, calculate the length, and select the polarization.
steps: Identify the frequency band (VHF).
Calculate the half-wave dipole length using the formula (468 / 50 = 9.36 feet).
Convert decimal feet to inches for precision (+/- 2 inches).
Select horizontal polarization to minimize signal absorption by vertical tree trunks.

conclusion.summary: We have analyzed the HF, VHF, and UHF bands, practiced the math behind resonance, and determined how terrain influences our choice of polarization.
conclusion.closingStatement: The antenna is the only part of the radio system you can truly 'field-expedientize.' Use the math and the environment to your advantage to ensure the Commander's intent is heard.

title: Executing Jam Resistance and COMSEC Procedures

introduction.gainAttention: Imagine you are in the middle of a CASEVAC request when the net suddenly goes silent or is filled with enemy propaganda. In a contested environment, the enemy is constantly listening and attempting to disrupt our command and control. Your ability to properly execute frequency hopping and COMSEC procedures is the only thing standing between a successful mission and a compromised unit.
introduction.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of Communications Security (COMSEC) and jam resistance, the technical requirements for synchronization, and the hands-on procedures for loading data into tactical radios.
objectives: TLO-103: Execute jam resistance and COMSEC procedures.
ELO-279: Define COMSEC and jam resistance terminology.
ELO-280: Explain the requirement for common timing and frequency data in frequency hopping operations.
ELO-281: Load COMSEC and frequency hopping data into the radio.

mainPoints.title: COMSEC and Jam Resistance Fundamentals
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C, Single Channel Radio (SCR) is the principal means of communication for maneuver units. To protect these links, we utilize two primary methods: COMSEC and Jam Resistance.
subPoints: COMSEC (Communications Security): The protection resulting from all measures designed to deny unauthorized persons information derived from telecommunications.
Jam Resistance: The ability of a communication system to withstand deliberate electronic interference.
Frequency Hopping (FH): A method of transmitting radio signals by rapidly switching a carrier among many frequency channels, using a pseudorandom sequence known to both transmitter and receiver.

mainPoints.title: Synchronization Requirements
mainPoints.content: For frequency hopping to function, all radios in the net must be synchronized. Without precise coordination, the receiver will not know which frequency the transmitter has 'hopped' to.
subPoints: Common Timing: All stations must be within a specific time tolerance (usually +/- 4 seconds for SINCGARS) to ensure they transition frequencies simultaneously.
Frequency Data (WOD/FMT): The Word of the Day (WOD) and Frequency Management Training (FMT) data provide the 'map' for the hopping sequence.
Net Identifiers: Specific codes that allow multiple nets to operate in the same area without interference.

mainPoints.title: Data Loading Procedures
mainPoints.content: Loading data requires the use of a Simple Key Loader (SKL) or similar fill device. This process must be done with strict adherence to technical manuals to prevent zeroizing the equipment.
subPoints: Verify the current COMSEC key version (Effective Edition).
Connect the fill device to the radio's DATA port.
Transfer the Transmission Security (TRANSEC) and COMSEC variables.
Perform a 'Cold Start' or 'Net Opening' procedure to verify synchronization.

practicalApplication.scenario: You are the RTO for a platoon-sized patrol. Before departure, you must configure two AN/PRC-117G radios for a secure, frequency-hopping net using the provided SKL and SOI data.
steps: Power on the radio and perform a Built-In Test (BIT).
Connect the SKL and load the assigned COMSEC keys.
Input the Frequency Hopping (FH) data, including the Net ID and WOD.
Synchronize the radio time with the GPS/Time source.
Conduct a radio check in FH/CT (Cipher Text) mode to confirm link establishment.

conclusion.summary: We have covered the definitions of COMSEC and jam resistance, the critical need for common timing in FH operations, and the technical steps to load a radio.
conclusion.closingStatement: Secure communications are not a luxury; they are a requirement for survival on the modern battlefield. Master these procedures now so you can execute them under pressure.

introduction.gainAttention: When your unit is operating beyond the reach of VHF line-of-sight—hundreds of miles from the nearest friendly base—the only link back to the MAGTF is through the satellites orbiting above. If you cannot establish a SATCOM link, you are isolated.
introduction.overview: This lesson focuses on the characteristics of SCR SATCOM, the technical requirements for antenna siting, and the configuration of the radio for satellite operations.
objectives: TLO-104: Implement SCR Satellite Communications (SATCOM).
ELO-282: Describe the characteristics and limitations of SCR SATCOM.
ELO-283: Determine the optimal site for SATCOM antenna placement.
ELO-284: Configure the radio for SCR SATCOM operations.

mainPoints.title: Characteristics and Limitations of SCR SATCOM
mainPoints.content: SATCOM provides the MAGTF with a mobile and flexible long-range communication capability that is not limited by terrestrial terrain.
subPoints: Range: Virtually unlimited as long as both stations are within the satellite's footprint.
Spectrum Availability: Extremely limited; SATCOM frequencies must be strictly coordinated and assigned by higher headquarters.
Interference: Susceptible to atmospheric conditions and electronic warfare, as well as 'footprint' interference from other users.

mainPoints.title: Antenna Siting and Horizon Angles
mainPoints.content: Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 7, the most critical factor in SATCOM is the physical placement of the antenna to ensure a clear path to the satellite.
subPoints: Line of Sight (LOS): There must be no physical obstructions (trees, buildings, mountains) between the antenna and the satellite.
Horizon Angles: Operators must calculate the elevation and azimuth to the satellite to ensure the signal clears local terrain.
Polarization: SATCOM typically uses circular polarization; ensure the antenna elements are correctly oriented.

mainPoints.title: Radio Configuration for SATCOM
mainPoints.content: Configuring for SATCOM requires specific settings that differ from standard LOS VHF/UHF operations.
subPoints: Select the correct SATCOM mode (DAMA or Dedicated).
Enter the assigned Uplink and Downlink frequencies.
Adjust power settings to ensure the signal reaches the transponder without over-modulating.
Verify the 'Acquisition' of the satellite signal via the radio's signal strength indicator.

practicalApplication.scenario: Your unit is established in a deep-reconnaissance hide site. You are tasked with setting up a SATCOM link to the COC. You have an AN/PRC-117G and an AV-2040 foldable SATCOM antenna.
steps: Identify the satellite's azimuth and elevation using the provided mission data.
Select a site with a clear view of the sky at the required coordinates.
Assemble and orient the SATCOM antenna using a compass.
Configure the radio to the assigned SATCOM channel.
Adjust the antenna position while monitoring the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) until a peak signal is achieved.

conclusion.summary: We have discussed the advantages of SATCOM range, the limitations of spectrum availability, and the technical requirements for antenna siting and radio configuration.
conclusion.closingStatement: The ability to reach back to the MAGTF from anywhere in the world is a powerful tool, but it requires technical precision in siting and configuration. Ensure your line-of-sight is clear and your settings are exact.

tlo.justification: Establishing a SATCOM link requires the Marine to configure equipment and coordinate external variables (spectrum) to achieve a functional communication architecture.
